fields.Name: Saint Peter's Basilica
fields.Alternate: San Pietro in Vaticano (Papal Basilica of Saint Peter in the Vatican)
fields.Description: The most important Roman Catholic shrine and the largest church in the world by interior area, volume, and length, built over the burial site of the apostle Simon Peter; Michelangelo designed its dome, and Gian Lorenzo Bernini added the baldachin and the encircling colonnade.
fields.Architect: Michelangelo (dome); Donato Bramante (original plan); Carlo Maderno (nave and façade); Gian Lorenzo Bernini (baldachin and colonnade)
fields.Caption 2: The dome was brought to completion by Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana
fields.Caption 3: The altar with Bernini's baldacchino

fields.Name: Saint Basil's Cathedral
fields.Alternate: Pokrovsky Cathedral, Cathedral of Vasily the Blessed
fields.Description: Nine chapels rising from one base around a central tower, each under its own brightly patterned onion dome, built to mark Ivan the Terrible's capture of Kazan; legend says Ivan had the architects blinded.
fields.Caption 2: From Vasilyevsky Descent, behind the flower beds
fields.Caption 3: The onion domes

fields.Name: Sagrada Família
fields.Description: Antoni Gaudí's basilica, begun in 1882 and still unfinished, with tree-like columns that branch toward the vault and a skyline of spires; Gaudí worked on it for 43 years and is buried in its crypt, and in 2025 its central Tower of Jesus Christ made it the tallest church in the world (172.5 m when complete).
fields.Caption 2: Columns

fields.Name: Hagia Sophia
fields.Description: Justinian's cathedral and the epitome of Byzantine architecture, built in five years by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus: its huge dome, carried on pendentives, seems to float on a ring of forty windows above the nave. A mosque from 1453, a museum from 1935, and a mosque again since 2020.
fields.Architect: Anthemius of Tralles; Isidore of Miletus
fields.Caption 1: With the minarets added under the Ottomans
fields.Caption 2: The hexapterygon (six-winged angel) on the north-east pendentive (lower right)

fields.Name: Santa Maria del Fiore
fields.Description: Florence's cathedral, whose dome, the largest brick dome ever built, Filippo Brunelleschi raised without centring, using a herringbone brick pattern and a double shell.
fields.Style: Italian Gothic with Renaissance elements, Gothic revival facade
fields.Architect: Filippo Brunelleschi (dome); Arnolfo di Cambio (original design); Emilio De Fabris (façade)
fields.Caption 2: Dome from below
fields.Caption 3: Nanni di Banco, The Madonna of the Girdle, Porta della Mandorla, 1414–21

fields.Name: Pisa Cathedral
fields.Alternate: Duomo di Pisa, Duomo di Santa Maria Assunta
fields.Description: The cathedral beside the Leaning Tower, begun by Buscheto in 1063 with spoils from Pisa's victory over the Saracens at Palermo; its striped marble and tiers of arcades define Pisan Romanesque.
fields.Caption 2: Detail of the façade of the cathedral
fields.Caption 3: Detail of the façade

fields.Name: Basilica di San Marco
fields.Alternate: Saint Mark's Basilica, Chiesa d'Oro (Church of Gold)
fields.Description: Venice's cathedral, built to house the relics of Saint Mark, smuggled out of Alexandria in 828: a Greek cross of five domes modelled on Constantinople's Church of the Holy Apostles, its interior sheathed in gold-ground mosaics. Its four bronze horses were looted from Constantinople in 1204; replicas now stand on the loggia.
fields.Caption 1: The west front on Piazza San Marco
fields.Caption 2: Mosaics in one of the domes

fields.Name: Córdoba Cathedral-Mosque
fields.Alternate: Mezquita-Catedral de Córdoba, Catedral de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción
fields.Description: The Umayyad mosque begun by Abd al-Rahman I in 785 on the site of a Visigothic church, where a forest of more than 800 columns carries double tiers of red-and-white striped horseshoe arches; made a church in 1236, it had a Renaissance cathedral built into its centre in the 16th century, which Charles V is said to have regretted.
fields.Caption 1: Aerial view with the Court of the Oranges
fields.Caption 2: The mihrab
fields.Caption 3: A chapel inside the former prayer hall

fields.Name: Notre Dame de Paris
fields.Description: The Catholic cathedral on the Île de la Cité, among the first buildings to use flying buttresses; the 2019 fire destroyed Eugène Viollet-le-Duc's 19th-century spire and the medieval oak roof frame, both rebuilt for its reopening in December 2024.
fields.Architect: Jean de Chelles (north transept front); Pierre de Montreuil (south transept front)
fields.Caption 1: The south side, with the spire and flying buttresses
fields.Caption 2: West façade
fields.Caption 3: The west rose window

fields.Name: Basilique du Sacré-Cœur
fields.Alternate: Basilica of the Sacred Heart of Paris
fields.Description: A Roman Catholic basilica on the hill of Montmartre, the highest point in Paris, built as a national act of penance after the defeat of 1870 and the Commune; its Romano-Byzantine domes are of a travertine that whitens as it weathers.
fields.Caption 2: Under construction in 1897

fields.Name: Saint Paul's Cathedral
fields.Alternate: Cathedral Church of St. Paul the Apostle
fields.Description: Christopher Wren's Anglican cathedral, the tallest building in London for over 250 years; its dome is three shells: an inner dome, a hidden brick cone carrying the lantern, and an outer timber dome.
fields.Caption 1: An aerial view of St Paul's Cathedral
fields.Caption 2: The choir and crossing beneath the dome

fields.Name: Kölner Dom
fields.Alternate: Cologne Cathedral, High Cathedral of Saint Peter
fields.Description: A Catholic cathedral, the most visited landmark in Germany, whose twin spires (157 m) made it the tallest building in the world from its completion in 1880 until the Washington Monument in 1884; its blackened stone is sandstone darkened by pollution.
fields.Caption 2: Never without steel net: the stones on the cathedral require constant renewal
fields.Caption 3: The cathedral beside the Hohenzollern Bridge at night

fields.Name: Milan Cathedral
fields.Description: One of the largest churches in the world, which took nearly six centuries to finish; Napoleon had its façade completed for his coronation as King of Italy in 1805.
fields.Caption 2: Roof structures
fields.Caption 3: Nave of the cathedral

fields.Name: Basilica of Our Lady of Aparecida
fields.Description: Brazil's national Marian shrine and the second-largest church in the world by interior area, after Saint Peter's, built to house the small clay statue of the Virgin that fishermen found in the Paraíba River in 1717; about 12 million pilgrims come each year.
fields.Caption 2: Cathedral ceiling
fields.Caption 3: The nave

fields.Name: Seville Cathedral
fields.Alternate: Catedral de Santa María de la Sede (Cathedral of Saint Mary of the See)
fields.Description: The largest Gothic cathedral in the world, built on the site of the city's Almohad great mosque, whose minaret survives as the Giralda bell tower; the tomb of Christopher Columbus is carried by four figures representing the kingdoms of Spain.
fields.Caption 2: La Giralda

fields.Name: Saint John the Divine Cathedral
fields.Description: An unfinished Gothic Revival cathedral nicknamed “St. John the Unfinished”: begun in 1892 in a Romanesque-Byzantine design, switched to Gothic by Ralph Adams Cram in 1911, and still without its towers.
fields.Architect: Ralph Adams Cram (Gothic redesign); Heins & LaFarge (original design)
fields.Caption 2: Looking up the Gothic façade

fields.Name: Our Lady of Licheń
fields.Description: One of the largest churches in the world and an important Polish pilgrimage site, commemorating the legend of a Polish soldier, wounded fighting under Napoleon, who had a vision of the Virgin Mary as Our Lady of Sorrows.
fields.Caption 1: The basilica and its bell tower at dusk
fields.Caption 2: The bell tower

fields.Name: Liverpool Cathedral
fields.Alternate: Cathedral Church of Christ in Liverpool, Liverpool Anglican Cathedral
fields.Description: A red-sandstone Gothic Revival Anglican cathedral, the largest cathedral in Britain and the longest in the world; Giles Gilbert Scott, later the designer of the red telephone box, won the competition for it at 22.
fields.Caption 2: Bell chamber within the tower

fields.Name: Our Lady of Peace Basilica
fields.Description: The largest church in the world by exterior area, modelled on Saint Peter's, built for President Félix Houphouët-Boigny in his home town, now the capital, and consecrated by John Paul II in 1990.
fields.Caption 2: The interior beneath the dome

fields.Name: Saint Isaac's Cathedral
fields.Description: A former Russian Orthodox cathedral whose gilded dome took over 100 kg of gold; made a museum of atheism in the Soviet era, it has remained a museum since.
fields.Caption 2: St. Isaac's Cathedral interior
fields.Caption 3: Design model of the cathedral, 1818–1821, designed by Montferrand, wood, plaster, metal, oil paint, gilding

fields.Name: Speyer Cathedral
fields.Description: The largest Romanesque church, founded by Conrad II about 1030 and the largest church in the world when finished; its crypt holds the tombs of eight German emperors and kings from 1039 to 1308.
fields.Caption 2: The east end and towers
fields.Caption 3: Double chapel of Saint Emmeram and Saint Catherine, upper level with opening to the bottom

fields.Name: Basílica da Santíssima Trindade
fields.Alternate: Basilica of the Most Holy Trinity
fields.Description: A modern basilica at the Fátima shrine, consecrated in 2007, ninety years after the apparitions; seating about 8,600, it is one of the largest Catholic churches in the world by capacity.
fields.Caption 2: The sanctuary esplanade seen from the basilica
fields.Caption 3: Reliefs on an interior wall

fields.Name: Ulmer Münster
fields.Description: A Lutheran minster begun in 1377 but finished only in 1890, when its spire was completed to the medieval plans; at 161.5 m it made the minster the tallest church in the world until the Sagrada Família passed it.
fields.Caption 1: Aerial view over the old town
fields.Caption 2: An undetonated WWII bomb deformed the steel construction over the choir

fields.Name: Lincoln Cathedral
fields.Alternate: Cathedral Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Lincoln
fields.Description: A medieval cathedral whose central spire made it taller than the Great Pyramid, and reportedly the tallest building in the world, from 1311 until the spire fell in 1548; the Lincoln Imp, carved in the Angel Choir, is the city's emblem.
fields.Caption 2: Romanesque frieze on the west front
fields.Caption 3: The central portal of the west front

fields.Name: Saint Olaf's Church
fields.Description: A church whose spire, 124 m (407 ft) high, reputedly made it the tallest building in the world from 1549 to 1625; it is named for Saint Olaf, King Olaf II of Norway.
fields.Caption 2: The spire behind a tower of the town wall

fields.Name: Beauvais Cathedral
fields.Description: The cathedral with the tallest Gothic choir vault ever built, about 48 m high; the vault collapsed in 1284 and the crossing tower in 1573, and the nave was never built. Called the “Parthenon of French Gothic.”
fields.Caption 2: The interior, looking towards the choir

fields.Name: St.-Marien-Kirche
fields.Description: A Brick Gothic Lutheran church partly modelled on the Marienkirche in Lübeck, whose steeple, reportedly 151 m, may have made it the tallest building in the world from 1625 to 1647; after a lightning fire it was capped with a Baroque dome, leaving it 104 m high.
fields.Caption 1: The church and its west tower
fields.Caption 2: The church above the square
fields.Caption 3: Looking up into the westwork's net and star vaults

fields.Name: Rouen Cathedral
fields.Alternate: Cathédrale primatiale Notre-Dame de l'Assomption de Rouen
fields.Description: A cathedral whose west façade Claude Monet painted more than thirty times in changing light; its cast-iron spire, built after lightning destroyed the old one in 1822, made it the world's tallest building from 1876 to 1880.
fields.Caption 1: The towers and spire above the city
fields.Caption 2: Carved detail of the organ case
fields.Caption 3: Carved altar in a side chapel

fields.Name: Strasbourg Cathedral
fields.Description: A cathedral of pink Vosges sandstone with only one completed tower, the tallest building in the world from 1647 to 1874 and famed for its astronomical clock; Johann Wolfgang von Goethe praised its façade in “On German Architecture.”
fields.Caption 2: Statues and tracery on the façade
fields.Caption 3: The west front

fields.Name: Peter and Paul Cathedral
fields.Description: The cathedral inside the Peter and Paul Fortress, burial place of nearly every Russian emperor from Peter the Great to Nicholas II, whose gilded needle spire, 122.5 m high and topped by an angel, makes it the world's tallest Orthodox bell tower.
fields.Caption 1: The cathedral and its bell tower
fields.Caption 2: The gilded spire
fields.Caption 3: Stained-glass window of Christ

fields.Name: Salisbury Cathedral
fields.Alternate: Cathedral Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary
fields.Description: The leading example of Early English Gothic, with the tallest church spire in the UK (123 m / 404 ft); it keeps one of the oldest working clocks in the world and the best surviving of the four original copies of Magna Carta.
fields.Architect: Elias of Dereham; Richard of Farleigh (tower and spire)
fields.Caption 2: The nave, with William Pye's decorative font visible in the foreground
fields.Caption 3: Spire and west façade

fields.Name: Metéora monasteries
fields.Description: Eastern Orthodox monasteries built on natural sandstone pillars in central Greece; of the two dozen at their peak, six still function.
fields.Caption 1: A monastery beneath the sandstone pillars
fields.Caption 2: A monastery on its rock pillar

fields.Name: Le Mont-Saint-Michel
fields.Description: A tidal island off Normandy crowned by the abbey church above a walled village; it held out against the English throughout the Hundred Years' War, served as a prison after the Revolution, and since 2014 has been reached by a bridge instead of the old causeway.
fields.Caption 2: Two bombards abandoned by English forces and currently on display

fields.Name: Rock-hewn churches of Lalibela
fields.Description: Eleven churches carved down into the rock under King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty as a “New Jerusalem,” all still active Ethiopian Orthodox churches; the cross-shaped Church of Saint George (Bete Giyorgis) is the best known.
fields.Caption 2: Biete Medhani Alem
fields.Caption 3: Biete Amanuel

fields.Name: Rock-hewn churches of Ivanovo
fields.Description: A group of churches, chapels, and monastic cells hewn out of solid rock, noted for their well-preserved medieval frescoes.
fields.Caption 1: The path to one of the church entrances
fields.Caption 2: The rocks near the church complex
fields.Caption 3: Fresco of Tsar Ivan Alexander as the church's donor

fields.Name: Rila Monastery
fields.Description: Bulgaria's most famous Eastern Orthodox monastery, founded in the 10th century by the hermit Saint John of Rila; it kept Bulgarian culture alive under Ottoman rule, and its striped arcaded courtyard and painted church were rebuilt in the 19th century.
fields.Caption 2: Portico

fields.Name: Churches of Peace
fields.Description: Two timber-framed Lutheran churches, at Jawor and Świdnica, owed to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which let Silesian Lutherans build churches only of wood, clay, and straw, outside the town walls and within a year; a third, at Głogów, burned in 1758.
fields.Location: Świdnica and Jawor, Lower Silesia, Poland
fields.Caption 1: The Church of Peace in Świdnica
fields.Caption 2: The timber interior and its galleries

fields.Name: Sümela Monastery
fields.Description: A Greek Orthodox monastery in the Pontic Mountains, hanging off a vertical cliff; abandoned in the 1923 population exchange, it keeps a rock church covered in frescoes of the 14th to 18th centuries, and a yearly Dormition liturgy resumed there in 2010.
fields.Date: Founded c. 386; present buildings mainly 19th century
fields.Caption 2: Frescoes inside the rock church
fields.Caption 3: The frescoed rock church in the cave

fields.Name: Paoay Church
fields.Description: A coral-stone and brick church braced by 24 carved buttresses against earthquakes, the “Earthquake Baroque” of the Spanish Philippines; one of the Baroque Churches of the Philippines on the UNESCO list.
fields.Caption 2: Interior
fields.Caption 3: Façade in 2012, prior to restoration

fields.Name: Borgund Stave Church
fields.Description: A Lutheran church built about 1180–1250 of pine staves, one of the oldest wooden buildings in Europe and the best preserved of Norway's 28 surviving stave churches; its tiered roofs carry carved dragon heads.
fields.Caption 2: One of the four dragon heads that adorn the church's gable ridges
fields.Caption 3: Interior, showing arcade, supporting columns, “Saint Andrew's crosses”, and gallery arches above

fields.Name: Khor Virap
fields.Description: An Armenian monastery and pilgrimage site built over the pit where Gregory the Illuminator was held for years before he converted King Tiridates III, making Armenia the first Christian state; Mount Ararat rises behind it.
fields.Caption 1: The monastery above the Ararat plain
fields.Caption 2: Beneath Mount Ararat
fields.Caption 3: A carved doorway

fields.Name: Trinity Church
fields.Description: A small Russian Orthodox church of Siberian cedar and larch, built in Siberia in 2003 and assembled at Russia's Bellingshausen Station on King George Island in 2004; one of the southernmost churches in the world, served by priests year-round.
fields.Location: King George Island, South Shetland Islands, Antarctica
fields.Date: Built 2003 in Siberia, shipped to Antarctica in 2004
fields.Caption 2: The entrance and bell tower

fields.Name: Skellig Michael Monastery
fields.Description: A Gaelic monastery of dry-stone beehive huts (clocháns) near the summit of an Atlantic rock off Ireland, built from about the 6th century; it served as Luke Skywalker's hideaway in the Star Wars films.
fields.Caption 1: A beehive hut (clochán) of the monastery
fields.Caption 2: The stone steps, with Little Skellig beyond
fields.Caption 3: Visitors climbing the monks' stairway

fields.Name: Basilica di San Vitale
fields.Description: An octagonal Byzantine church ringed by an ambulatory, consecrated in 547 and famous for its mosaics of Justinian and Theodora with their courts; it inspired Charlemagne's Palatine Chapel at Aachen.
fields.Caption 2: The mosaic of Justinian and his retinue
fields.Caption 3: Dome interior

fields.Name: Euphrasian Basilica
fields.Description: An early Byzantine basilica famous for its golden 6th-century mosaics; a large marble ciborium modelled on that of San Marco in Venice was built over its altar in 1277.
fields.Caption 2: The entrance, with a mosaic in the lunette
fields.Caption 3: The nave and apse

fields.Name: Saint Sophia Cathedral
fields.Description: A Russian Orthodox cathedral in the Novgorod Kremlin, among the oldest surviving churches in Russia and one of the first Slavic churches to depart from the Byzantine style, its plain walls and narrow windows closer to Romanesque.
fields.Caption 2: Bells displayed inside
fields.Caption 3: The cathedral within the kremlin

fields.Name: Abbaye aux Hommes
fields.Description: A Romanesque abbey that William the Conqueror founded as penance for marrying his cousin Matilda, who founded the nearby Abbaye aux Dames; he is buried there, and its sexpartite rib vaults are an early step toward Gothic.
fields.Caption 2: The choir of the abbey church of Saint-Étienne, with the tomb slab of William the Conqueror

fields.Name: Trierer Dom
fields.Description: The oldest church in Germany, begun under Constantine the Great in the 4th century and rebuilt after each of many destructions in the style of its time; some original Roman brickwork still shows outside.
fields.Caption 2: The cloister
fields.Caption 3: Seen from the cloister garden

fields.Name: Sé Velha
fields.Description: A Romanesque cathedral that looks like a small fortress with high, crenellated walls, the only Portuguese cathedral from the Reconquista to survive relatively intact.
fields.Caption 2: The Porta Especiosa, a Renaissance portal
fields.Caption 3: The apse and lantern tower

fields.Name: Abbaye Sainte-Marie-Madeleine de Vézelay
fields.Description: A pilgrimage abbey church, the outstanding example of Burgundian Romanesque, which claimed the relics of Mary Magdalene; its tympanum shows Christ sending the Apostles out to the peoples of the world, and Bernard of Clairvaux preached the Second Crusade here in 1146.
fields.Caption 2: Reliquary of Mary Magdalene in the crypt
fields.Caption 3: Tympanum of the central portal in the narthex

fields.Name: Worms Cathedral
fields.Description: A Romanesque church, one of the three Imperial Cathedrals of the Holy Roman Empire on the Rhine, in the city that gave its name to the Concordat of Worms (1122) and the Diet of Worms (1521).
fields.Caption 2: Bottom left Peter and Paul, bottom right Mary, upper right Brother Conrad
fields.Caption 3: Romanesque tympanon of St Nicholas

fields.Name: Basilica di San Nicola
fields.Description: A Romanesque pilgrimage church for Catholics and Orthodox Christians alike, built to house the relics of Saint Nicholas, stolen from Myra by sailors from Bari in 1087.
fields.Caption 2: The façade seen through a grille
fields.Caption 3: A carved Romanesque capital

fields.Name: Notre Dame de Reims
fields.Description: The coronation church of the French kings, whose west portal carries the Smiling Angel; heavily shelled in the First World War and later restored.
fields.Caption 2: High altar
fields.Caption 3: Detail of the west front

fields.Name: Chartres Cathedral
fields.Description: The best-preserved High Gothic cathedral, rebuilt in about thirty years after a fire of 1194; it keeps most of its 12th- and 13th-century stained glass, the Royal Portal of its earlier west front, and a labyrinth in the nave floor.
fields.Caption 2: The north rose window
fields.Caption 3: The Royal Portal of the west front, in a 19th-century photograph

fields.Name: Basilica of Saint Denis
fields.Description: The abbey church north of Paris whose choir, rebuilt by Abbot Suger in 1140–1144 with rib vaults, pointed arches, and wide stained-glass windows, is counted the first Gothic building; the burial place of nearly all the kings of France.
fields.Caption 2: The west front

fields.Name: York Minster
fields.Alternate: Cathedral and Metropolitical Church of St Peter
fields.Description: One of the largest Gothic cathedrals in northern Europe, stepping through Early English, Decorated, and Perpendicular Gothic; its Great East Window (1405–1408) is the largest expanse of medieval stained glass in England.
fields.Caption 1: Flying buttresses and the central tower
fields.Caption 2: The south transept and its rose window
fields.Caption 3: Chapter House ceiling and stained glass

fields.Name: Catedral de Santa María de Burgos
fields.Description: A vast cathedral begun in 1221 on French Gothic models, to which Juan de Colonia added openwork Flamboyant spires; it holds the tomb of El Cid.
fields.Caption 1: The cathedral above the old town
fields.Caption 2: The Golden Staircase
fields.Caption 3: El Cid's coffer hanging in a chapel

fields.Name: Roskilde Cathedral
fields.Description: Scandinavia's first Gothic cathedral built of brick and the burial church of Danish monarchs since the 15th century, with about forty royal tombs.
fields.Date: c. 1170–1280; side chapels added up to the 19th century
fields.Caption 2: The east end
fields.Caption 3: The cathedral seen from the Bispegården (Bishop's house)

fields.Name: Stephansdom
fields.Description: Vienna's Catholic cathedral, nicknamed “Steffl,” Romanesque and Gothic, its roof patterned with some 230,000 glazed tiles.
fields.Caption 1: The cathedral and its south tower
fields.Caption 2: Ducal Crypt
fields.Caption 3: The nave

fields.Name: Mosteiro da Batalha
fields.Alternate: Batalha Monastery, Mosteiro de Santa Maria da Vitória (Monastery of Saint Mary of the Victory)
fields.Description: A Dominican monastery, the finest Flamboyant Gothic building in Portugal, built to thank the Virgin for the victory over Castile at Aljubarrota (1385); its roofless Unfinished Chapels are a showpiece of the Manueline style.
fields.Architect: Afonso Domingues; Master Huguet (Founder's Chapel and royal cloister); Mateus Fernandes (Unfinished Chapels)
fields.Caption 2: Main nave

fields.Name: La Sainte-Chapelle
fields.Description: A royal chapel in the Palais de la Cité, the residence of the French kings, commissioned by Louis IX to house his Passion relics, among them the Crown of Thorns; its upper chapel, walled almost entirely in stained glass, is a model of 13th-century High Gothic.
fields.Location: Palais de la Cité, Paris, France
fields.Caption 2: Painted columns of the lower chapel
fields.Caption 3: Arcade and windows of the upper chapel

fields.Name: Tempietto
fields.Description: Donato Bramante's small circular martyrium in the courtyard of San Pietro in Montorio, on the traditional site of Saint Peter's crucifixion; ringed by Doric columns, it is the first building of the High Renaissance and the model for centrally planned churches.
fields.Caption 2: The rear, with the ring of Doric columns and the balustrade

fields.Name: Santa Maria Novella
fields.Description: Florence's great Dominican church: a Gothic nave behind a marble façade that Leon Battista Alberti completed in 1470 by setting a classical temple front, joined by scrolled volutes, on the Gothic lower storey; inside is Masaccio's Holy Trinity.
fields.Architect: Leon Battista Alberti (upper façade); Fra Sisto; Fra Ristoro da Campi
fields.Caption 2: The Gothic brick flank of the church

fields.Name: El Escorial
fields.Description: Philip II's vast complex outside Madrid, at once monastery, royal palace, museum, and school.
fields.Location: San Lorenzo de El Escorial, Community of Madrid, Spain
fields.Caption 1: The monastery-palace from the hills above
fields.Caption 2: High altar of the Basilica
fields.Caption 3: Portion of the formal gardens (Gardens of the Friars) adjacent to north façade of the monastery

fields.Name: Catedral Nueva de la Asunción de la Virgen
fields.Description: A Late Gothic and Baroque cathedral built beside the Romanesque Old Cathedral, which it was meant to replace; a carved astronaut on its north portal was added in a 1992 restoration.
fields.Caption 1: The Old and New Cathedrals from above
fields.Caption 2: The tower and dome
fields.Caption 3: A Plateresque doorway

fields.Name: Katedrala sv. Jakova
fields.Description: The most important Renaissance building in Dalmatia, built entirely of stone without mortar, with innovative stone vaults and dome and a frieze of 71 carved heads.
fields.Caption 2: The cathedral and its dome

fields.Name: Cappella Sistina
fields.Description: The papal chapel in the Vatican, built for Sixtus IV and named after him, where the conclave meets to elect the pope. Behind a plain exterior, its walls were frescoed by Sandro Botticelli, Domenico Ghirlandaio, and others, and Michelangelo painted its ceiling (1508–1512) and the Last Judgment on the altar wall.
fields.Caption 2: Michelangelo, The Creation of Adam, on the ceiling
fields.Caption 3: Botticelli, The Trials of Moses, on the south wall

fields.Name: Saint Hedwig's Basilica
fields.Description: Berlin's first Catholic church after the Reformation, modelled on the Pantheon and built for the city's Catholics on land given by Frederick the Great; the seat of the archbishop of Berlin.
fields.Architect: Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff (original design); Hans Schwippert (postwar reconstruction)
fields.Caption 2: Design drawing of the church
fields.Caption 3: Historic photograph of the church and square

fields.Name: Frauenkirche, Munich
fields.Description: A Late Gothic brick church built in only twenty years (1468–1488), whose twin towers, capped with onion domes in 1525, are the symbol of Munich; a black footprint in the entrance is said to be the Devil's.
fields.Caption 1: The twin towers above the old town
fields.Caption 2: The nave

fields.Name: Frauenkirche, Dresden
fields.Description: A Baroque Lutheran church whose great stone dome dominates Dresden's skyline; destroyed in the 1945 bombing and left as a ruin through the East German years, it was rebuilt in 1994–2005 with original stones where possible, which show dark among the new.

fields.Name: Saint Mary's Church
fields.Description: The archetype of north German Brick Gothic, whose 38.5 m nave vault is the highest brick vault in the world; some seventy Baltic churches copy it, and the bells that fell in the 1942 air raid lie where they landed.
fields.Caption 2: The nave and its painted vaults
fields.Caption 3: The bells that fell in the 1942 air raid, left where they landed

fields.Name: Palazzo Pubblico
fields.Description: The seat of the Republic of Siena's government, whose Torre del Mangia was built to the height of the cathedral, a sign that church and state held equal power; inside, Ambrogio Lorenzetti's Allegory of Good and Bad Government lines the council hall, the Sala dei Nove.

fields.Name: Altes Museum
fields.Description: A Neoclassical museum for the Prussian royal collection, fronted by a colonnade of eighteen Ionic columns and centred on a rotunda modelled on the Pantheon; it opened Berlin's Museum Island in 1830.
fields.Caption 2: The eighteen-column Ionic front on the Lustgarten

fields.Name: Pantheon
fields.Alternate: Santa Maria ad Martyres (Saint Mary and the Martyrs)
fields.Description: Hadrian's temple to all the gods, a porticoed rotunda whose coffered dome, 43.3 m across with an open oculus, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome; the portico inscription credits Marcus Agrippa, whose earlier temple Hadrian rebuilt, and its consecration as a church in 609 saved it.
fields.Caption 2: Giovanni Paolo Panini's painting of the interior, c. 1734
fields.Caption 3: Tomb of Victor Emmanuel II

fields.Name: Burj Khalifa
fields.Description: The tallest building and structure in the world since 2009, 829.8 m high; built as Burj Dubai, it was renamed at its 2010 opening for Khalifa bin Zayed, ruler of Abu Dhabi and president of the UAE, who had rescued the project financially.
fields.Caption 2: The tower above the Dubai skyline

fields.Name: Villa Savoye
fields.Description: A white villa on pilotis outside Paris, the fullest statement of Le Corbusier's Five Points of Architecture: pilotis, a roof garden, a free plan, ribbon windows, and a free façade.
fields.Caption 2: The living room opening onto the roof terrace

fields.Name: Flatiron Building
fields.Description: A wedge-shaped skyscraper, named for its shape, filling the triangular block where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue at Madison Square; among the first steel-framed skyscrapers in New York, it is clad in limestone and terracotta.
fields.Caption 2: A typical floor in 1903
fields.Caption 3: From street level

fields.Name: Guggenheim Museum
fields.Description: A spiral rotunda viewed by descending a continuous ramp; Frank Lloyd Wright worked on it for sixteen years and died six months before it opened in 1959, and artists complained that its sloping walls made paintings hard to hang.
fields.Caption 1: The spiralling exterior on Fifth Avenue
fields.Caption 2: The auditorium

fields.Name: Fallingwater
fields.Description: A house built for the Pittsburgh department-store owner Edgar J. Kaufmann, its cantilevered concrete terraces hanging over a waterfall on Bear Run, which is heard rather than seen from inside.
fields.Caption 2: The hatch for the living-room stairs
fields.Caption 3: The living-room cantilever as seen from the bridge leading to the house

fields.Name: Buckingham Palace
fields.Description: The London residence and administrative headquarters of the monarch, a royal home since Queen Victoria's accession in 1837; a German bomb destroyed its chapel in the Second World War.
fields.Architect: John Nash (conversion into a palace); Edward Blore (east wing); Aston Webb (east front)
fields.Caption 1: East Front of the palace seen from the Victoria Memorial
fields.Caption 2: The west front, facing the garden

fields.Name: Space Needle
fields.Description: An observation tower built for the 1962 World's Fair (the Century 21 Exposition), with a revolving restaurant at the top; a 2018 renovation added a rotating glass floor.
fields.Architect: John Graham & Company; Victor Steinbrueck; Edward E. Carlson
fields.Caption 2: Scaffold surrounding top section during 2017–2018 renovation
fields.Caption 3: Looking south-east over downtown

fields.Name: Sydney Opera House
fields.Description: A performing-arts centre on Bennelong Point whose roof is a cluster of white shell vaults, all cut from the surface of a single sphere and clad in over a million tiles; Jørn Utzon is said to have hit on the idea while peeling an orange.
fields.Caption 2: The opening ceremony, 1973
fields.Caption 3: The steps of the Opera House

fields.Name: Casa Batlló
fields.Description: A house remodelled for the textile industrialist Josep Batlló with an organic, skeletal façade of bone-like columns and almost no straight lines, clad in a colourful mosaic of broken ceramic tiles; its scaled, humped roof is read as the back of the dragon slain by Saint George.
fields.Caption 2: Atrium (light well)

fields.Name: Eiffel Tower
fields.Description: Built as the entrance to the 1889 World's Fair, the tallest man-made structure in the world from 1889 to 1930 at 324 metres (1,063 ft), and now the cultural icon of France.
fields.Caption 2: At night, beyond the Trocadéro fountains
fields.Caption 3: The 1889 World's Fair

fields.Name: Great Pyramid of Giza
fields.Alternate: Pyramid of Khufu, Pyramid of Cheops
fields.Description: The tomb of Khufu, built of limestone and granite about 2560 BCE, the largest of the Giza pyramids and the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, the only one still standing; at 146.6 m it was the tallest man-made structure until Lincoln Cathedral's spire in 1311.
fields.Caption 2: Nineteenth-century painting of visitors on the summit
fields.Caption 3: The stepped limestone core

fields.Name: Taj Mahal
fields.Description: An Islamic mausoleum of white Makrana marble, built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his favourite wife, Mumtaz Mahal; he is buried beside her.
fields.Caption 2: The mosque beside the mausoleum

fields.Name: Dome of the Rock
fields.Description: The oldest surviving major Islamic monument, built under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik over the Foundation Stone, sacred to Jews, Christians, and Muslims: an octagon ringed by an ambulatory under a gilded wooden dome, its outside faced in tiles added under Suleiman the Magnificent.
fields.Location: Temple Mount (Haram al-Sharif), Old City of Jerusalem
fields.Architect: Raja ibn Haywa; Yazid ibn Salam (attributed)
fields.Caption 2: Interior

fields.Name: Casa Milà
fields.Description: An apartment block built for Pere Milà and Roser Segimon, mocked when new for its undulating stone façade, with no straight line in it, and its twisted iron balconies; nicknamed La Pedrera (“the quarry”), it has a roof of chimneys and ventilation shafts sculpted into hooded figures.
fields.Caption 2: The painted entrance hall
fields.Caption 3: Roof chimneys known as espantabruixes (witch scarers)

fields.Name: One World Trade Center
fields.Description: The main tower of the rebuilt World Trade Center and the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere, its height of 1,776 ft (541.3 m) recalling the year of the Declaration of Independence; from the street it appears to taper to a point.
fields.Caption 2: From the September 11 memorial

fields.Name: Petronas Towers
fields.Description: Twin 88-storey towers joined by a skybridge, the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004; their plan, an eight-pointed star based on the Islamic Rub el Hizb, and their façade motifs come from Islamic art.
fields.Caption 2: The towers above the Suria KLCC mall

fields.Name: Empire State Building
fields.Description: An American icon, 443.2 m (1,454 ft) to its tip, and the world's tallest building from 1931 to 1970; after the World Trade Center fell in 2001 it was again New York's tallest until One World Trade Center passed it in 2012.
fields.Caption 2: One World Trade Center, in the distance, overtook the Empire State Building's height on 30 April 2012
fields.Caption 3: Lit in rainbow colours for Pride, 2015

fields.Name: Chrysler Building
fields.Description: Built as the headquarters of the Chrysler Corporation, the tallest building in the world from 1930 to 1931; its stainless-steel crown of sunburst arches ends in a spire, assembled secretly inside and hoisted in 1929 to beat 40 Wall Street, and its corner eagles copy Chrysler hood ornaments.
fields.Caption 2: Lobby
fields.Caption 3: Looking up the tower

fields.Name: Gothic
fields.Description: The medieval style of pointed arches, rib vaults, and flying buttresses, which let churches rise higher and turn their walls into stained glass; it began in Abbot Suger's choir at Saint-Denis around 1140.
fields.Notes: Rib vaults and flying buttresses made great height and huge windows possible, and tracery divides the windows. Preceded by Romanesque and followed by the Renaissance; revived as Gothic Revival in the 18th and 19th centuries.
fields.Caption 1: The West Front of Wells Cathedral
fields.Caption 2: The Old New Synagogue
fields.Caption 3: Early Gothic interior at Alcobaça, looking east

fields.Name: Romanesque
fields.Description: Architectural style of medieval Europe characterized by semi-circular arches.
fields.Notes: Thick walls, small windows, and round arches give a fortress-like look; it combines Roman and Byzantine features and in England is called Norman. Succeeded by Gothic.
fields.Caption 2: Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio
fields.Caption 3: A carved capital with vines and fruit

fields.Name: Renaissance
fields.Description: European style of the 15th and 16th centuries emphasizing symmetry, proportion, geometry, and the regularity of its parts.
fields.Notes: Symmetrical façades, round arches, and hemispherical domes revive Greek and Roman forms; it followed Gothic and was succeeded by Baroque.
fields.Caption 2: Brunelleschi's Ospedale degli Innocenti (begun 1419), Florence
fields.Caption 3: Palladio's Villa La Rotonda, Vicenza

fields.Name: Neuschwanstein Castle
fields.Description: A Romanesque Revival palace built for Ludwig II of Bavaria as a homage to Richard Wagner, whose operas its murals illustrate; Ludwig lived there only 172 days, and it inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle.
fields.Caption 2: The castle in its mountain setting
fields.Caption 3: An eastward view over the Alpsee towards the Alps

fields.Name: Byzantine
fields.Description: Architectural style of the Eastern Roman Empire: a large dome over a square central space, round arches, and gold-ground mosaics.
fields.Notes: From the founding of Constantinople in 330 to its fall in 1453: the dome on pendentives over a square, gold-ground mosaics, and brick-and-stone walls, epitomized by Hagia Sophia.
fields.Caption 2: An opus sectile marble floor before a church doorway

fields.Name: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
fields.Description: A titanium-clad museum on the Nervión, whose curves Frank Gehry designed with CATIA, aerospace software, and whose success gave its name to the “Bilbao effect”; Jeff Koons's flower-covered Puppy guards the entrance.
fields.Caption 2: The museum at night on the Nervión

fields.Name: Forbidden City
fields.Description: The vast palace complex at the centre of Beijing, home of 24 Ming and Qing emperors from 1420 to 1912; its buildings follow strict symmetry along a north–south axis, and yellow roof tiles were reserved for the emperor.
fields.Caption 2: Tiananmen Gate

fields.Name: Great Wall of China
fields.Description: Not one wall but many, built by different dynasties from the 7th century BCE along China's northern borders against raiding nomads; the brick-and-stone sections most visitors see are Ming, and that it is visible from the Moon is a myth.
fields.Caption 1: The wall along the mountain ridges
fields.Caption 2: Visitors climbing a restored section

fields.Name: Temple of Heaven
fields.Description: A complex built under the Yongle Emperor where Ming and Qing emperors prayed for good harvests; its round, triple-roofed Hall of Prayer stands in a square precinct: heaven round, earth square.
fields.Caption 1: The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests
fields.Caption 2: The hall's upper roofs

fields.Name: Giant Wild Goose Pagoda
fields.Description: A seven-storey Tang Buddhist pagoda built in 652 to hold the scriptures the monk Xuanzang brought back from India and translated there; it leans slightly to the west.
fields.Caption 2: Avalokiteshvara Hall

fields.Name: Potala Palace
fields.Description: The fortress-palace of the Dalai Lamas and their winter home for over 300 years, thirteen storeys and 117 m (384 ft) high on the side of Marpo Ri (“Red Hill”) at 3,700 m (12,100 ft), with over 1,000 rooms, 10,000 shrines, and 200,000 statues.
fields.Caption 2: The White and Red Palaces
fields.Caption 3: Historic photograph of the palace

fields.Name: Shanghai Tower
fields.Description: The tallest building in Shanghai and the third-tallest in the world: nine cylindrical sections stacked inside a double transparent skin whose outer layer twists as it rises.
fields.Caption 2: View north from 118F observation deck

fields.Name: Oriental Pearl Tower
fields.Description: Shanghai's TV tower, eleven spheres of different sizes linked by enormous columns, with a revolving restaurant at 267 m (876 ft); the tallest structure in China from 1994 to 2007.
fields.Architect: East China Architectural Design & Research Institute
fields.Caption 1: Lujiazui Roundabout and Oriental Pearl Tower in the background
fields.Caption 2: The bottom-most sphere and its foundations

fields.Name: Skytree
fields.Description: A broadcasting and observation tower, at 634 m the tallest tower in the world, built to rise above the radio interference of Tokyo's many skyscrapers; its form recalls a five-storey pagoda.
fields.Caption 1: At night, reflected in a canal
fields.Caption 2: Worm's-eye view of the tower
fields.Caption 3: Seen from a side street

fields.Name: Horyuji Temple
fields.Description: A Buddhist temple whose main hall is the world's oldest wooden building, with a five-storey pagoda and Buddhist art of the 6th and 7th centuries.
fields.Style: Japanese architecture; Chinese and Korean influences
fields.Caption 1: The Golden Hall and five-storey pagoda
fields.Caption 2: The temple approach and the pagoda
fields.Caption 3: A scroll in the temple's treasure hall

fields.Name: Himeji Castle
fields.Description: The finest surviving example of Japanese castle architecture, called the White Egret Castle for its brilliant white walls and supposed resemblance to a bird taking flight.
fields.Caption 1: After the five-year restoration of the roof and walls
fields.Caption 2: From inside the fortifications
fields.Caption 3: The castle keep and stone ramparts

fields.Name: Sanjusangen-do
fields.Description: A Tendai Buddhist temple whose hall, about 120 m long, holds a large seated thousand-armed Kannon flanked by 1,000 standing ones; archers once competed to shoot arrows the length of its veranda.
fields.Caption 2: Statue of Basū Sennin, one of the guardian deities
fields.Caption 3: The central Thousand-armed Kannon

fields.Name: El Castillo in Chichen Itza
fields.Description: The Maya step pyramid at the centre of Chichen Itza, whose 365 steps encode the solar year; at the equinoxes a serpent of shadow descends its balustrade.
fields.Caption 2: The restored stairway
fields.Caption 3: Aerial view of Chichén Itzá

fields.Name: Angkor Wat
fields.Description: A Khmer temple complex and, at 162.6 hectares (402 acres), the largest religious monument in the world; built as a Hindu temple to Vishnu, it was gradually turned into a Buddhist one.
fields.Caption 1: The front of the main complex
fields.Caption 2: The Churning of the Sea of Milk, in the bas-relief gallery
fields.Caption 3: The central towers, standing for the five peaks of Mount Meru

fields.Name: Colosseum
fields.Description: An elliptical amphitheatre, the icon of Imperial Rome, seating 50,000 to 80,000 for gladiator contests, animal hunts, mock battles, and dramas; its exterior rises in four levels, the lower three of 80 arches each.
fields.Caption 2: Seen past cypresses
fields.Caption 3: The outer arcades

fields.Name: Faisal Mosque
fields.Description: Pakistan's national mosque, a modern domeless design whose eight-sided main hall was inspired by a Bedouin tent; its prayer hall holds about 10,000, and with its courtyards and grounds it is said to hold up to 300,000.
fields.Caption 2: The mosque against the Margalla Hills
fields.Caption 3: The mosque and its four minarets at dusk

fields.Name: Alhambra
fields.Description: The Nasrid palace-fortress on a hill above Granada, the last seat of Muslim rule in Spain until the city fell in 1492, famed for the stucco, tile, and muqarnas of its courts, among them the Court of the Lions and the Hall of the Abencerrajes; Charles V later built a Renaissance palace inside it.
fields.Caption 2: The Court of the Lions, in an early photograph

fields.Name: Citadel of Aleppo
fields.Description: A hilltop fortress used since the 3rd millennium BCE and one of the oldest and largest castles in the world; most of what stands is Ayyubid, entered by a bridge over the moat to a fortified gate. Damaged in the Syrian civil war and under repair.
fields.Caption 2: Aleppo citadel Museum
fields.Caption 3: The roof of the baths

fields.Name: Borobudur
fields.Description: The world's largest Buddhist temple, a Mahayana monument built under the Sailendra dynasty: nine stacked platforms topped by a central stupa and ringed by 72 Buddhas in perforated stupas, forming a mandala seen from above.
fields.Style: Javanese Buddhist architecture; influences of Indian Gupta art
fields.Caption 2: Relief carving on one of the galleries

fields.Name: Lakshmana Temple
fields.Alternate: Laxmana Temple, Chaturbhuja Temple of Khajuraho, Ramachandra Temple of Khajuraho
fields.Description: A Hindu temple to Vaikuntha Vishnu with every element of the Nagara temple: entrance porch (ardha-mandapa), pillared halls (mandapa and maha-mandapa), antechamber (antarala), and the sanctum (garbhagriha) holding the main image.
fields.Caption 2: Sculpture on the temple walls

fields.Name: Lotus Temple
fields.Description: A Baháʼí House of Worship, open to people of all religions and one of the most visited buildings in the world: on a nine-sided circular plan, 27 freestanding marble-clad “petals” form a giant lotus flower.
fields.Caption 2: The Lotus Temple's petal-shaped shells

fields.Name: Ajanta Caves
fields.Description: About thirty Buddhist caves cut into rock in two phases, from the 2nd century BCE and the 5th century CE, whose murals of the Jataka tales are the finest surviving ancient Indian painting.
fields.Date: First phase: 2nd century BCE; second phase: 400–650 CE
fields.Caption 2: Monks at a rock-cut cave entrance

fields.Name: Chand Baori
fields.Description: A monumental rectangular stepwell descending 13 storeys into the ground, beside a large Hindu shrine; built to store rainwater in an arid region, its cool depths made it a gathering place in hot weather.
fields.Caption 2: The colonnade of arches around the stepwell

fields.Name: Khajuraho Monuments
fields.Description: A group of Hindu and Jain temples built under the Chandela dynasty, famous for erotic sculpture, though only about a tenth of it is erotic and most shows daily life; about 25 of perhaps 85 temples survive.
fields.Style: Nagara style of Hindu temple architecture
fields.Caption 1: A temple and its clustered spires
fields.Caption 2: Temples of the Western Group on their platforms
fields.Caption 3: The spires rising to the main shikhara

fields.Name: Golden Temple
fields.Description: The holiest gurdwara of Sikhism, built by Guru Arjan in the Amrit Sarovar pool with four doors, open to all; Ranjit Singh covered it in gold in the 1830s, and Operation Blue Star damaged it in 1984.
fields.Date: First Sikh shrine on the site: 1589; current structure built between 1809–1830
fields.Caption 2: Atta Mandi Deori, one of the gates

fields.Name: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi
fields.Description: The mosque Muhammad built beside his house in 622, the second-holiest site in Islam; its Green Dome covers his tomb and those of Abu Bakr and Umar, and giant retractable umbrellas shade the piazza.
fields.Location: Medina, Al Madinah Province, Saudi Arabia
fields.Caption 2: Interior of the Saudi expansion
fields.Caption 3: The courtyard, with a retractable umbrella canopy

fields.Name: Great Mosque of Mecca
fields.Description: The mosque surrounding the Kaaba, which Muslims face in prayer: the holiest mosque in Islam and the goal of the Hajj, overlooked by the Abraj Al Bait clock tower.
fields.Date: 7th century, continuously altered and expanded until today
fields.Caption 1: Aerial view of the mosque around the Kaaba
fields.Caption 2: The Hijr Ismail

fields.Name: Harpa Concert Hall
fields.Description: A concert hall and conference centre whose steel frame is clad in geometric panels of coloured glass inspired by Iceland's basalt landscape, a façade designed with Ólafur Elíasson.
fields.Architect: Henning Larsen Architects (with Ólafur Elíasson, façade)
fields.Caption 1: The glass façade above the waterfront
fields.Caption 2: The concert hall on the harbour in winter

fields.Name: Heydar Aliyev Center
fields.Description: A cultural centre of continuous white curving surfaces without a single sharp angle, winner of the Design Museum's Design of the Year in 2014; named after Heydar Aliyev, Communist leader of Soviet Azerbaijan and later president of independent Azerbaijan.
fields.Caption 2: The centre at night

fields.Name: Cathedral of Brasília
fields.Alternate: Catedral Metropolitana Nossa Senhora Aparecida (Metropolitan Cathedral of Our Lady of Aparecida)
fields.Description: The cathedral of Brazil's capital, whose sixteen curved concrete columns form a hyperboloid crown; visitors enter through a dark tunnel into a nave lit by stained glass, under suspended angels.
fields.Caption 1: The ring of hyperboloid concrete columns
fields.Caption 2: Interior with angel sculptures
fields.Caption 3: The stained-glass roof

fields.Name: Milwaukee Art Museum
fields.Description: Santiago Calatrava's Quadracci Pavilion on Lake Michigan, a tall arched glass hall whose Burke Brise Soleil, a pair of steel wings, opens by day and folds down over it at night like a bird's.
fields.Caption 2: The Burke Brise Soleil, its wings open above the Quadracci Pavilion
fields.Caption 3: Inside the Quadracci Pavilion

fields.Name: Dancing House
fields.Description: An office building for the Dutch insurer Nationale-Nederlanden, nicknamed Fred and Ginger after Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers: its glass tower, “Ginger”, leans against a concrete one, “Fred”, like a pair of dancers.
fields.Caption 2: The site in 1945 and 2010
fields.Caption 3: The building on the Vltava embankment

fields.Name: Ryugyong Hotel
fields.Description: An unfinished pyramid-shaped skyscraper about 330 m tall, the tallest structure in North Korea; begun in 1987, it stalled for years and has never opened, and an LED display was added to its façade in 2018.
fields.Caption 2: The top, some time after construction resumed

fields.Name: Great Mosque of Djenné
fields.Description: Often called the largest mud-brick building in the world, its smooth plaster coat bristling with bundles of palm sticks that serve as decoration and permanent scaffolding; because the rains erode it, the town replasters it every year in a festival.
fields.Date: Current structure completed in 1907. First mosque on the site: 13th century.
fields.Caption 2: Ruins of the earlier mosque, before the 1907 rebuilding
fields.Caption 3: The same ruins on a 1904 postcard

fields.Name: The Shard
fields.Description: A glass-clad pyramidal skyscraper of 95 storeys, 309.6 m (1,016 ft) tall, the tallest building in the United Kingdom; Renzo Piano took his cues from the railway lines beside the site, London's spires, and the masts of sailing ships.
fields.Caption 2: The tower lit up at night

fields.Name: Santuario de Las Lajas
fields.Description: A Gothic Revival basilica built on a bridge across the canyon of the Guáitara River, about 100 m above the water, where an image of the Virgin is said to have appeared on the rock face.
fields.Caption 1: The church on its bridge across the Guáitara gorge
fields.Caption 2: The vaulted ceiling
fields.Caption 3: The façade seen from the bridge

fields.Name: Lloyd's building
fields.Description: The home of the insurance market Lloyd's of London, with its staircases, lifts, and service ducts on the outside, leaving an open atrium within; in 2011 it became the youngest building to be given Grade I listing.
fields.Caption 1: Looking up at the exposed services on the tower's exterior
fields.Caption 2: Looking straight ahead, “The Walkie-Talkie” (20 Fenchurch Street) fills the view

fields.Name: Parkroyal Collection Pickering
fields.Description: A “hotel-in-a-garden” in downtown Singapore with 15,000 m² of sky gardens, green walls, and water features, which keeps its energy use low with solar cells, motion sensors, rainwater harvesting, and reclaimed water.
fields.Caption 2: The tower above its garden terraces
fields.Caption 3: The planted terraces over the street

fields.Name: Paro Taktsang
fields.Description: A monastery clinging to a cliff about 900 m above the Paro valley, built in 1692 around the cave where Padmasambhava, who brought Buddhism to Bhutan, is said to have flown on a tigress in the 8th century, hence its name, the Tiger's Nest.
fields.Date: Built in 1692. Meditation cave established in 8th century.
fields.Caption 2: Prayer wheel
fields.Caption 3: Pine forest in the area

fields.Name: Ranganathaswamy Temple
fields.Description: The largest functioning Hindu temple in the world, dedicated to Ranganatha, a form of Vishnu: it fills the island of Srirangam in the Kaveri River within seven concentric walls, and its 21 gopurams include the Rajagopuram, about 73 m tall, finished only in 1987.
fields.Date: Established in 9th century, rebuilt in 14th century, continuously expanded in 16th–17th centuries.
fields.Caption 2: A carved pillar figure

fields.Name: Santuário Dom Bosco
fields.Description: A church dedicated to John Bosco, whose 1883 dream of a utopian city between the 15th and 20th parallels is taken as a prophecy of Brasília: 80 concrete columns form pointed arches filled with twelve shades of blue Murano glass, so that the interior feels like a night sky.
fields.Caption 2: A carved door panel

fields.Name: Bublik Apartments
fields.Description: A ring-shaped Soviet apartment block of prefabricated panels, about 155 m across, with 913 flats in Moscow's Ramenki district; legend says five such rings were planned to form the Olympic rings for the 1980 Games, but only two were built.
fields.Caption 2: The curving façade from the street

fields.Name: Shah-i-Zinda
fields.Description: A necropolis of tiled mausoleums along a single avenue, said to hold the grave of Kusam ibn Abbas, a cousin of Muhammad; many mausoleums for the Timurid dynasty were added in the 14th century.
fields.Date: Continuously expanded from 9th–15th centuries. Reconstruction work done during 16th–19th centuries.
fields.Caption 2: The domed mausoleums
fields.Caption 3: Glazed tilework

fields.Name: Parthenon
fields.Description: The temple of Athena on the Acropolis and the most important surviving building of Classical Greece, built under Pericles with sculpture overseen by Phidias, whose gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos stood inside; its columns swell slightly (entasis). A Venetian shell blew it apart in 1687, and Lord Elgin removed much of its sculpture in 1801–1812.
fields.Caption 2: The east façade
fields.Caption 3: Surviving part of the east pediment

fields.Name: Baroque
fields.Description: European architecture style from the 17th and early 18th century. Characterized by luxurious ornamentation, grandeur, and curved and oval shapes that create a sense of motion.
fields.Notes: Oval and curving spaces, domes with painted interiors, trompe-l'oeil ceilings, and grand stairways aim at drama and movement. It followed the Renaissance and gave way to Neoclassicism; Rococo is its lighter, asymmetric late phase.
fields.Caption 1: Interior of the Basilica of Superga
fields.Caption 2: Ceiling of the Church of the Gesù

fields.Name: Templo de San Francisco Acatepec
fields.Description: A colonial church near Cholula whose whole façade and bell tower are faced in Talavera, the glazed pottery of Puebla, set in brick; often paired with nearby Santa María Tonantzintla, whose interior is covered in Indigenous-style stucco.
fields.Caption 2: Detail of the Talavera tilework

fields.Name: Neoclassical
fields.Description: Architectural style from 18th and 19th century Europe. Emphasis on symmetry, simple geometry, and clear lines, inspired by Ancient Greco-Roman Classical architecture.
fields.Notes: A reaction against Baroque and Rococo excess that returned to plain, planar forms; it was spurred by Enlightenment archaeology, especially the excavations at Pompeii and Herculaneum, and became international.
fields.Caption 2: Soufflot's Panthéon (1790)

fields.Name: Hagia Irene
fields.Description: One of the oldest churches in Constantinople, where the First Council of Constantinople met in 381; never made a mosque, it served the Ottomans as an arsenal, and its apse keeps a large mosaic cross from the Iconoclast period.
fields.Caption 2: With Hagia Sophia behind
fields.Caption 3: A huge cross in mosaic in the apse, iconoclastic work

fields.Name: Palace of Fine Arts
fields.Description: A Beaux-Arts rotunda and colonnade built for the 1915 Panama–Pacific Exposition as a crumbling Roman ruin, after Giovanni Battista Piranesi's engravings and Arnold Böcklin's Isle of the Dead; the only exposition building still on its original site, it was rebuilt in concrete in the 1960s.
fields.Caption 2: The rotunda
fields.Caption 3: Colonnade

fields.Name: Hoover Dam
fields.Description: A concrete arch-gravity dam in Black Canyon on the Arizona–Nevada border, built during the Depression and finished two years early, with Art Deco styling by Gordon Kaufmann and the winged Figures of the Republic by Oskar J. W. Hansen; called Boulder Dam from 1933 until Congress restored Hoover's name in 1947.
fields.Location: Black Canyon, Nevada and Arizona, United States
fields.Caption 2: Turbine/generator controls in power plant beneath Hoover Dam
fields.Caption 3: The dam from the air, with its intake towers

fields.Name: Grand Central Terminal
fields.Description: A Beaux-Arts station whose main concourse ceiling carries a painted zodiac, reversed because it was copied from a medieval manuscript's outside-in view; the Supreme Court's 1978 ruling in Penn Central v. New York City, upholding landmark laws, saved it from demolition.
fields.Caption 2: The Main Concourse

fields.Name: Rockefeller Center
fields.Description: A complex of Art Deco towers around a sunken plaza, built through the Depression with murals and reliefs commissioned across it, home of the Christmas tree and the Prometheus statue; Diego Rivera's mural Man at the Crossroads was destroyed there in 1934 because it included Lenin.
fields.Caption 2: Looking up the façade of 1221 Avenue of the Americas
fields.Caption 3: Radio City Music Hall

fields.Name: Leaning Tower of Pisa
fields.Description: The freestanding bell tower of Pisa Cathedral, which began to lean during construction because of soft ground; engineering work from 1993 to 2001 reduced the tilt. Legend says Galileo dropped balls from it to show that falling speed does not depend on weight.
fields.Architect: Bonanno Pisano; Giovanni di Simone; Tommaso di Andrea Pisano
fields.Caption 1: The tower from above, leaning to the south
fields.Caption 2: The tower behind the cathedral on the Piazza dei Miracoli
fields.Caption 3: The blind arcades of its base

fields.Name: Tower Bridge
fields.Description: A combined bascule and suspension bridge with Gothic Revival stone cladding over a steel frame, often confused with London Bridge; its original steam engines survive, and in 1952 a double-decker bus jumped the gap as the bascules began to rise.
fields.Caption 2: The south arch

fields.Name: Big Ben
fields.Description: The clock tower at the north end of the Palace of Westminster, renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012; Big Ben is properly the great bell inside it, which cracked soon after it was hung in 1859.
fields.Caption 1: With the north end of the Palace of Westminster
fields.Caption 2: Scaffolding during the 2017–2022 restoration

fields.Name: Brandenburg Gate
fields.Description: A Neoclassical gate modelled on the Propylaea and topped by the Quadriga, which Napoleon carried off to Paris in 1806; it came back in 1814, when its Victoria was given an Iron Cross. The gate stood in the death strip of the Berlin Wall, and Ronald Reagan gave his “Tear down this wall!” speech in front of it in 1987.
fields.Caption 2: From Pariser Platz

fields.Name: Arc de Triomphe
fields.Description: A triumphal arch begun by Napoleon after Austerlitz, carrying François Rude's relief La Marseillaise, at the centre of the Place Charles de Gaulle, from which twelve avenues radiate; beneath it lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, whose flame is rekindled every evening.
fields.Caption 2: The arch and its sculpture groups
fields.Caption 3: The coffered vault

fields.Name: Christ the Redeemer
fields.Description: A soapstone-clad Art Deco figure on Corcovado, thirty metres tall with a twenty-eight-metre span, designed by the Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa with a face sculpted by Gheorghe Leonida and assembled from parts made in France; named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.
fields.Architect: Paul Landowski (sculptor); Heitor da Silva Costa (engineer); Carlos Oswald (initial design); Albert Caquot (structure)
fields.Caption 2: From below

fields.Name: Sydney Harbour Bridge
fields.Description: A steel through-arch bridge, locally the Coathanger, whose arch spans 503 m and carries road, rail, and footways; it opened a year before work on the Golden Gate began.
fields.Caption 1: Three-span bridge linking Millers Point with Balls Head and Balmain, proposed by Ernest Stowe in 1922
fields.Caption 2: The Hell Gate Bridge, which inspired its design
fields.Caption 3: BridgeClimb participants, wearing the mandatory special jumpsuits

fields.Name: Mount Rushmore
fields.Description: The heads of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln carved into granite in the Black Hills, on land taken from the Lakota; Gutzon Borglum died in 1941 and his son Lincoln finished the work, stopping short of the planned waist-length figures.
fields.Caption 2: The carved mountain above its forested slopes
fields.Caption 3: Gutzon Borglum's plaster model in the sculptor's studio

fields.Name: Little Mermaid
fields.Description: A bronze figure on a rock in the harbour, commissioned by Carl Jacobsen of Carlsberg after he saw a ballet of Hans Christian Andersen's story; its head was modelled on the ballerina Ellen Price and its body on the sculptor's wife, and it has been beheaded twice.
fields.Caption 2: The statue on its rock at Langelinie

fields.Name: Angel of the North
fields.Description: A weathering-steel figure twenty metres tall with a fifty-four-metre wingspan, standing over the A1 on the site of a colliery bath house; its wings tilt 3.5 degrees forward, and it is built to withstand winds of over 160 km/h (100 mph).
fields.Caption 2: The sculpture's outstretched wings, in silhouette

fields.Name: Panama Canal locks
fields.Description: Stepped lock chambers that lift ships twenty-six metres to Gatun Lake, filled by gravity alone; each original chamber is 305 m by 33.5 m, the source of the “Panamax” limit on ship size, and electric locomotives called mules guide ships through.
fields.Architect: George Washington Goethals; John Frank Stevens
fields.Caption 2: A tanker and tugs in the canal

fields.Name: Chunnel
fields.Description: Three bored tunnels fifty kilometres long beneath the Strait of Dover, whose undersea section of about 38 km is the longest of any tunnel in the world.
fields.Caption 2: Eurostar 3015 at Calais Frethun, heading north to the UK

fields.Name: Itaipu Dam
fields.Description: A hydroelectric dam on the Paraná between Brazil and Paraguay, for years the largest generator of electricity in the world; its reservoir drowned the Guaíra Falls, once among the largest waterfalls in the world by volume.
fields.Caption 2: The dam undergoes expansion work

fields.Name: Palm Jumeirah
fields.Description: An artificial archipelago of dredged sand and rock in the shape of a palm tree, visible from orbit; the Atlantis hotel stands at the tip of its crescent breakwater.
fields.Caption 2: The artificial archipelago from the air
fields.Caption 3: The monorail

fields.Name: Winchester Mystery House
fields.Description: A mansion of roughly 160 rooms extended continuously for decades by Sarah Winchester, widow of the rifle magnate, with stairs that end at ceilings and doors that open onto walls or sheer drops; legend says she kept building to appease the ghosts of those killed by Winchester rifles.
fields.Caption 2: A corner turret
fields.Caption 3: The gardens

fields.Name: Biosphere 2
fields.Description: A sealed glass-and-steel ecological facility where eight people lived for two years (1991–1993), a mission troubled by falling oxygen; now a research station run by the University of Arizona.
fields.Caption 1: The habitat and biomes at dusk
fields.Caption 2: A lung dome, with the biomes behind

fields.Name: Thorncrown Chapel
fields.Description: A chapel of 425 windows in a wooden lattice, built in the Ozark woods from parts small enough for two people to carry to the site; E. Fay Jones, an apprentice of Frank Lloyd Wright, won the AIA Gold Medal in 1990.
fields.Caption 1: The chapel in the Ozark woods
fields.Caption 2: Looking up through the timber lattice
fields.Caption 3: The interior

fields.Name: Salginatobel Bridge
fields.Description: A reinforced-concrete three-hinged arch over an alpine ravine, won in a 1929 competition as the cheapest design and held up as proof that concrete could be both structural and beautiful; the first international historic civil engineering landmark named outside the United States.
fields.Caption 2: Along the deck
fields.Caption 3: The arch and the deck piers

fields.Name: Therme Vals
fields.Description: A bathhouse built into a hillside from 60,000 slabs of local Valser quartzite, lit through slots so that the water is read by sound and temperature as much as by sight.
fields.Caption 2: Detail of the gneiss courses beside glass

fields.Name: Bruder Klaus Field Chapel
fields.Description: A chapel built by farmers who stacked 112 tree trunks as a wigwam, cast concrete around them, and then burned the wood out over three weeks, leaving a charred interior.
fields.Caption 2: The charred interior, cast around tree trunks later burned away

fields.Name: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art
fields.Description: A low glass circle with no front or back, entered from any side, with galleries as boxes floating in an open plan; it houses Leandro Erlich's Swimming Pool.
fields.Caption 1: Aerial view of the circular building
fields.Caption 2: Leandro Erlich's The Swimming Pool
fields.Caption 3: Sound-tube sculptures in the grounds

fields.Name: New Museum
fields.Description: Off-kilter aluminum-mesh boxes stacked on the Bowery, each shifted off the one below to let skylights and terraces into the galleries: the first art museum built from the ground up in downtown Manhattan. Its architects won the Pritzker Prize in 2010.
fields.Caption 2: Resource Center

fields.Name: Leça Swimming Pools
fields.Description: Tidal pools made by low concrete walls that simply close off natural pools among the rocks, so the sea does the shaping; the changing rooms sit below the seafront road so as not to block the view. An early work by Álvaro Siza, who won the Pritzker Prize in 1992.
fields.Caption 2: A pool among the seaside rocks
fields.Caption 3: The entrance ramp between concrete walls

fields.Name: Kursaal
fields.Description: Two tilted translucent glass cubes on the beach at the river mouth, which Rafael Moneo described as two rocks stranded there; home of the San Sebastián International Film Festival, it won the 2001 Mies van der Rohe Prize.
fields.Caption 1: The translucent glass cube by the sea
fields.Caption 2: Lit at night
fields.Caption 3: Waves breaking in front of the auditorium

fields.Name: Casa Luis Barragán
fields.Description: Luis Barragán's own house, plain toward the street and opening inward to courtyards of saturated pink, yellow, and violet stucco; a staircase without a handrail climbs to a walled roof terrace open only to the sky.
fields.Caption 2: The rooftop terrace's coloured walls
fields.Caption 3: The street front

fields.Name: Torres de Satélite
fields.Description: Five concrete prisms 30 to 52 metres tall, painted in flat colours, standing in a highway median as the gateway to the new Ciudad Satélite suburb of Mexico City; seven were planned.
fields.Caption 2: The towers above the Periférico freeway
fields.Caption 3: The towers against a stormy sky

fields.Name: Camino Real Hotel
fields.Description: A low hotel of coloured planes and water courts built for the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, in Ricardo Legorreta's signature magenta and yellow, with a magenta lattice wall at the entrance.
fields.Caption 1: The lattice screen wall on the forecourt
fields.Caption 2: Detail of the lattice screen

fields.Name: Heritance Kandalama
fields.Description: A hotel a kilometre long, built into a cliff facing Sigiriya and planted so that the jungle swallows it, hiding it from the reservoir below.
fields.Caption 2: The planted terraces of the hotel

fields.Name: Sangath
fields.Description: Balkrishna Doshi's own studio, half sunk into the ground under vaults finished in broken china mosaic to throw off the heat; its name means “moving together through participation,” and Doshi won the Pritzker Prize in 2018.

fields.Name: Jawahar Kala Kendra
fields.Description: An arts centre laid out as nine squares after the Vedic mandala, with one square displaced as in the original plan of Jaipur, where a hill forced one square of the grid out of place.
fields.Caption 2: The central open-air courtyard (kund)

fields.Name: Gando Primary School
fields.Description: A school built by the village from compressed local clay bricks, under a raised corrugated roof that shades the classrooms and draws hot air out; it won Diébédo Francis Kéré the 2004 Aga Khan Award.
fields.Caption 2: The clay-brick school under its raised roof

fields.Name: National Museum of African American History and Culture
fields.Description: A bronze-coloured filigree corona of three inverted tiers, drawn from a Yoruba caryatid, its lattice echoing ironwork made by enslaved craftsmen in Charleston and New Orleans; most of the building is underground.
fields.Caption 2: The museum's bronze-coloured corona at night, beside the Washington Monument

fields.Name: Portland Building
fields.Description: A squat cube in cream, terracotta, and blue with oversized applied ornament, widely taken as the first major postmodern public building; leaky and dark inside, it was gutted and rebuilt in 2017–2020, and the statue Portlandia kneels over its entrance.
fields.Caption 2: Reconstruction under way

fields.Name: Piazza d'Italia
fields.Description: A public square for New Orleans's Italian-American community, its concentric colonnades in every classical order rendered in stainless steel and neon around a map of Italy in the paving; it decayed within a decade and was called the first postmodern ruin.
fields.Caption 2: Beneath an arch
fields.Caption 3: The entrance arch from the street

fields.Name: San Cataldo Cemetery
fields.Description: A cemetery of stripped archetypal forms, drained of detail so that only the type remains, around a roofless cube ossuary pierced by rows of square windows, like an abandoned house; designed by Aldo Rossi with Gianni Braghieri after a 1971 competition.
fields.Caption 2: The adjoining 19th-century cemetery by Cesare Costa

fields.Name: Neue Staatsgalerie
fields.Description: A museum wrapped around a circular open-air sculpture court, mixing travertine masonry with a bright green rubber floor and pink and blue steel handrails; a public footpath ramps through the court, and stones lie on the lawn as if fallen from the wall, exposing the masonry as cladding.
fields.Caption 1: The rotunda in the museum's entrance

fields.Name: World Trade Center
fields.Description: Two 110-storey towers, briefly the tallest buildings in the world, built as load-bearing steel tubes with closely spaced perimeter columns, which is why the windows were only 46 centimetres wide; Philippe Petit walked a wire between them in 1974, and they were destroyed on 11 September 2001.
fields.Caption 1: The plaza at dusk, with Fritz Koenig's The Sphere
fields.Caption 2: The plaza beneath the towers
fields.Caption 3: The Twin Towers from across the Hudson

fields.Name: Pruitt-Igoe
fields.Description: A public housing project of 33 slab blocks, opened in 1954 and cleared by 1976; Charles Jencks declared its demolition, begun in 1972, the death of modern architecture. Minoru Yamasaki later designed the World Trade Center.
fields.Caption 2: The demolition of one of the blocks, 1972

fields.Name: United Nations Secretariat Building
fields.Description: A green glass slab with blank marble end walls, one of the first glass curtain-wall towers in New York, designed by an international board of architects that included Le Corbusier and Oscar Niemeyer, whose joint scheme was built.
fields.Architect: Wallace Harrison; Le Corbusier; Oscar Niemeyer
fields.Caption 2: Meeting room within the building
fields.Caption 3: The building from the southwest

fields.Name: Yale Art and Architecture Building
fields.Description: Thirty-seven floor levels in seven storeys, faced in ribbed “corduroy” concrete hammered by hand; students loathed it, and a 1969 fire of unknown cause gutted part of it. Restored in 2008, it was renamed for Paul Rudolph.
fields.Caption 2: The concrete towers from across the street
fields.Caption 3: Street-level steps beside the building

fields.Name: Whitney Museum of American Art (Breuer Building)
fields.Description: An inverted granite ziggurat stepping out over Madison Avenue, with seven trapezoidal windows scattered across its face; after the Whitney moved to Renzo Piano's building in 2015, it housed the Met Breuer (2016–2020) and Frick Madison (2021–2024), and since 2025 Sotheby's.
fields.Caption 1: The stepped granite block on Madison Avenue
fields.Caption 2: The lobby under its grid of round ceiling lights
fields.Caption 3: A cantilevered upper floor and one of the trapezoid windows

fields.Name: Kaufmann Desert House
fields.Description: A glass-and-steel pinwheel for Edgar J. Kaufmann, the client who had commissioned Fallingwater, made an icon of desert modernism by Julius Shulman's 1947 photograph at dusk.
fields.Caption 1: The Kaufman House from the pool deck
fields.Caption 2: The house against the San Jacinto Mountains

fields.Name: Schindler House
fields.Description: A house of tilt-up concrete slabs with canvas sliding walls and rooftop sleeping baskets, built as two studios for two couples, the Schindlers and Clyde and Marian Chace, with no conventional bedrooms; often called the first modern house in California.
fields.Caption 2: The garden front

fields.Name: Eames House
fields.Description: Case Study House No. 8, sponsored by Arts & Architecture magazine: a house and studio assembled from off-the-shelf industrial catalogue parts, its steel frame raised in a day and a half and infilled with coloured panels. Charles and Ray Eames lived and worked there for the rest of their lives.
fields.Caption 2: Eames Studio

fields.Name: Chemosphere
fields.Description: An octagonal house on a single concrete stem anchoring it to a 45-degree slope too steep to build on, reached by a funicular; once called the most modern home in the world.
fields.Caption 2: The house on its hillside, above the Hollywood Hills

fields.Name: Bavinger House
fields.Description: A logarithmic spiral of local sandstone wound around a steel mast, with the living areas hung from cables as suspended pods; demolished in 2016.
fields.Caption 1: The house in the woods near Norman, its roof spiralling around a steel mast
fields.Caption 2: The sandstone spiral, studded with green glass, hung by cables from the mast

fields.Name: Erechtheion
fields.Description: An Ionic temple on the Acropolis that housed the cult of Athena Polias and the sacred olive tree, famous for its Porch of the Caryatids; Lord Elgin took one of the six caryatids to the British Museum, and those on site are now replicas.
fields.Caption 2: The Porch of the Caryatids

fields.Name: Stonehenge
fields.Description: A prehistoric ring of standing sarsen stones with lintels, its main axis aligned with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset; its bluestones came about 240 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales, and a 2024 study traced the Altar Stone to northeast Scotland.
fields.Caption 2: Sun through a trilithon

fields.Name: Machu Picchu
fields.Description: An Inca citadel on a ridge above the Urubamba valley, built for the emperor Pachacuti about 1450 and abandoned about a century later, unknown to the Spanish; Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention in 1911.
fields.Caption 2: Main square of Aguas Calientes
fields.Caption 3: The citadel among the Andean peaks

fields.Name: Petra
fields.Description: A Nabataean city whose temple façades are carved into rose-red rock, reached through the Siq, a narrow gorge; its best-known façade, Al-Khazneh (the Treasury), appears in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade.
fields.Caption 1: Al Deir, “The Monastery”, a monument closely resembling Al Khazneh though less ornate
fields.Caption 2: The Treasury, seen from the Siq
fields.Caption 3: Al-Khazneh, the Treasury, at night

fields.Name: Persepolis
fields.Description: The ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, begun by Darius I about 518 BCE; reliefs on the stairways of its Apadana audience hall show delegations from 23 subject peoples bringing tribute. Alexander the Great burned it in 330 BCE.
fields.Caption 1: Reliefs of Persian and Median guards on the stairway
fields.Caption 2: In the National Museum of Iran

fields.Name: Ziggurat of Ur
fields.Description: A massive stepped mud-brick platform for a temple to the moon god Nanna, built under the Third Dynasty of Ur; Leonard Woolley excavated it in the 1920s and 1930s, and its lower façade and stairways were rebuilt in the 1980s under Saddam Hussein.
fields.Caption 2: Excavated foundations

fields.Name: Pont du Gard
