fields.Description: A three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge over the Gardon, 48.8 m high, the tallest surviving Roman aqueduct bridge; its aqueduct carried water about 50 km to Nemausus (Nîmes) while falling only about 12 m along its length.
fields.Caption 1: The three tiers of arches over the Gardon
fields.Caption 2: The road bridge adjacent to the aqueduct

fields.Name: Baths of Caracalla
fields.Description: A vast imperial Roman bath complex of soaring vaulted halls, which inspired the waiting room of New York's original Pennsylvania Station.
fields.Caption 2: The surviving walls of the baths

fields.Name: Trajan's Column
fields.Description: A marble column wound with a spiral relief of the Dacian Wars that would run about 200 m if unrolled; Trajan's ashes were placed in its base, and a statue of Saint Peter has replaced his on top since 1587.
fields.Caption 1: The column and its spiral frieze
fields.Caption 2: The column in Trajan's Forum, with the domed churches beyond

fields.Name: Teotihuacan
fields.Description: A Mesoamerican city laid out on a grid, whose Avenue of the Dead runs over 2 km past the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon; the Aztecs found it long abandoned and named it “the place where the gods were created.”
fields.Location: San Martín de las Pirámides, State of Mexico, Mexico
fields.Caption 1: Pyramid of the Sun, with the Avenue of the Dead and the Pyramid of the Moon
fields.Caption 2: Steps of the Pyramid of the Moon complex
fields.Caption 3: Carved feline head

fields.Name: Great Zimbabwe
fields.Description: A dry-stone city built without mortar, with a conical tower in its Great Enclosure; it gave the modern country its name.
fields.Caption 1: The conical tower in the Great Enclosure
fields.Caption 2: Dry-stone walls at dusk
fields.Caption 3: A narrow passage between the walls

fields.Name: Durham Cathedral
fields.Description: A Norman cathedral on a rock above a bend of the River Wear, beside the castle, whose nave has the earliest surviving rib vaults on a large scale; it holds the shrine of Saint Cuthbert and the tomb of the Venerable Bede.
fields.Caption 2: Cloisters, south and west ranges
fields.Caption 3: Cloisters, south range

fields.Name: Canterbury Cathedral
fields.Description: The mother church of the Anglican Communion, where Thomas Becket was murdered in 1170.
fields.Caption 2: The 12th-century quire
fields.Caption 3: 'Becket's crown' chapel at the far east end of the cathedral

fields.Name: Westminster Abbey
fields.Description: The coronation church since 1066, home of Poets' Corner and the Coronation Chair.
fields.Caption 1: The north side, with the north transept and the nave's flying buttresses
fields.Caption 2: The west front and its two towers, finished to Nicholas Hawksmoor's design in 1745
fields.Caption 3: The cloister

fields.Name: Amiens Cathedral
fields.Description: The largest cathedral in France by interior volume, its nave vaults rising about 42 m; a labyrinth in the nave floor names its three master masons, and John Ruskin wrote The Bible of Amiens about its sculpture.
fields.Caption 2: The nave
fields.Caption 3: A rose window

fields.Name: Sainte-Foy
fields.Description: A pilgrimage church on the road to Santiago, with a famous tympanum of the Last Judgement, which holds the gold reliquary statue of Sainte Foy.
fields.Caption 2: The abbey church above the village of Conques

fields.Name: Doge's Palace
fields.Description: The Venetian Gothic seat of the Republic's government, built in phases from the 14th century with no single architect and linked to the prisons by the Bridge of Sighs; its corner sculptures are attributed to Filippo Calendario.
fields.Caption 1: The palace and the Campanile from the lagoon
fields.Caption 2: The courtyard façade
fields.Caption 3: The courtyard, with the domes of St Mark's

fields.Name: Krak des Chevaliers
fields.Description: A concentric Crusader castle held by the Knights Hospitaller, which T. E. Lawrence called the finest castle in the world.
fields.Caption 2: Smoke coming from the castle, during the Syrian Civil War
fields.Caption 3: The inner court seen from the south

fields.Name: Castel del Monte
fields.Description: Frederick II's octagonal castle with eight octagonal towers, shown on the Italian one-cent euro coin.
fields.Caption 1: The octagonal castle and its main portal
fields.Caption 2: A stair in one of the towers
fields.Caption 3: A rib vault

fields.Name: Tower of London
fields.Description: A Norman fortress on the Thames begun by William the Conqueror, whose keep is the White Tower; it houses the Crown Jewels and is guarded by the Yeomen Warders, and legend says the kingdom will fall if its ravens leave.
fields.Caption 2: The White Tower and the river wall

fields.Name: Cluny Abbey
fields.Description: A Benedictine abbey that headed hundreds of dependent monasteries; its third church, begun in 1088, was the largest in Christendom until the new Saint Peter's, and was largely demolished after the French Revolution, leaving part of one transept.
fields.Caption 1: Cluny (Saône-et-Loire, France) - The abbey buildings (18th c.)
fields.Caption 2: The site of the abbey church, looking east through the west door
fields.Caption 3: The surviving south transept of the abbey church

fields.Name: Süleymaniye Mosque
fields.Description: Mimar Sinan's great imperial mosque overlooking the Golden Horn, whose grounds hold the tombs of Suleiman the Magnificent and Roxelana.
fields.Caption 2: The mosque above the Golden Horn
fields.Caption 3: The sebil (water fountain) beside Sinan's tomb

fields.Name: Selimiye Mosque
fields.Description: Mimar Sinan's masterpiece, built for Selim II when the architect was about eighty: its dome, set on eight piers, rivals Hagia Sophia's in width, and its four slender minarets are the tallest in Ottoman architecture.
fields.Caption 2: The ablution fountain in the courtyard
fields.Caption 3: The dome and four minarets

fields.Name: Sultan Ahmed Mosque
fields.Description: The Blue Mosque, famous for its blue İznik tiles and its six minarets, a number that only the Great Mosque of Mecca then had.
fields.Caption 2: The painted domes of the interior
fields.Caption 3: The cascading domes and minarets

fields.Name: Registan
fields.Description: The public square of Timurid Samarkand, framed by three madrasas: Ulugh Beg, Sher-Dor, and Tilya-Kori.
fields.Caption 2: The Sher-Dor Madrasa
fields.Caption 3: The three madrasas at night

fields.Name: Great Mosque of Kairouan
fields.Description: The oldest surviving mosque in the Maghreb, with a massive square minaret; its hypostyle plan became a model across North Africa.
fields.Caption 2: The minaret and courtyard
fields.Caption 3: Hypostyle prayer hall

fields.Name: Mosque of Ibn Tulun
fields.Description: Cairo's oldest mosque in its original form, built of fired brick around a vast open courtyard, with a spiral minaret.
fields.Caption 2: One of the stucco-decorated windows
fields.Caption 3: View (from the minaret) of the ziyada or outer enclosure that surrounds most of the mosque

fields.Name: Shah Mosque
fields.Description: A Safavid mosque on Naqsh-e Jahan Square, covered in seven-colour tilework; its entrance faces the square, while the mosque behind turns 45 degrees to face Mecca.
fields.Caption 2: Muqarnas vault of the entrance portal
fields.Caption 3: The tiled dome from inside

fields.Name: Tōdai-ji
fields.Description: A temple housing Japan's Great Buddha in the Daibutsuden, long the world's largest wooden building even though its 1709 rebuilding is only two-thirds of the original width.
fields.Caption 2: Statue of Tamonten (also named Bishamonten)
fields.Caption 3: The Chūmon (middle gate)

fields.Name: Kinkaku-ji
fields.Description: A Zen temple whose top two storeys are covered in gold leaf; a monk burned it down in 1950, it was rebuilt in 1955, and Yukio Mishima fictionalized the arson in The Temple of the Golden Pavilion.
fields.Caption 2: The pavilion across the mirror pond in spring
fields.Caption 3: The pavilion in autumn

fields.Name: Ryōan-ji
fields.Description: A Zen temple famous for its dry rock garden of fifteen stones, of which only fourteen are visible from any one viewpoint.
fields.Caption 2: The temple gate

fields.Name: Katsura Imperial Villa
fields.Description: An imperial retreat admired for its restrained modular timber design, which Bruno Taut praised as a forerunner of modernism.
fields.Caption 2: A garden path in autumn
fields.Caption 3: A teahouse across the garden pond

fields.Name: Ise Grand Shrine
fields.Description: A Shinto shrine ritually rebuilt every twenty years in the Shikinen Sengū, a ceremony held over sixty times.
fields.Caption 1: Uji Bridge, the entrance to the Inner Shrine
fields.Caption 2: The Gekū (Outer Shrine)

fields.Name: Summer Palace
fields.Description: An imperial garden landscape around Kunming Lake and Longevity Hill, rebuilt by the Empress Dowager Cixi after its destruction in 1860.

fields.Name: Shwedagon Pagoda
fields.Description: A gilded stupa about 100 m tall, covered in gold plate and said to enshrine relics of four Buddhas.
fields.Caption 2: The great stupa and its ring of smaller shrines

fields.Name: Meenakshi Temple
fields.Description: A Dravidian temple to Meenakshi and Sundareswarar, with towering polychrome gopurams.
fields.Caption 1: The view from one of the gopurams
fields.Caption 2: Illuminated during the Navaratri festival
fields.Caption 3: Various gopurams as seen from the West tower

fields.Name: Brihadeeswarar Temple
fields.Description: A Chola granite temple built by Raja Raja Chola I, its vimana over 60 m tall.
fields.Caption 2: A gopuram (gateway tower)

fields.Name: Konark Sun Temple
fields.Description: A temple conceived as the sun god's chariot, with carved stone wheels, known to European sailors as the Black Pagoda.
fields.Caption 1: Hub of one of the temple's carved stone chariot wheels
fields.Caption 2: The temple's tiered sanctuary
fields.Caption 3: Carved rim and spoke of a chariot wheel

fields.Name: Red Fort
fields.Description: A Mughal walled palace-fortress of red sandstone, from which India's prime minister addresses the nation each Independence Day.
fields.Caption 2: The Delhi Gate, almost identical in appearance to the Lahori Gate
fields.Caption 3: The barrel-vaulted structure located just beyond the Lahore Gate served as a market

fields.Name: Humayun's Tomb
fields.Description: A garden tomb that established the Mughal charbagh model, a direct precursor of the Taj Mahal.
fields.Caption 2: The tomb across its water channel
fields.Caption 3: The tomb and its garden, in an early photograph

fields.Name: Fatehpur Sikri
fields.Description: Akbar's short-lived Mughal capital in red sandstone, entered by the Buland Darwaza and abandoned within about fifteen years, reportedly for lack of water.
fields.Caption 2: The city walls
fields.Caption 3: A courtyard seen through a colonnade

fields.Name: Qutb Minar
fields.Description: A fluted five-storey minaret of red sandstone and marble, about 73 m tall, begun in 1199 under the first sultan of Delhi; beside it stands an uncorroded iron pillar.
fields.Caption 2: Ruins in the Qutb complex
fields.Caption 3: The complex's gardens and ruins

fields.Name: Villa La Rotonda
fields.Description: A villa square in plan with four identical porticoed façades, the model for Chiswick House, Monticello, and countless others.
fields.Caption 2: The villa from the park
fields.Caption 3: Interior of the rotonda

fields.Name: San Giorgio Maggiore
fields.Description: An island church whose white marble façade, facing the Piazzetta across the basin, fuses two classical temple fronts.
fields.Caption 1: The island church from St Mark's Campanile
fields.Caption 2: The campanile above the gardens
fields.Caption 3: The Istrian stone façade

fields.Name: Il Redentore
fields.Description: A votive church built in thanks for Venice's deliverance from the plague of 1575–1577, still the focus of the city's annual Festa del Redentore.
fields.Caption 2: Section drawing of the nave and dome
fields.Caption 3: Cross-section through the dome

fields.Name: Ospedale degli Innocenti
fields.Description: A foundling hospital whose arcaded loggia opens the Renaissance, often called the first true Renaissance building.
fields.Caption 2: The rectangular women's cloister on the east side

fields.Name: Pazzi Chapel
fields.Description: A chapter house of geometric clarity in the cloister of Santa Croce, its plan built from squares and circles.
fields.Caption 2: St Andrew, glazed terracotta roundel in the lunette above the door
fields.Caption 3: Interior

fields.Name: Palazzo Rucellai
fields.Description: A palace for the Rucellai family whose façade first applied superimposed classical orders to a house, built by Bernardo Rossellino to Leon Battista Alberti's design.
fields.Caption 2: The rusticated façade

fields.Name: Sant'Andrea, Mantua
fields.Description: A church whose façade adapts a Roman triumphal arch and whose barrel-vaulted nave influenced Baroque church design.
fields.Caption 1: The coffered vault of the entrance porch
fields.Caption 2: The triumphal-arch façade

fields.Name: Laurentian Library
fields.Description: A library vestibule almost filled by a cascading staircase, its walls of blind windows and recessed columns breaking classical rules on purpose: a defining work of Mannerism.
fields.Caption 2: The reading room viewed from the top of the stairs
fields.Caption 3: The vestibule

fields.Name: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane
fields.Description: Francesco Borromini's first independent commission, a small Baroque church with an undulating façade and an oval dome.
fields.Caption 2: The dome with its intricate geometrical pattern
fields.Caption 3: The façade on the street corner

fields.Name: Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza
fields.Description: A Baroque church on a star-hexagon plan, crowned by a corkscrew lantern unique in Rome.
fields.Caption 2: The lantern
fields.Caption 3: The dome from below, its plan a six-pointed star

fields.Name: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
fields.Description: An oval Baroque church entered on its short axis, which Gian Lorenzo Bernini reportedly regarded as his most perfect work.
fields.Caption 2: Main altar - Martyrdom of Saint Andrew (1668) including dome, side chapels, and lantern
fields.Caption 3: The Lantern at Sant’Andrea al Quirinale

fields.Name: Blenheim Palace
fields.Description: A vast English Baroque country house given to the Duke of Marlborough, the birthplace of Winston Churchill, with grounds by Lancelot “Capability” Brown.
fields.Caption 2: West front with its stone belvederes
fields.Caption 3: The park and lake

fields.Name: Karlskirche
fields.Description: A Viennese Baroque church built in thanks for deliverance from the plague of 1713, flanked by two columns modelled on Trajan's.
fields.Caption 2: Detail of Johann Michael Rottmayr's dome fresco
fields.Caption 3: The nave and dome

fields.Name: Palace of Versailles
fields.Description: The royal palace whose Hall of Mirrors set the model for European courts, with gardens by André Le Nôtre; the treaty ending the First World War was signed there in 1919.
fields.Caption 2: The gilded gate
fields.Caption 3: A painted ceiling

fields.Name: Monticello
fields.Description: Thomas Jefferson's Palladian plantation house with a central dome, shown on the reverse of the U.S. nickel.
fields.Caption 2: Under the dome

fields.Name: United States Capitol
fields.Description: The domed seat of the U.S. Congress on Capitol Hill, its cast-iron dome completed during the Civil War.
fields.Architect: William Thornton (original design); Benjamin Latrobe; Charles Bulfinch; Thomas U. Walter (wings and cast-iron dome)
fields.Caption 2: The Capitol Rotunda beneath the dome, Washington, D.C.
fields.Caption 3: Inauguration of Abraham Lincoln in 1861, before the partially complete Capitol dome

fields.Name: Lincoln Memorial
fields.Description: A Doric temple housing Daniel Chester French's seated Lincoln, the setting of the 1963 March on Washington.
fields.Caption 2: The memorial by night

fields.Name: Park Güell
fields.Description: A hillside park of mosaic terraces and organic stonework, its serpentine bench faced in trencadís, a mosaic of broken tiles.
fields.Caption 2: Main terrace
fields.Caption 3: Viaduct

fields.Name: Bauhaus Dessau
fields.Description: The school building whose glass curtain wall announced the new architecture; it housed the Bauhaus from its opening in 1926 until the Nazi-led city council forced the school out of Dessau in 1932.
fields.Caption 1: The workshop wing and studio block
fields.Caption 2: The vocational-school wing, with its ribbon windows
fields.Caption 3: The glass curtain wall of the workshop wing

fields.Name: Fagus Factory
fields.Description: A shoe-last factory whose glass corners turn without visible support, often cited as the first truly modern building.
fields.Caption 1: The glazed corner of the main building
fields.Caption 2: A storehouse block
fields.Caption 3: The main building's entrance

fields.Name: Wainwright Building
fields.Description: An early steel-framed skyscraper whose unbroken brick piers stress its height; it embodies Louis Sullivan's dictum “form ever follows function.”
fields.Caption 2: The intricate frieze along the top of the building along with the bull's-eye windows
fields.Caption 3: The building in 1907

fields.Name: Carson, Pirie, Scott Building
fields.Description: A department store with lavish cast-iron ornament at street level and a plain grid frame above; its rounded corner entrance anchors State Street.
fields.Caption 1: The rounded corner at State and Madison
fields.Caption 2: Cast-iron ornament above the corner entrance

fields.Name: Robie House
fields.Description: A Prairie School house in Chicago's Hyde Park whose low roofs cantilever far beyond their supports, with long, thin Roman bricks stressing the horizontal.
fields.Caption 1: The cantilevered roof over the west terrace
fields.Caption 2: The long, low street front
fields.Caption 3: Art-glass windows designed by Wright

fields.Name: Unity Temple
fields.Description: A church built as a cube of poured concrete and lit from above, one of the first monumental buildings in exposed reinforced concrete.
fields.Caption 1: Clerestory windows at the top of the façade
fields.Caption 2: Detail of one of the piers
fields.Caption 3: The auditorium's pulpit from the north

fields.Name: Johnson Wax Headquarters
fields.Description: An open office hall carried on slender dendriform columns and lit by tubes of Pyrex glass instead of windows.
fields.Caption 1: The Research Tower and the administration building
fields.Caption 2: The complex behind its brick wall

fields.Name: Taliesin West
fields.Description: Frank Lloyd Wright's desert studio and winter home of canvas and local stone, the base of the Taliesin Fellowship.
fields.Caption 1: Fountain and terrace, with dining and dormitory area beyond
fields.Caption 2: The desert garden and the drafting-studio roof

fields.Name: Barcelona Pavilion
fields.Description: Germany's pavilion at the 1929 International Exposition, a flow of space between freestanding walls of onyx and travertine under a flat roof; demolished in 1930 and rebuilt in 1986.
fields.Caption 2: The pavilion's travertine walls and pool
fields.Caption 3: A Barcelona chair against onyx and marble

fields.Name: Farnsworth House
fields.Description: A steel-and-glass weekend house raised above a floodplain, whose construction ended in a famous lawsuit with its client, Edith Farnsworth.
fields.Caption 2: The glass walls, raised above the Fox River's floodplain
fields.Caption 3: Underside of the house

fields.Name: Seagram Building
fields.Description: A bronze-and-glass tower set back behind a granite plaza, which prompted New York's incentive zoning rules.
fields.Architect: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe; Philip Johnson
fields.Caption 1: The tower behind its plaza on Park Avenue
fields.Caption 2: The building as seen from the ground on 53rd Street
fields.Caption 3: The columns at the lobby's northwestern corner

fields.Name: Glass House
fields.Description: Philip Johnson's own home, a transparent pavilion in the landscape whose only enclosed room is a brick cylinder holding the bathroom; it answers Ludwig Mies van der Rohe's Farnsworth House, which Johnson saw in drawings before it was built.
fields.Caption 1: The house on its lawn: glass walls on a black steel frame
fields.Caption 2: The single open room, divided only by a brick cylinder and free-standing furniture

fields.Name: Notre-Dame du Haut
fields.Description: A pilgrimage chapel with a sweeping curved roof and thick walls pierced by deep, coloured windows, a sharp turn from Le Corbusier's earlier machine aesthetic.
fields.Caption 1: The chapel on its hill above Ronchamp

fields.Name: Unité d'Habitation
fields.Description: A slab housing block on pilotis with a shopping street inside it, the prototype for post-war mass housing across Europe.
fields.Caption 2: Loggias with coloured balcony panels
fields.Caption 3: The roof terrace

fields.Name: Chandigarh Capitol Complex
fields.Description: The government complex of the new capital of Punjab, buildings of monumental board-marked concrete: the Palace of Assembly, the High Court, and the Secretariat.
fields.Caption 1: The reflecting pool in front of it
fields.Caption 2: The hyperboloid roof of the Assembly Chamber
fields.Caption 3: The Tower of Shadows

fields.Name: Villa Mairea
fields.Description: A modernist country villa for Harry and Maire Gullichsen, named after her, softened by timber, brick, and forest imagery: clusters of rattan-wrapped steel columns in the living room echo the surrounding pine forest.
fields.Caption 2: An ivy-covered wing
fields.Caption 3: The pool and sauna

fields.Name: Paimio Sanatorium
fields.Description: A tuberculosis sanatorium designed around sunlight, air, and quiet, from the patient's point of view: calm ceiling colours for those lying in bed, quiet washbasins, and the bent-plywood Paimio chair, angled to ease breathing.
fields.Caption 2: Sun deck at the top floor of the building

fields.Name: Salk Institute
fields.Description: Symmetrical research laboratories framing a bare travertine court open to the Pacific, with a channel of water running down its axis toward the ocean; Luis Barragán persuaded Louis Kahn to leave the court empty, as “a façade to the sky.” Founded by Jonas Salk, developer of the polio vaccine.
fields.Caption 2: The study towers above the fountain
fields.Caption 3: Stairs between the study towers

fields.Name: Kimbell Art Museum
fields.Description: A museum of repeated concrete cycloid vaults, each with a slot at its crown that lets in daylight, which aluminum reflectors spread across the concrete; Renzo Piano added a pavilion in 2013.
fields.Caption 2: One of the porticos at the front of the museum
fields.Caption 3: A gallery under the cycloid vaults, lit from the slit at each crown

fields.Name: National Assembly of Bangladesh
fields.Description: A monumental parliament set in a lake, its assembly chamber ringed by offices whose walls are cut with huge circles, triangles, and rectangles that shade the interior; begun in 1961 for Pakistan and finished in 1982, eight years after Louis Kahn's death.
fields.Caption 2: A façade with geometric openings

fields.Name: Gateway Arch
fields.Description: A stainless-steel catenary arch marking westward expansion, 192 m tall and as wide at its base, the tallest arch in the world; tram capsules inside its legs carry visitors to an observation deck at the top.
fields.Caption 1: The arch above the St. Louis skyline at night
fields.Caption 2: From the air, framing the Old Courthouse
fields.Caption 3: One of the tram capsules that climb its legs

fields.Name: TWA Flight Center
fields.Description: A terminal of swooping thin-shell concrete evoking flight, dedicated on 28 May 1962, nine months after Eero Saarinen's death; it reopened in 2019 as the TWA Hotel.
fields.Caption 1: The lunch counter and café of the original terminal
fields.Caption 2: The entrance front under its wing-like concrete shells
fields.Caption 3: The crowded terminal

fields.Name: Habitat 67
fields.Description: Housing built for Expo 67 in Montreal from Moshe Safdie's thesis project: 354 identical prefabricated concrete boxes stacked so that each flat has a roof garden on the one below.
fields.Caption 2: Stacked concrete units

fields.Name: Centre Pompidou
fields.Description: A cultural centre with its structure and services worn on the outside to free the interior, the ducts colour-coded: blue for air, green for water, yellow for electricity, and red for movement, as on the escalator tube.
fields.Caption 2: The exposed pipes and escalator tubes on the façade

fields.Name: 30 St Mary Axe
fields.Description: A tapering tower in the City of London nicknamed the Gherkin, whose diagrid frame allows column-free floors and whose spiralling light wells help ventilate it naturally.
fields.Caption 2: The diagrid glazing

fields.Name: Reichstag dome
fields.Description: A glass dome with a public ramp above the German parliament chamber, from which visitors look down on the Bundestag as a symbol of transparency.
fields.Caption 2: The mirrored cone from below

fields.Name: Louvre Pyramid
fields.Description: A glass-and-steel pyramid forming the museum's entrance, commissioned by François Mitterrand for the Grand Louvre project; critics mocked it at first, and a popular myth says it has 666 panes (it has 673).
fields.Caption 2: Courtyard of the Museum of Louvre, and its pyramid
fields.Caption 3: Hall Napoléon visitors centre with views of museum through the glass pyramid

fields.Name: Bank of China Tower
fields.Description: A faceted tower braced by a visible triangular frame, whose sharp angles were criticized on feng shui grounds.
fields.Caption 1: The tower among its Central neighbours
fields.Caption 2: The triangular bracing

fields.Name: Vanna Venturi House
fields.Description: A small house for Robert Venturi's mother whose split gable mocks modernist purity, a founding work of postmodernism.
fields.Caption 2: The garden side of the house

fields.Name: Jewish Museum Berlin
fields.Description: A zinc-clad zigzag, its plan often read as a fractured Star of David, cut through by empty voids that commemorate absence.
fields.Caption 2: Jewish Museum and the Libeskind Building

fields.Name: Beijing National Stadium
fields.Description: The stadium of the 2008 Olympics, wrapped in an interwoven steel lattice that gave it the nickname the Bird's Nest; the artist Ai Weiwei consulted on the design, then distanced himself from the Games as propaganda.
fields.Caption 2: The interwoven steel members that gave it the name Bird's Nest

fields.Name: Tate Modern
fields.Description: Giles Gilbert Scott's Bankside Power Station converted into a museum around its Turbine Hall, which hosts large commissions such as Ólafur Elíasson's The Weather Project (2003).
fields.Architect: Giles Gilbert Scott (original power station); Herzog & de Meuron (conversion)
fields.Caption 2: The former power station

fields.Name: CCTV Headquarters
fields.Description: A continuous loop of a tower folded into a hollow rectangle, locally nicknamed Big Pants.
fields.Caption 2: The loop of the building

fields.Name: Seattle Central Library
fields.Description: A faceted glass-and-steel library of stacked, shifting platforms, whose Books Spiral runs the collection along one continuous ramp.
fields.Caption 2: The reading area under the glass diagrid
fields.Caption 3: A red corridor on the meeting-room floor

fields.Name: Church of the Light
fields.Description: A small concrete chapel, built on a tight budget, whose altar wall is slit with a cross of daylight; a freestanding wall cuts diagonally through the box, and Tadao Ando wanted the cross left open to the air.
fields.Caption 1: A concrete stair beneath a cross-shaped opening
fields.Caption 2: The cross of light behind the altar

fields.Name: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum
fields.Description: A raised concrete museum on the axis of the Peace Park, aligned with the memorial cenotaph and the A-Bomb Dome.
fields.Caption 2: A second museum building
fields.Caption 3: Human Shadow Etched in Stone

fields.Name: Yoyogi National Gymnasium
fields.Description: A suspension-roofed arena built for the 1964 Olympics, whose sweeping cable roof recalls traditional Japanese forms.
fields.Caption 1: The arena during a basketball game
fields.Caption 2: The suspended roof above the plaza

fields.Name: Niterói Contemporary Art Museum
fields.Description: A saucer-shaped museum on a cliff above Guanabara Bay, reached by a curving red ramp.
fields.Caption 2: The saucer on its pedestal
fields.Caption 3: Guanabara Bay through the gallery windows

fields.Name: Guangzhou Opera House
fields.Description: Twin boulder-like volumes of glass and granite by the Pearl River, which Zaha Hadid likened to pebbles in a stream.
fields.Caption 2: The opera house in fog

fields.Name: Marina Bay Sands
fields.Description: Three towers carrying a boat-shaped SkyPark with a 150 m infinity pool.
fields.Caption 2: The Apple store sphere on the bay at night
fields.Caption 3: The Merlion, with the hotel across the bay

fields.Name: Willis Tower
fields.Description: The former Sears Tower, whose nine bundled tubes step back as it rises, the tallest building in the world for 25 years.
fields.Caption 2: The wall of the tower from the Skydeck
fields.Caption 3: Bottom of the tower

fields.Name: John Hancock Center
fields.Description: A tapering Chicago skyscraper with exposed X-bracing, an early trussed tube that made its height economical.

fields.Name: Taipei 101
fields.Description: A pagoda-inspired tower with a giant tuned mass damper, the tallest building in the world from 2004 to 2010.
fields.Caption 2: The tuned mass damper

fields.Name: Golden Gate Bridge
fields.Description: A suspension bridge across the Golden Gate strait, painted international orange, with the longest suspension span in the world until 1964.
fields.Architect: Joseph Strauss; Irving Morrow (Art Deco design and colour); Leon Moisseiff (suspension design)
fields.Caption 2: The deck from the top of a tower
fields.Caption 3: Atop a tower, looking toward the city

fields.Name: Crystal Palace
fields.Description: A prefabricated iron-and-glass hall built in Hyde Park for the Great Exhibition, then moved to Sydenham, where it burned down in 1936.
fields.Caption 1: The Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, 1851
fields.Caption 2: The transept, built high enough to enclose the park's elms

fields.Name: Göbekli Tepe
fields.Description: Circles of carved T-shaped limestone pillars on a hilltop, the oldest known monumental architecture, built before agriculture, pottery, or the wheel.
fields.Caption 2: Enclosure of T-shaped limestone pillars
fields.Caption 3: Carved animal relief on a T-shaped pillar

fields.Name: Skara Brae
fields.Description: A cluster of Neolithic stone houses linked by covered passages, preserved under sand until a storm uncovered it in 1850; their stone dressers and beds still stand.
fields.Caption 1: A house in the Neolithic village
fields.Caption 2: The stone dresser and hearth inside a house

fields.Name: House of the Vettii
fields.Description: The best-preserved Roman domus, a townhouse built around an atrium and a garden peristyle, owned by two freedmen and painted in the Fourth Style.
fields.Caption 2: The atrium, painted by Luigi Bazzani, 1895

fields.Name: Cliff Palace
fields.Description: The largest cliff dwelling in North America, a village of about 150 sandstone rooms and kivas set in a canyon alcove, abandoned within a century of its completion.
fields.Caption 2: The cliff dwelling beneath its overhang

fields.Name: Sultanhanı Caravanserai
fields.Description: The largest caravanserai in Anatolia, a fortified courtyard inn with a covered hall and a raised mosque, one of a chain spaced a day's travel apart on the trade roads.
fields.Caption 2: The vaulted winter hall

fields.Name: Generalife
fields.Description: The summer palace of the Nasrid rulers above the Alhambra, a retreat of pavilions, water channels, and terraced gardens, and the best-surviving medieval Islamic garden.
fields.Caption 2: Water garden

fields.Name: Church of Saint Francis of Assisi
fields.Description: A Baroque church with a curved façade and a carved soapstone portal by Aleijadinho, who lost the use of his hands to disease and carved with tools strapped to his wrists.
fields.Caption 1: The façade and its round towers
fields.Caption 2: Carved altarpieces in the nave

fields.Name: The Iron Bridge
fields.Description: The first major bridge built of cast iron, a single arch of thirty metres over the Severn gorge, cast by Abraham Darby III; its joints copy carpentry rather than metalwork.
fields.Caption 1: The east side, showing the dark red paint of the 2018 restoration
fields.Caption 2: Elias Martin's painting of the bridge under construction, 1779

fields.Name: Red House
fields.Description: A red-brick, L-shaped house with a steep tiled roof and no classical detail, built for William Morris, who furnished it with his own designs: the founding building of the Arts and Crafts movement.
fields.Caption 2: A mural inside the house

fields.Name: Letchworth Garden City
fields.Description: The first garden city, a planned town of low-density housing set in a permanent green belt, built to realize Ebenezer Howard's To-morrow: A Peaceful Path to Real Reform (1898); the model for the later British new towns.
fields.Caption 2: 217 Icknield Way: Winner of best £150 cottage competition at the 1905 Cheap Cottages Exhibition

fields.Name: Rashtrapati Bhavan
fields.Description: A domed palace of red and cream sandstone on a raised platform, the centrepiece of imperial New Delhi, mixing classical order with Indian chhatris and chhajjas; now the residence of India's president.
fields.Caption 2: The banqueting hall, set for a state dinner
fields.Caption 3: Jaipur Column

fields.Name: Thiepval Memorial
fields.Alternate: Memorial to the Missing of the Somme
fields.Description: A brick and stone mass of interlocking arches on a ridge, carrying the names of more than 72,000 men of the Somme who have no known grave.
fields.Caption 2: The 'Somme 1916' roundel

fields.Name: Hearst Castle
fields.Description: A hilltop estate of towers, terraces, and imported European interiors, built for William Randolph Hearst by Julia Morgan, the first woman admitted to study architecture at the École des Beaux-Arts.
fields.Caption 2: The library, with some of Hearst's collection of ancient Greek vases on the bookshelves

fields.Name: Mayakovskaya
fields.Description: A Moscow Metro platform hall of slender steel columns under shallow oval domes with mosaic ceilings; a copy won the Grand Prize at the 1939 New York World's Fair, and in 1941 the station served as an air-raid shelter and command post.
fields.Caption 2: The station's arched central hall

fields.Name: Cenotaph for Newton
fields.Description: An unbuilt design for a sphere 150 metres across in a cypress-planted base, pierced to throw starlight on the interior; never meant to be affordable, it is the best-known drawing of French revolutionary architecture.
fields.Caption 1: Section, with the armillary sphere at the centre
fields.Caption 2: Elevation
fields.Caption 3: The interior by night, its vault pierced to show the stars

fields.Name: Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana
fields.Description: A white travertine cube of six storeys of identical arches, the symbol of Mussolini's EUR district, built for a world's fair that the war cancelled.
fields.Caption 1: The arcaded cube on its stepped podium
fields.Caption 2: During construction, 1940

fields.Name: New Gourna
fields.Description: A village of mud-brick houses roofed with Nubian vaults built without centring, by local labour, against the concrete of official planning; Hassan Fathy set out its ideas in Architecture for the Poor.
fields.Caption 2: Foundation tablet

fields.Name: Poundbury
fields.Description: An urban extension of traditional streets and squares in local stone and render, built on Duchy of Cornwall land at the direction of the then Prince of Wales as an argument against post-war planning.

fields.Name: Ningbo History Museum
fields.Description: A tilted mass split by ravine-like passages, walled in bricks and tiles salvaged from demolished villages and laid by local masons; Wang Shu won the Pritzker Prize in 2012.
fields.Caption 1: South gate of Ningbo Museum, designed by Wang Shu
fields.Caption 2: Model of Ningbo city in Tang Dynasty

fields.Name: Vitruvius
fields.Description: A Roman military engineer under Augustus whose De architectura is the only treatise on building to survive from antiquity, and the source of the rule that architecture must have firmitas (strength), utilitas (usefulness) and venustas (beauty).
fields.Notes: Leonardo's Vitruvian Man illustrates his account of human proportion; Leon Battista Alberti and Andrea Palladio both wrote in answer to him.
fields.Caption 2: Roman house plan after Vitruvius

fields.Name: Great Mosque of Samarra
fields.Description: An Abbasid mosque, the largest in the world when built, enclosed by a vast rectangle of brick wall; beside it stands the Malwiya, a freestanding spiral minaret 52 metres high climbed by an external ramp.
fields.Caption 1: The Minaret and the mosque Wall
fields.Caption 2: The Malawiyya minaret, standing on the north side of the mosque
fields.Caption 3: The spiral Malwiya Minaret (9th century)

fields.Name: Orsanmichele
fields.Description: A Florentine grain market turned church, whose exterior niches the guilds filled with statues by Donatello, Lorenzo Ghiberti, Andrea del Verrocchio, and Nanni di Banco; most of the originals are now in the museum upstairs, Donatello's Saint George in the Bargello.
fields.Caption 1: Orcagna's tabernacle: the Assumption of the Virgin
fields.Caption 2: Orcagna's tabernacle: the Dormition of the Virgin

fields.Name: Hôtel Tassel
fields.Description: A Brussels townhouse usually called the first Art Nouveau building: Victor Horta exposed its iron structure instead of hiding it, made the stair hall the centre of the plan instead of a corridor, and carried its whiplash line from the iron into the mosaics and wall painting.
fields.Caption 3: Huis Tassel

fields.Name: Majolica House
fields.Description: An apartment block whose street front is covered edge to edge in glazed tiles in a floral pattern, built as Otto Wagner moved from historicism toward a frankly modern surface; his book Modern Architecture argued that new materials demanded new forms.
fields.Caption 2: The façade's majolica tiles of flowering vines

fields.Name: Looshaus
fields.Description: An unornamented office and apartment block facing the Hofburg, so bare above its marble base that the Viennese called it the house without eyebrows and the emperor is said to have kept his curtains shut against it: Adolf Loos's Ornament and Crime, which called decoration wasted labour, built in stone.
fields.Caption 2: Colonnade and mezzanine bay windows

fields.Name: Glasgow School of Art
fields.Description: An art school on a steep site, its severe stone street front broken by tall studio windows and ironwork; its library, a cage of squared timber posts, was the most admired interior in Britain before fires gutted the building in 2014 and again in 2018. Charles Rennie Mackintosh worked with Margaret Macdonald and the rest of the Glasgow Four.
fields.Caption 2: A scale model of the GSA's Mackintosh building

fields.Name: Royal Saltworks at Arc-et-Senans
fields.Description: An industrial town laid out as a half circle around the director's house, so that supervision radiated from the centre: the only built part of Claude-Nicolas Ledoux's ideal city of Chaux. Ledoux also built the Paris toll gates.

fields.Name: Basilica of the Fourteen Holy Helpers
fields.Description: A pilgrimage church whose interior is built from interlocking ovals rather than a nave, so the vaults never settle into a single axis and the altar stands free in the middle; Balthasar Neumann also built the Würzburg Residence, whose staircase carries the largest fresco in the world, by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo.
fields.Caption 2: The basilica above the Main valley

fields.Name: The Pentagon
fields.Description: The headquarters of the American defence establishment, built in sixteen months during the Second World War: five concentric rings joined by ten spokes, so that any two points are within a seven-minute walk. Its plan came from the shape of the original site, hemmed in by roads, and was kept after the site moved.
fields.Caption 2: The west side after the 11 September 2001 attack

fields.Name: Getty Center
fields.Description: A museum complex on a ridge above Los Angeles, reached by a cable-hauled tram and laid out on two grids at 22.5 degrees to each other; Richard Meier, who works almost only in white, clad it in travertine, cut so that the fossils show, to let it sit in the landscape.
fields.Caption 2: A stairway leading down to the Central Garden

fields.Name: Institut du Monde Arabe
fields.Description: An institute whose south wall is a grid of photosensitive metal diaphragms that open and close like camera apertures, filtering light through a pattern drawn from the mashrabiya screen; Jean Nouvel later built the Torre Agbar in Barcelona and the Louvre Abu Dhabi.
fields.Caption 2: Impression of the metallic brise soleil seen from the inside out
fields.Caption 3: The south façade

fields.Name: Centre Pompidou-Metz
fields.Description: A gallery under a hexagonal timber lattice roof modelled on a Chinese woven hat, with three rectangular gallery tubes pushed through it at different heights; Shigeru Ban is best known for emergency shelters and churches of cardboard tubes, work that won him the Pritzker Prize in 2014.

fields.Name: Flying buttress
fields.Description: An arched exterior support that carries the outward thrust of a roof across an open gap to a free-standing pier, letting the wall between be opened into glass.
fields.Notes: Its adoption is what allowed Gothic churches to rise so high and hold so much window.
fields.Caption 1: Flying buttresses over a side aisle of St. Mary's Church, Lübeck
fields.Caption 2: Flying buttress of Reims Cathedral, as drawn by Villard de Honnecourt
fields.Caption 3: Flying buttresses around the apse of Notre-Dame de Paris

fields.Name: Ribbed vault
fields.Description: A ceiling whose skeleton of arched stone bands takes the load, so the panels between can be filled with light webbing.
fields.Notes: Distributes weight to piers rather than along the whole wall; with the pointed arch and flying buttress it defines Gothic construction.
fields.Caption 1: Ribbed vault in St. Marienstern Abbey
fields.Caption 2: Gothic rib vaulting over the nave of Tours Cathedral
fields.Caption 3: Rib-vaulted ceiling of Noyon Cathedral, one of the first Gothic cathedrals

fields.Name: Groin vault
fields.Description: Formed where two barrel roofs cross at right angles, giving four arched openings and sharp diagonal edges where the curved surfaces meet.
fields.Notes: Standard in Roman and Romanesque building; the edges are called groins.
fields.Caption 1: Renaissance groin vault in Santa Maria dei Carmini
fields.Caption 2: A groin vault (with pointed Gothic profile) viewed from the underside
fields.Caption 3: Groin vaults in the cloister of Tournus Abbey, France

fields.Name: Barrel vault
fields.Description: A continuous semicircular ceiling of unchanging cross-section, in effect a single arch drawn out along the length of a space.
fields.Notes: Also called a tunnel roof; needs continuous support along both walls, which limits window openings.
fields.Caption 2: Coffered barrel vault over the Temple of Jupiter at Diocletian's Palace
fields.Caption 3: Painted barrel vault of the abbey church of Saint-Savin-sur-Gartempe (c. 1100)
fields.Caption 4: Pointed barrel vault over the nave of Fontenay Abbey (1147)

fields.Name: Fan vault
fields.Description: A ceiling of inverted half-cones covered with ribs of equal curvature spreading from each springing point.
fields.Notes: A peculiarly English Perpendicular form; King's College Chapel, Cambridge, and Bath Abbey are the great examples.
fields.Caption 2: Fan vaulting over the nave of Bath Abbey
fields.Caption 3: King's College Chapel, Cambridge

fields.Name: Pendentive
fields.Description: A curved triangular section of masonry that carries a circular base above a square bay, filling each corner.
fields.Notes: The Byzantine solution to setting a round shape on a square plan; Hagia Sophia is the decisive demonstration.
fields.Caption 2: Correggio's dome fresco in San Giovanni Evangelista (1520–21)
fields.Caption 3: The dome and pendentives of Çamlıca Mosque

fields.Name: Squinch
fields.Description: A small arch or lintel thrown across an interior corner to convert a square bay into an octagon that a round base can sit on.
fields.Notes: The Persian and Islamic alternative to the pendentive.
fields.Caption 1: Squinches supporting the dome of Odzun Basilica (early 8th century)
fields.Caption 2: Squinches in the Baptistery of San Giovanni in Fonte

fields.Name: Oculus
fields.Description: A circular opening at the crown of a roof or in a wall, open or glazed.
fields.Notes: The one in the Pantheon is nearly nine metres across and is the building's only light source.
fields.Caption 2: Renaissance oculus with figures of War and Peace, Cour Carrée, Louvre
fields.Caption 3: Un œil de bœuf à Lyon

fields.Name: Tympanum
fields.Description: The recessed area enclosed by an arch above a doorway's lintel, usually carved with figures.
fields.Notes: Romanesque and Gothic churches place a Last Judgement here; also the triangular face of a Greek pediment.
fields.Caption 1: Tympanum of the church of Sant Esteve
fields.Caption 2: Last Judgement tympanum of the Abbey Church of Sainte-Foy (c. 1107–25), Conques
fields.Caption 3: Tympanum of the Abbey of Sainte-Foy, Conques

fields.Name: Clerestory
fields.Description: A row of windows in the upper stage of a wall, above the roofs of the aisles that flank it.
fields.Notes: Lights the central vessel of a basilica or church from above.
fields.Caption 2: Interior elevation of a Gothic cathedral, with clerestory highlighted
fields.Caption 3: St. Nicholas' Church

fields.Name: Triforium
fields.Description: A shallow arcaded passage or blind gallery in the middle storey of a church wall, between the arcade and the upper windows.
fields.Notes: Occupies the space over the aisle roof.
fields.Caption 1: A Romanesque triforium gallery in the Cathedral of Saint Mary Major

fields.Name: Ambulatory
fields.Description: A curved aisle running behind the high altar, allowing pilgrims to circulate without disturbing the service.
fields.Notes: Often gives onto a ring of radiating chapels; a chevet in French planning.
fields.Caption 2: Ambulatory of Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari
fields.Caption 3: Vaults of the ambulatory of the Basílica del Voto Nacional

fields.Name: Narthex
fields.Description: An entrance porch or antechamber across the west end of a church, before the main body of the building.
fields.Notes: In the early church, the place for catechumens, and penitents who could not enter the nave.
fields.Caption 1: Floorplan of the Chora Church, showing both inner and outer narthex
fields.Caption 2: In the narthex of a small Orthodox church, looking through the doorway into the nave and Holy Doors
fields.Caption 3: The inner narthex of Hagia Sophia, Istanbul

fields.Name: Transept
fields.Description: The arm that crosses the main axis of a church at right angles, giving the plan the shape of a cross.
fields.Notes: Where it meets the nave and choir is the crossing, often carrying a tower or dome.
fields.Caption 1: Canterbury Cathedral from the air: the long nave and choir crossed by two transepts, Canterbury, England
fields.Caption 2: The south transept of York Minster, York, England
fields.Caption 3: The south transept and its rose window, Notre-Dame de Paris, Paris
fields.Caption 4: The crossing of Amiens Cathedral, Amiens, France, where the transept meets the nave

fields.Name: Apse
fields.Description: A semicircular or polygonal recess, usually roofed with a half-dome, terminating the east end of a church.
fields.Notes: Inherited from the Roman basilica; usually holds the altar.
fields.Caption 1: Early Christian apse with a semi-dome, Sant'Apollinare in Classe
fields.Caption 2: Surviving apse of the Basilica of Santa Giulia
fields.Caption 3: The chevet of Saint-Ouen, ringed by radiating chapels

fields.Name: Spandrel
fields.Description: The roughly triangular surface between the outer curve of an arch and the rectangle enclosing it, or between two adjacent arches.
fields.Notes: In steel-framed towers, the panel between the head of one window and the sill above it.
fields.Caption 1: Winged victories in the spandrels of the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel, Paris
fields.Caption 2: Spandrels of a bridge over the Orb at Roquebrun, France

fields.Name: Voussoir
fields.Description: One of the wedge-shaped blocks that together make up the curve of an arch.
fields.Notes: The central one at the crown is the keystone.
fields.Caption 1: Carved voussoirs over a tower-house doorway
fields.Caption 2: Old College, University of Edinburgh (William Henry Playfair): bevelled blocks mark each voussoir
fields.Caption 3: A keystone arch in a 16th-century Mannerist courtyard

fields.Name: Keystone
fields.Description: The wedge at the very crown of an arch, the last piece set and the one that locks the rest into place.
fields.Notes: Often enlarged and carved as a decorative feature.
fields.Caption 1: Keystone carved as a lion's head
fields.Caption 2: A rusticated doorway with a carved keystone

fields.Name: Pilaster
fields.Description: A shallow rectangular projection from a wall, shaped and capitalled like a column but structurally part of the wall itself.
fields.Notes: Used to articulate a facade without engaging a true colonnade.
fields.Caption 2: Two decorative Corinthian pilasters in the Church of Saint-Sulpice
fields.Caption 3: Ornamental pilaster design, German print, before 1921

fields.Name: Entablature
fields.Description: The horizontal band a classical colonnade carries, divided into architrave, frieze, and cornice.
fields.Notes: Its treatment differs by order and is one of the clearest ways to identify which is in use.
fields.Caption 1: The back of the entablature of the Gate of Athena Archegetis
fields.Caption 2: Entablature of the Temple of Venus Genetrix
fields.Caption 3: Entablatures at Caesarea Maritima

fields.Name: Architrave
fields.Description: The lowest of the three bands a classical colonnade carries, resting directly on the capitals.
fields.Notes: Plain in the Doric order, divided into three stepped bands in the Ionic.
fields.Caption 1: Architrave of the Temple of Mars Ultor in the Forum of Augustus
fields.Caption 2: Architrave in the Basilica of San Salvatore
fields.Caption 3: The Parthenon, Athens: the architrave runs above the columns

fields.Name: Frieze
fields.Description: The middle band of a classical entablature, between the architrave and the cornice, often carrying sculpture.
fields.Notes: In the Doric order it alternates triglyphs and metopes; the Parthenon's continuous one is the most famous.
fields.Caption 2: The Circus (Bath), UK. Architectural detail of the frieze showing the alternating triglyphs and metope
fields.Caption 3: Doric frieze of the Temple of Hephaestus (449–415 BCE)
fields.Caption 4: Frieze of animals and myths at the base of the Hoysaleswara temple

fields.Name: Cornice
fields.Description: The projecting uppermost band of an entablature, or any horizontal moulding crowning a wall.
fields.Notes: Throws rainwater clear of the face below.
fields.Caption 2: Cornice by Michelangelo on the Palazzo Farnese, Rome
fields.Caption 3: Cornice of the Maison Carrée, a Corinthian Roman temple, with dentils nearest the wall

fields.Name: Pediment
fields.Description: The low triangular gable closing the end of a ridged roof above a classical portico.
fields.Notes: Its recessed face is a tympanum; the broken and segmental varieties are Baroque devices.
fields.Caption 1: Pediment of the Madeleine, with sculpture by Henri Lemaire (1826–34)
fields.Caption 2: Types of pediment; “curved” and “broken” examples at the lower right
fields.Caption 3: Neoclassical pediment of the Madeleine

fields.Name: Metope
fields.Description: The square panel, plain or carved in relief, set between the grooved blocks of a Doric frieze.
fields.Notes: Those from the Parthenon show the battle of Lapiths and centaurs.
fields.Caption 1: A carved metope in the Museo Archeologico Regionale
fields.Caption 2: Parthenon metope: a Lapith fighting a centaur, Athens
fields.Caption 3: Archaic metope, National Archaeological Museum of Paestum

fields.Name: Triglyph
fields.Description: The vertically grooved block, cut with three bars, that punctuates a Doric frieze.
fields.Notes: Thought to represent the ends of ceiling beams in an earlier timber system.
fields.Caption 2: Triglyphs and metopes on the Temple of Hephaestus, Athens

fields.Name: Doric order
fields.Description: The plainest and stoutest of the Greek systems: a fluted shaft rising without a base to a simple cushion and square slab.
fields.Notes: Its frieze alternates triglyphs and metopes; the Parthenon is the supreme example.
fields.Caption 1: The Doric order of the Parthenon, Athens
fields.Caption 2: Painted details of ancient Greek architecture
fields.Caption 3: A Doric temple at Paestum, Italy

fields.Name: Ionic order
fields.Description: The Greek system identified at once by the pair of spiral scrolls on either side of its capital.
fields.Notes: Slenderer than the Doric and set on a moulded base; the Erechtheion is the standard example.
fields.Caption 2: Volute capital, Temple of Apollo at Didyma
fields.Caption 3: Capital from the Erechtheion, Athens

fields.Name: Corinthian order
fields.Description: The most ornate Greek system, its capital a deep bell wrapped in two tiers of acanthus leaves.
fields.Notes: Vitruvius tells the story of Callimachus inventing it after seeing a basket overgrown at a girl's grave.
fields.Caption 2: Corinthian colonnade of the Temple of Bacchus (150–250 CE)
fields.Caption 3: Corinthian capitals of the Choragic Monument of Lysicrates (330s BCE)

fields.Name: Tuscan order
fields.Description: A Roman simplification of the plainest Greek system: an unfluted shaft on a base, with an undecorated frieze.
fields.Notes: The most severe of the five orders codified in the Renaissance.
fields.Caption 1: St Paul's, Covent Garden by Inigo Jones (1633), “the handsomest barn in England”
fields.Caption 2: Doorway framed by plain, unfluted pilasters
fields.Caption 3: The five orders compared, with the Tuscan first

fields.Name: Composite order
fields.Description: A Roman conflation putting the scrolls of one Greek system above the acanthus foliage of another.
fields.Notes: The fifth of the canonical orders; the Arch of Titus is an early appearance.
fields.Caption 1: Composite capitals of the Arch of Titus, Rome
fields.Caption 2: Unlike the Composite capital, this Ionic capital
fields.Caption 3: Composite capitals on the Showakan, Tokyo

fields.Name: Caryatid
fields.Description: A carved female figure standing in place of a column and carrying an entablature on her head.
fields.Notes: The Erechtheion porch has six; the male equivalent is an atlas or telamon.
fields.Caption 1: Porch of the Maidens (Caryatids), Acropolis New Museum
fields.Caption 2: The caryatid porch of the Erechtheion, Athens
fields.Caption 3: The caryatid standing in contrapposto, originally part of the Erechtheion, Athens

fields.Name: Cantilever
fields.Description: A beam or slab anchored at one end only, projecting into space with no support beneath its far end.
fields.Notes: Wright's terraces at Fallingwater are the famous demonstration in reinforced concrete.
fields.Caption 2: The Pierre Pflimlin Bridge under construction
fields.Caption 3: Howrah Bridge

fields.Name: Curtain wall
fields.Description: A non-loadbearing outer skin hung on the frame of a building, carrying nothing but its own weight and the wind.
fields.Notes: Made the fully glazed tower possible; the Seagram Building is the canonical statement.
fields.Caption 2: A building under construction, showing the frame behind the curtain wall
fields.Caption 3: Curtain walls are also used on residential structures
fields.Caption 4: Oriel Chambers

fields.Name: Post and lintel
fields.Description: The simplest structural system: two uprights carrying a horizontal member across the gap between them.
fields.Notes: Trabeated construction; Stonehenge and the Greek temple both work this way, and it cannot span far in stone.
fields.Caption 1: Stonehenge, an example of Neolithic architecture post and lintel construction, Wiltshire, England
fields.Caption 2: Post-and-lintel construction in the Airavatesvara Temple
fields.Caption 3: Leinster House in Dublin retains column-shaped pilasters under a pediment for aesthetic reasons

fields.Name: Corbel
fields.Description: A block projecting from a wall to carry weight, or a series of such blocks each oversailing the one below to close a gap.
fields.Notes: Corbelled construction predates the true arch; the Treasury of Atreus is roofed this way.
fields.Caption 1: Carved stone corbel under a balcony
fields.Caption 2: Corbels under a balcony
fields.Caption 3: Carved corbel beside a doorway

fields.Name: Machicolation
fields.Description: A floor opening in a projecting parapet through which defenders could drop missiles on attackers at the wall's foot.
fields.Notes: Carried on corbels; a standard feature of the later medieval castle.
fields.Caption 2: 15th-century machicolations of Craigmillar Castle
fields.Caption 3: Machicolation at Cahir Castle, Ireland

fields.Name: Crenellation
fields.Description: A parapet notched into alternating raised blocks and gaps, giving cover and openings to shoot through.
fields.Notes: The raised parts are merlons, the gaps embrasures; battlements in ordinary speech.
fields.Caption 2: Battlements on the Great Wall of China
fields.Caption 3: Crenellated battlements of Bodiam Castle, England

fields.Name: Rustication
fields.Description: Masonry cut with deeply recessed joints and often a roughened face, used to give a lower storey weight and severity.
fields.Notes: A Renaissance palace device; the Palazzo Medici Riccardi grades it from rough to smooth as it rises.
fields.Caption 2: Rusticated stone blocks
fields.Caption 3: Two different styles of rustication in the Palazzo Medici-Riccardi
fields.Caption 4: Rusticated ground floor of the Palazzo Medici Riccardi, Florence

fields.Name: Quoin
fields.Description: The dressed stones at the external corner of a building, usually larger and of contrasting texture to the wall.
fields.Notes: Both structural reinforcement and decoration.
fields.Caption 1: Quoins at the corner of a house
fields.Caption 2: Porch quoins of the Palazzo Giusti
fields.Caption 3: Rustic quoins and keystone on the main entrance to the Palazzo Giusti

fields.Name: Mullion
fields.Description: A slender upright bar dividing a window into separate lights.
fields.Notes: The horizontal equivalent is a transom.
fields.Caption 1: A bifora: a two-light window divided by a central mullion
fields.Caption 2: A mullioned window in the church of San Francesco of Lodi
fields.Caption 3: A window mullion at St Mary's Church, Fertagh, Ireland

fields.Name: Tracery
fields.Description: The stone framework of intersecting ribs holding the glass in the upper part of a Gothic window.
fields.Notes: Plate tracery is pierced from a solid panel; bar tracery is assembled from moulded stone.
fields.Caption 1: Plate tracery in the north rose window of Laon Cathedral
fields.Caption 2: Plate tracery in the Dean's Eye rose window of Lincoln Cathedral (c. 1225)
fields.Caption 3: Window tracery of a Gothic cathedral in Kraków

fields.Name: Rose window
fields.Description: A large circular opening filled with radiating tracery and stained glass, usually over a church's main door or transept ends.
fields.Notes: Notre-Dame de Paris and Chartres have the most celebrated.
fields.Caption 1: The north rose of Notre-Dame de Paris
fields.Caption 2: Exterior of the rose at Strasbourg Cathedral
fields.Caption 3: Interior of the rose at Strasbourg Cathedral

fields.Name: Hypostyle hall
fields.Description: An interior whose roof rests on rows of columns spread across the whole floor, so the space is a forest of supports.
fields.Notes: The Great Hall at Karnak is the largest; the plan also governs the early congregational mosque.
fields.Caption 2: Brick-vaulted hypostyle prayer hall on tiled piers
fields.Caption 3: Design of the Great Hypostyle Hall constructed around c. 1290–1224 BCE

fields.Name: Iwan
fields.Description: A rectangular hall walled on three sides and opening through a great arch on the fourth.
fields.Notes: The four-part plan built around these is the classic Persian madrasa and mosque arrangement.
fields.Caption 2: An iwan at Hatra
fields.Caption 3: Taq-e Bostan

fields.Name: Muqarnas
fields.Description: A honeycomb of small niche-like cells stepped out one above another to make a transition between wall and dome.
fields.Notes: Stalactite vaulting; the Alhambra's Hall of the Two Sisters is the showpiece.
fields.Caption 1: The muqarnas hood of a Seljuk portal
fields.Caption 2: Muqarnas seen from below in the entrance iwan of the Shah Mosque (17th century), Isfahan
fields.Caption 3: Muqarnas dome in the Hall of the Two Sisters, Alhambra (14th century), Granada

fields.Name: Minaret
fields.Description: The slender tower attached to a mosque from which the call to prayer is given.
fields.Notes: The spiral one at Samarra and the pencil-thin Ottoman pairs are the extremes of the type.
fields.Caption 1: Minaret of the Great Mosque of Kairouan
fields.Caption 2: The spiral Malwiya Minaret, Great Mosque of Samarra, Iraq
fields.Caption 3: The pencil-thin minarets of the Blue Mosque, Istanbul, Turkey

fields.Name: Mihrab
fields.Description: The niche in a mosque wall marking the direction of Mecca.
fields.Notes: Set in the qibla wall and usually the most richly decorated element in the building.
fields.Caption 1: Mihrab of the Great Mosque of Córdoba
fields.Caption 2: Mihrab in the Prophet's Mosque
fields.Caption 3: 8th-century marble mihrab from the al-Khassaki Mosque, now in the Iraq Museum

fields.Name: Stupa
fields.Description: A solid hemispherical mound raised over relics, circled by worshippers on a processional path.
fields.Notes: Sanchi is the great surviving example; the form develops into the pagoda further east.
fields.Caption 2: Stupa at Samye Monastery
fields.Caption 3: Shwedagon Pagoda, Yangon

fields.Name: Torii
fields.Description: The freestanding gateway of two uprights and two crossbars that marks the entrance to a Shinto shrine.
fields.Notes: The one at Itsukushima stands in the water.
fields.Caption 1: The torii of Itsukushima Shrine, standing in the water
fields.Caption 2: Buddhist goddess Benzaiten, a torii visible on her head
fields.Caption 3: Torana gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, a possible forerunner of the torii

fields.Name: Ziggurat
fields.Description: A stepped tower of receding rectangular terraces raised as a temple platform in ancient Mesopotamia.
fields.Notes: The one at Ur is the best preserved; approached by monumental stairs rather than internal rooms.
fields.Caption 2: Reconstructed façade and stairway of the Ziggurat of Ur, c. 2100 BCE, Iraq
fields.Caption 3: Reconstruction drawing of the White Temple on its platform (3500–3000 BCE)

fields.Name: Peristyle
fields.Description: A continuous row of columns surrounding a building or enclosing a courtyard.
fields.Notes: The colonnade around a Greek temple's cella, or around the open court of a Roman house.
fields.Caption 1: A peristyle courtyard with its surviving columns
fields.Caption 2: Reconstruction of a Roman peristyle around a courtyard
fields.Caption 3: Peristyle in Diocletian's Palace

fields.Name: Atrium
fields.Description: The central top-lit court of a Roman house, open to the sky over a basin that caught rainwater.
fields.Notes: The basin is the impluvium; in modern usage, any tall glazed internal court.
fields.Caption 1: A modern multi-storey atrium, lit from a glazed roof
fields.Caption 2: Atrium with its impluvium in a Roman house
fields.Caption 3: The atrium of the House of the Small Fountain, Pompeii

fields.Name: Loggia
fields.Description: A gallery or room open to the air on at least one side, its openings formed by an arcade or colonnade.
fields.Notes: Often on an upper storey; the Loggia dei Lanzi in Florence is a public example.
fields.Caption 2: Renaissance loggia of Poznań Town Hall

fields.Name: Portico
fields.Description: A roofed porch carried on columns, forming the entrance front of a building.
fields.Notes: Named by column count: tetrastyle for four, hexastyle for six, octastyle for eight.
fields.Caption 2: Temple of Portunus
fields.Caption 3: The hexastyle Temple of Concord at Agrigentum (c. 430 BCE)

fields.Name: Colonnade
fields.Description: A continuous line of columns carrying an entablature or a run of arches.
fields.Notes: Gian Lorenzo Bernini's oval embrace of Saint Peter's Square is the grandest.
fields.Caption 2: A colonnade of Corinthian columns
fields.Caption 3: Luxor Temple
fields.Caption 4: The colonnaded street of Palmyra from the hills

fields.Name: Cupola
fields.Description: A small crowning structure, usually domed, set on a roof or on top of a larger dome as a lantern.
fields.Notes: Frequently glazed to light the space below.
fields.Caption 1: Cupolas on the towers of Montefiascone Cathedral
fields.Caption 2: Domed kiosk crowning a minaret of the Tomb of Jahangir
fields.Caption 3: Brunelleschi's dome of Florence Cathedral

fields.Name: Ogee arch
fields.Description: A pointed opening whose two sides each reverse curvature, concave above and convex below, meeting in a slender point.
fields.Notes: A Venetian Gothic and Decorated English signature.
fields.Caption 1: Sedilia under three ogee arches, St Andrew's Church, Pickworth, 14th century
fields.Caption 2: The ogee curve: two S-curves meeting in a point
fields.Caption 3: A piscina under an ogee arch, St Peter's Church, Easington

fields.Name: Horseshoe arch
fields.Description: An opening whose curve continues past the half-circle so that it narrows again before reaching the springing.
fields.Notes: Ubiquitous in Moorish Spain; the Great Mosque of Córdoba stripes them in red and white.
fields.Caption 1: Horseshoe arches in the Palace of Ardashir (3rd century CE), in which the springers of the arches
fields.Caption 2: Horseshoe arches in the Umayyad palace at the Citadel of Amman (early 8th century, partially restored)
fields.Caption 3: A horseshoe arch in the Church of Saint Jacob

fields.Name: Gargoyle
fields.Description: A carved waterspout projecting from a roofline, throwing rainwater clear of the wall through its open mouth.
fields.Notes: A carved figure with no spout is properly a grotesque.
fields.Caption 1: A gargoyle on the Auberge de France
fields.Caption 2: Gargoyles of Notre-Dame de Paris
fields.Caption 3: Dragon-headed gargoyle of the Tallinn Town Hall

fields.Name: Volute
fields.Description: A spiral scroll ornament, most familiar in pairs on either side of an Ionic capital.
fields.Notes: Also used singly as a Baroque device linking a nave clerestory to lower side chapels.
fields.Caption 1: Volute on the steps of San Bieito de Fefiñáns
fields.Caption 2: Examples of Ionic volutes
fields.Caption 3: The volutes of an Ionic capital, Erechtheion

fields.Name: Stylobate
fields.Description: The uppermost step of the platform on which a Greek temple's columns stand.
fields.Notes: The Parthenon's curves upward slightly at the centre to correct the eye.
fields.Caption 1: Triple-stepped crepidoma with stylobate at top, in the Doric Temple of Segesta
fields.Caption 2: The stylobate blocks of the Old Athena Temple beside the Parthenon, Athens
fields.Caption 3: The steps and stylobate of the Parthenon, Athens

fields.Name: Cella
fields.Description: The enclosed inner chamber of a classical temple, housing the cult statue.
fields.Notes: The naos in Greek usage; ringed by the peristyle in a peripteral temple.
fields.Caption 2: Greek Temple of Apollo at Paestum with centrally located cella
fields.Caption 3: The Maison Carrée at Nîmes with its cella offset behind the hexastyle portico

fields.Name: Baldachin
fields.Description: A canopy on columns raised over an altar, throne or tomb.
fields.Notes: Gian Lorenzo Bernini's twisted bronze one over the tomb of Saint Peter is the most celebrated.
fields.Caption 2: Enthroned Virgin Mary with cloth of honour by Hans Memling
fields.Caption 3: Louis XIV's state bed in the Chambre du Roi

fields.Name: Cloister
fields.Description: A covered walk enclosing a rectangular open court, arcaded toward the garth and attached to a monastic church.
fields.Notes: The circulation spine of a monastery, linking church, chapter house, and refectory.
fields.Caption 1: Small cloister of the Certosa di Pavia
fields.Caption 2: The cloister (1240) at Salisbury Cathedral
fields.Caption 3: The Cloisters (1351–77) at Gloucester Cathedral

fields.Name: Campanile
fields.Description: A bell tower, in Italian practice usually built free-standing beside a church rather than attached to it.
fields.Notes: The one at Pisa is the leaning example; Giotto's stands beside Florence Cathedral.
fields.Caption 2: The Giralda, bell tower of Seville Cathedral
fields.Caption 3: Bell tower of Dürnstein Abbey
fields.Caption 4: Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben) from the dome on Methodist Central Hall

fields.Name: Crypt
fields.Description: A vaulted chamber wholly or partly below the floor of a church, generally holding tombs or relics.
fields.Notes: Often the oldest surviving fabric of a rebuilt church.
fields.Caption 1: Crypt of Henry the Lion, Brunswick Cathedral
fields.Caption 2: A crypt at Wola Gułowska
fields.Caption 3: A 17th-century crypt found in 1911

fields.Name: Coffer
fields.Description: A sunken rectangular or polygonal panel in a ceiling or the underside of a dome.
fields.Notes: Lightens the structure as well as decorating it; the Pantheon's dome is stepped in five rings of them.
fields.Caption 1: Coffered ceiling of the Pantheon (126 CE), Rome
fields.Caption 2: Gothic coffered ceiling with carved human heads at Wawel Castle (Kraków)
fields.Caption 3: Coffered vault of the Arch of Titus

fields.Name: Dentil
fields.Description: A small rectangular block, one of a closely set row under a cornice, resembling a line of teeth.
fields.Notes: An Ionic and Corinthian enrichment taken up throughout classical revivals.
fields.Caption 2: Close-up of dentils above a Corinthian capital
fields.Caption 3: Long view of same

fields.Name: Acanthus
fields.Description: The deeply cut, spiny-leaved plant form carved in two tiers around a Corinthian capital.
fields.Notes: The single most persistent ornament in Western architecture.
fields.Caption 2: Timeline of acanthus styles: a) Greek; b) Roman; c) Byzantine; d) Romanesque
fields.Caption 3: Acanthus mollis leaf

fields.Name: Rococo
fields.Description: A light, asymmetric, and playful late phase of Baroque decoration, worked in pale colours, gilt, shellwork, and scrolling curves.
fields.Notes: Centred on French interiors of the early 18th century; the Amalienburg and the Wieskirche are high points.
fields.Caption 1: The Salon de la Princesse in the Hôtel de Soubise
fields.Caption 2: François de Cuvilliés, the Hall of Mirrors in the Amalienburg, Munich, 1734–1739
fields.Caption 3: Dominikus Zimmermann, the Wieskirche, Bavaria, 1745–1754

fields.Name: Art Nouveau
fields.Description: A turn-of-the-century decorative manner built on whiplash curves and forms taken from stems, tendrils, and insect wings.
fields.Notes: Hector Guimard's Paris Métro entrances and Victor Horta's Brussels houses are landmarks; called Jugendstil in Germany and Modernisme in Catalonia.
fields.Caption 2: Hector Guimard's entrance to the Abbesses Métro station, Paris
fields.Caption 3: Victor Horta's staircase in the Hôtel Tassel, Brussels (1893)

fields.Name: Art Deco
fields.Description: An interwar style of stepped, streamlined, and geometric ornament in rich materials, at once machine-age and luxurious.
fields.Notes: Named from the 1925 Paris exposition; the Chrysler Building is its skyscraper.
fields.Caption 2: Art Deco hotels on Ocean Drive, Miami Beach
fields.Caption 3: The Eastern Columbia Building, Los Angeles (1930), in turquoise terracotta

fields.Name: Brutalism
fields.Description: A postwar manner of massive, blocky forms in raw board-marked concrete, with structure and services left frankly visible.
fields.Notes: From beton brut, raw concrete; the Barbican and Boston City Hall are characteristic.
fields.Caption 2: Teresa Carreño Cultural Complex
fields.Caption 3: The Barbican Estate, London (1965–1976), by Chamberlin, Powell and Bon
fields.Caption 4: Boston City Hall (1968), by Kallmann McKinnell & Knowles

fields.Name: Deconstructivism
fields.Description: A late-century approach fragmenting a building into skewed, colliding, and apparently unstable forms.
fields.Notes: Named after the 1988 show at the MoMA, whose seven exhibitors were Frank Gehry, Zaha Hadid, Daniel Libeskind, Rem Koolhaas, Peter Eisenman, Bernard Tschumi, and Coop Himmelb(l)au.
fields.Caption 1: Hysolar Institute, University of Stuttgart (Behnisch & Partner), 1987–89
fields.Caption 2: Olivetti Valentine typewriter (1969) by Ettore Sottsass
fields.Caption 3: The Wotruba Church (1976)

fields.Name: Postmodernism
fields.Description: A reaction against modernist severity that brought back ornament, colour, historical quotation, and wit.
fields.Notes: Robert Venturi answered Mies's 'less is more' with 'less is a bore'; the Portland Building and the Piazza d'Italia are landmarks.
fields.Caption 2: Robert Venturi's Vanna Venturi House (1964), Philadelphia
fields.Caption 3: Charles Moore's Piazza d'Italia (1978), New Orleans
fields.Caption 4: Robert Venturi's Guild House (1965)

fields.Name: International Style
fields.Description: The interwar modern manner of rectilinear volumes, unbroken glazed skins, white or neutral surfaces, and no applied ornament.
fields.Notes: Named by Henry-Russell Hitchcock and Philip Johnson for their 1932 exhibition at the MoMA.
fields.Caption 1: Tower C of Place de Ville
fields.Caption 2: Equitable Building, Atlanta
fields.Caption 3: The PSFS Building (Loews Philadelphia Hotel) in 1985

fields.Name: Bauhaus
fields.Description: The functional, unornamented idiom of the German school that fused craft with industrial design.
fields.Notes: Founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919; the school moved to Dessau, then Berlin, and was closed in 1933.
fields.Caption 1: The Dessau school building from the air
fields.Caption 2: The studio wing, with its balconies
fields.Caption 3: Marcel Breuer's tubular-steel Wassily chairs in the Dessau building

fields.Name: Beaux-Arts
fields.Description: A grand academic classicism of symmetrical planning, paired columns, sculptural enrichment, and monumental stairs.
fields.Notes: Taught in Paris and exported to America; Grand Central Terminal and the Paris Opera belong to it.
fields.Caption 1: Grand Central Terminal, New York City
fields.Caption 2: Façade of the Petit Palais
fields.Caption 3: Grand Staircase of the Palais Garnier, Paris
fields.Caption 4: The CEC Palace at night

fields.Name: Palladianism
fields.Description: A strict revival of the calm symmetry, temple porticoes, and harmonic proportion of a 16th-century Veneto architect.
fields.Notes: Spread by the Quattro Libri; Chiswick House and Monticello descend from it.
fields.Caption 2: Palladio's Villa Godi, 1537–42

fields.Name: Mannerism
fields.Description: A 16th-century style, named for the Italian maniera, that used classical elements in deliberately unorthodox ways to create tension and ambiguity.
fields.Notes: Giulio Romano's Palazzo Te lets its triglyphs slip out of place; Michelangelo's Laurentian Library vestibule and staircase is the other great example.
fields.Caption 2: Villa Farnese, Caprarola
fields.Caption 3: Michelangelo's Laurentian Library vestibule, Florence

fields.Name: Gothic Revival
fields.Description: A 19th-century return to pointed arches, tracery, and medieval silhouette, often argued on moral as well as visual grounds.
fields.Notes: Augustus Pugin and John Ruskin were its advocates; the Palace of Westminster and Saint Pancras are its monuments.
fields.Caption 2: Sint-Petrus-en-Pauluskerk (1899–1908), Ostend
fields.Caption 3: The Cathedral of St. John the Baptist, Savannah, Georgia
fields.Caption 4: Palace of Westminster, London

fields.Name: Prairie School
fields.Description: An early American modern manner of low horizontal masses, broad sheltering eaves, and open flowing interiors.
fields.Notes: Wright's Robie House is the definitive statement.
fields.Caption 2: Harold C. Bradley House, by Louis Sullivan and George Grant Elmslie

fields.Name: Chicago School
fields.Description: The commercial idiom of the first steel-framed towers, with broad tripartite windows and ornament confined to the frame.
fields.Notes: Louis Sullivan's “form follows function” is its motto; Daniel Burnham, John Wellborn Root, and William Le Baron Jenney were the other principals.
fields.Caption 2: The Chicago Building by Holabird & Roche (1904–1905)
fields.Caption 3: The steel frame of the Fisher Building (1895–96)

fields.Name: Constructivism
fields.Description: An early Soviet manner of exposed structural frames, dynamic diagonals, and forms derived from industry.
fields.Notes: Vladimir Tatlin's unbuilt tower for the Third International is its emblem.
fields.Caption 1: Vladimir Tatlin, Monument to the Third International (Tatlin's Tower), 1919
fields.Caption 2: Print shop of Ogonyok magazine, designed by El Lissitzky

fields.Name: De Stijl
fields.Description: A Dutch movement composing buildings from sliding rectangular planes in primary colours with black and white.
fields.Notes: The Rietveld Schröder House is the only full architectural realization.
fields.Caption 2: Café De Unie (J. J. P. Oud, 1925; rebuilt 1986)

fields.Name: Metabolism
fields.Description: A Japanese postwar movement conceiving buildings as organisms of replaceable plug-in parts capable of growth.
fields.Notes: Kisho Kurokawa's Nakagin Capsule Tower (1972, demolished 2022) was the built demonstration.
fields.Caption 1: The Nakagin Capsule Tower displayed small apartment units (capsules) attached to a central building core
fields.Caption 2: Kikutake used a photo of Marina City to illustrate the idea of capsules plugged onto a central tower
fields.Caption 3: Urban master plan of Skopje 1963

fields.Name: High-tech
fields.Description: A manner that treats structure and services as the architecture, putting ducts, lifts, and bracing on the outside.
fields.Notes: The Centre Pompidou and Lloyd's of London; also called structural expressionism.
fields.Caption 2: John Hancock Center, Chicago
fields.Caption 3: Aachen University Hospital (1985)

fields.Name: Organic architecture
fields.Description: An approach seeking a building continuous with its site and unified in all its parts, growing from the ground rather than set on it.
fields.Notes: Wright's term; Fallingwater over its waterfall is the argument in built form.
fields.Caption 1: Fallingwater by Frank Lloyd Wright, Mill Run, Pennsylvania
fields.Caption 2: Försters Weinterrassen by Udo Heimermann (2000)
