fields.Caption 3: Exposed bedrock at the Rådhuset metro station

fields.Name: Streamline Moderne
fields.Description: A late phase of interwar design favouring curved corners, long horizontal lines, and nautical rails, as if shaped by wind.
fields.Notes: Diners, cinemas, and ocean liners; a stripped, aerodynamic descendant of Art Deco.

fields.Name: Romanesque Revival
fields.Description: A 19th-century return to round arches, heavy rusticated walls, and squat towers.
fields.Notes: Henry Hobson Richardson's Trinity Church in Boston gave the American version his name, Richardsonian Romanesque.
fields.Caption 1: South face of the Garrison Church
fields.Caption 2: The Smithsonian Institution Building
fields.Caption 3: H. H. Richardson's Trinity Church (1872–77)

fields.Name: Greek Revival
fields.Description: An early 19th-century manner reproducing the temple front, with plain Doric or Ionic porticoes and low pediments.
fields.Notes: The style of banks, courthouses, and state capitols across the young United States.
fields.Caption 2: Brandenburg Gate (1791), Berlin

fields.Name: Second Empire
fields.Description: A mid 19th-century French manner recognized at once by its steep double-pitched roof with dormers.
fields.Notes: The mansard roof is named for François Mansart; the New Louvre wings built under Napoleon III set the pattern, and Philadelphia City Hall is a large American example.
fields.Caption 2: The Opéra Garnier (1862–1875)
fields.Caption 3: Philadelphia City Hall (1871–1901)

fields.Name: Queen Anne
fields.Description: A late Victorian domestic manner of asymmetric plans, turrets, wrap-around porches, and mixed wall textures.
fields.Notes: Has little to do with the actual reign of Queen Anne; Richard Norman Shaw popularized it in Britain.
fields.Caption 1: Winslow Hall (1700), possibly by Christopher Wren
fields.Caption 2: Hanbury Hall (c. 1706)

fields.Name: Arts and Crafts
fields.Description: A movement rejecting industrial production for handwork, honest materials, and vernacular building traditions.
fields.Notes: William Morris and Philip Webb's Red House is the founding building; John Ruskin supplied the argument.
fields.Caption 2: William Morris, Artichoke embroidered panel, designed 1877
fields.Caption 3: William Morris's design for Trellis wallpaper, 1862
fields.Caption 4: Pugin's house, The Grange (1843)

fields.Name: Expressionism
fields.Description: An early 20th-century manner of distorted, sculptural, and often crystalline forms charged with emotion.
fields.Notes: Erich Mendelsohn's Einstein Tower in Potsdam and Hans Poelzig's Grosses Schauspielhaus in Berlin are its key buildings.

fields.Name: Neo-futurism
fields.Description: A contemporary manner of sweeping curved shells and continuous flowing surfaces, made possible by computer modelling.
fields.Notes: Santiago Calatrava's City of Arts and Sciences in Valencia and Zaha Hadid's Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku are typical.
fields.Caption 1: Great Court of the British Museum (2000)
fields.Caption 2: Futuroscope
fields.Caption 3: Nanjing International Youth Cultural Centre

fields.Name: Mughal
fields.Description: An Indo-Islamic imperial manner of bulbous domes, cusped arches, pietra dura inlay, and formal water gardens.
fields.Notes: The Taj Mahal, Humayun's Tomb, and Fatehpur Sikri are its monuments; it peaked under Shah Jahan in the 17th century.
fields.Caption 2: Humayun's Tomb, Delhi
fields.Caption 3: Fatehpur Sikri
fields.Caption 4: The Panch Mahal

fields.Name: Ottoman
fields.Description: An imperial Turkish manner of great central domes buttressed by half-domes, with slender pencil minarets.
fields.Notes: Mimar Sinan is its master; the Süleymaniye and the Selimiye at Edirne are his.
fields.Caption 2: Prayer hall of the Green Mosque
fields.Caption 3: Imperial Hall in the Harem of Topkapı Palace

fields.Name: Carolingian
fields.Description: The first medieval revival of Roman building under a Frankish emperor, with westworks and monumental gatehouses.
fields.Notes: The Palatine Chapel at Aachen is the surviving centrepiece.
fields.Caption 1: The Palatine Chapel, now the core of Aachen Cathedral
fields.Caption 2: Lorsch Abbey gatehouse

fields.Name: Norman
fields.Description: The English name for the round-arched, thick-walled manner brought after 1066, with cushion capitals and chevron ornament.
fields.Notes: Durham Cathedral, whose rib vaults anticipate Gothic, is the great example.
fields.Caption 1: The early rib-vaulted interior of Lessay Abbey

fields.Name: Tudor
fields.Description: An English late-medieval domestic manner of exposed timber framing, tall clustered chimneys, and four-centred arches.
fields.Notes: Hampton Court Palace is the grandest survival.
fields.Caption 1: Window of the Senior Combination Room, Magdalene College
fields.Caption 2: Hardwick Hall, an Elizabethan prodigy house
fields.Caption 3: Ormonde Castle

fields.Name: Georgian
fields.Description: A restrained English classicism of symmetrical brick fronts, sash windows in regular bays and a pedimented door.
fields.Notes: Named for the four Georges who reigned from 1714 to 1830; the terraces and squares of Bath and Dublin are its showpieces.
fields.Caption 1: Middle-class house in a cathedral close, with minimal classical detail
fields.Caption 2: The Circus (begun 1754)
fields.Caption 3: Function rules at Massachusetts Hall at Harvard University, 1718–20

fields.Name: Stalinist
fields.Description: A monumental Soviet classicism of tiered, spired towers laden with socialist ornament.
fields.Notes: The Seven Sisters of Moscow; also called Socialist Classicism.
fields.Caption 1: The main building of Moscow State University
fields.Caption 2: Kotelnicheskaya Embankment Building
fields.Caption 3: Hotel Ukraina, one of “Stalin's high-rises”

fields.Name: Vernacular
fields.Description: Building made without architects, from local materials and inherited practice, shaped by climate and use.
fields.Notes: Trulli, yurts, stave churches, and adobe pueblos all belong to it.
fields.Caption 2: A traditional Kinnauri house in the Kath Kuni style
fields.Caption 3: 16th-century half-timbered and later village buildings

fields.Name: Karnak
fields.Description: Vast temple complex at Thebes dedicated chiefly to Amun and built over two thousand years; its Great Hypostyle Hall has 134 columns.
fields.Caption 2: Open papyrus umbel capitals and architrave on the central columns of the Hypostyle Hall

fields.Name: Abu Simbel
fields.Description: Two rock-cut temples of Ramesses II in Nubia, the larger fronted by four colossal seated statues of the king. In the 1960s they were cut into blocks and raised above the rising waters of Lake Nasser.
fields.Caption 2: The temples in 1820, before excavation

fields.Name: Luxor Temple
fields.Description: Egyptian temple on the east bank at Thebes, joined to Karnak by an avenue of sphinxes; one of its two obelisks now stands in the Place de la Concorde.
fields.Caption 2: The colonnade of Amenhotep III's forecourt in ruins, photographed 1870–1888

fields.Name: Ishtar Gate
fields.Description: The glazed-brick northern gate of Babylon, built c. 575 BCE under Nebuchadnezzar II and faced with blue tiles bearing dragons and aurochs. A reconstruction stands in Berlin's Pergamon Museum.
fields.Caption 1: The reconstruction in the Pergamon Museum
fields.Caption 2: One of the mušḫuššu dragons from the gate

fields.Name: Temple of Olympian Zeus
fields.Description: A colossal ruined temple at the centre of Athens, begun in the 6th century BCE and finished under Hadrian some 638 years later. Fifteen of its original 104 Corinthian columns still stand.
fields.Caption 2: Its Corinthian columns

fields.Name: Delphi
fields.Description: The sanctuary of Apollo on the slopes of Mount Parnassus, seat of the Pythia, the oracle consulted across the Greek world, which the Greeks held to be the navel of the world.
fields.Caption 2: The polygonal wall, 1902

fields.Name: Knossos
fields.Description: The Bronze Age palace complex of Minoan Crete, linked with the labyrinth of King Minos; Arthur Evans excavated it and partly rebuilt it in concrete.
fields.Caption 2: The Throne Room, with its gypsum throne and restored griffin frescoes

fields.Name: Hadrian's Wall
fields.Description: A Roman frontier wall of stone and turf about 118 km long across northern Britain, begun in 122 CE, with forts and milecastles along its length.
fields.Caption 2: Surviving sections in the hilly central sector

fields.Name: Arch of Constantine
fields.Description: A triumphal arch beside the Colosseum celebrating Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312, built partly from reliefs taken from monuments of Trajan, Hadrian, and Marcus Aurelius.
fields.Caption 1: South side, from the Via Triumphalis

fields.Name: Great Mosque of Damascus
fields.Description: One of the largest and oldest mosques in the world. Christian and Muslim tradition alike consider it the burial place of John the Baptist's head, a tradition originating in the 6th century.
fields.Caption 2: Remains of an old Roman-era triple doorway in the exterior southern wall of the mosque

fields.Name: Tikal
fields.Description: The ruins of a major Classic Maya city in the rainforest of the Petén Basin in northern Guatemala, whose steep temple-pyramids rise above the canopy.
fields.Caption 2: Temple II above the Great Plaza

fields.Name: King's College Chapel
fields.Description: The chapel of King's College, Cambridge, built in stages from 1446 to 1515; a masterpiece of Perpendicular Gothic with the world's largest fan vault.

fields.Name: Siena Cathedral
fields.Description: Siena's Gothic cathedral, banded in black and white marble, with Nicola Pisano's pulpit and an inlaid marble floor. A vast planned extension was abandoned after the Black Death of 1348.
fields.Caption 2: Floor plan

fields.Name: Palazzo Medici Riccardi
fields.Description: The Medici family's Florentine palace, whose rusticated walls grow smoother storey by storey; its chapel holds Benozzo Gozzoli's Procession of the Magi.
fields.Caption 2: Michelangelo's “kneeling windows”, a feature later copied by the Medici at their Palazzo Pitti

fields.Name: Il Gesù
fields.Alternate: Chiesa del Santissimo Nome di Gesù (Church of the Most Holy Name of Jesus)
fields.Description: The mother church of the Jesuits in Rome. Its wide single nave and two-storey façade became the model for Counter-Reformation churches.
fields.Architect: Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola (plan and interior); Giacomo della Porta (façade)
fields.Caption 2: The ceiling fresco and dome

fields.Name: Trevi Fountain
fields.Description: Rome's largest fountain, an 18th-century Baroque work: Oceanus rides a shell chariot drawn by two sea horses, one calm and one wild.
fields.Caption 2: The fountain in a photochrom print, about 1890–1900

fields.Name: Spanish Steps
fields.Description: A stairway of 135 steps linking the Piazza di Spagna to Trinità dei Monti, built 1723–25 with a French bequest; it widens and narrows in terraces.
fields.Caption 2: The site before the construction of the stairs in a late 17th century engraving by Giovanni Battista Falda

fields.Name: Les Invalides
fields.Description: Louis XIV's hospital and home for old soldiers, whose gilded Dôme church holds Napoleon's tomb; it now houses the Musée de l'Armée.
fields.Architect: Jules Hardouin-Mansart (Église du Dôme); Libéral Bruant (hospital)
fields.Caption 2: Hardouin-Mansart's plan of the complex (about 1700)

fields.Name: Palais Garnier
fields.Description: Second Empire opera house built for Napoleon III, with a grand staircase, a Chagall ceiling, and the underground lake of The Phantom of the Opera.
fields.Caption 2: The auditorium, under Chagall's 1964 ceiling

fields.Name: Alcázar of Seville
fields.Alternate: Real Alcázar de Sevilla (Royal Alcázar of Seville)
fields.Description: A royal palace built over the Islamic-era citadel of Seville, centred on Pedro I's 14th-century Mudéjar palace; its upper floors are still a royal residence.
fields.Caption 2: The Sala de las Bóvedas preserves elements of Alfonso X's Gothic palace (13th century)

fields.Name: Belém Tower
fields.Description: Manueline fortress in the Tagus at Lisbon, ceremonial gateway for the Portuguese navigators, carved with ropes, armillary spheres, and a rhinoceros.
fields.Caption 2: The tower

fields.Name: Schönbrunn Palace
fields.Description: The Habsburgs' summer palace in Vienna, rebuilt for Maria Theresa, with 1,441 rooms, a formal park, and the oldest zoo in the world.
fields.Architect: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach; Nicolò Pacassi
fields.Caption 2: Schönbrunn from the main entrance

fields.Name: Einstein Tower
fields.Description: Erich Mendelsohn's Expressionist observatory on the Telegrafenberg in Potsdam, built to house a solar telescope for testing Einstein's theory of relativity.
fields.Caption 1: The observatory ensemble on the Telegrafenberg
fields.Caption 2: A rear view of Erich Mendelsohn's Einstein Tower

fields.Name: Berliner Philharmonie
fields.Description: Tent-like concert hall whose terraced “vineyard” seating surrounds the orchestra; home of the Berlin Philharmonic.
fields.Caption 1: The concert hall and chamber music hall
fields.Caption 2: Handel's Judas Maccabaeus performed by the Kulturbund Deutscher Juden orchestra

fields.Name: Winter Palace
fields.Description: The tsars' Baroque winter residence on the Neva, stormed by the Bolsheviks in 1917 and now part of the Hermitage Museum.
fields.Caption 2: The south façade on Palace Square

fields.Name: Moscow Kremlin
fields.Description: A fortified complex at the historic centre of the Russian capital, walled in red brick with twenty towers, enclosing five palaces and four cathedrals and overlooking Red Square.
fields.Architect: Pietro Antonio Solari; Marco Ruffo; Aristotile Fioravanti; Aloisio da Milano
fields.Caption 1: The south wall and its towers above the Moskva River, with the Grand Kremlin Palace and the cathedrals behind
fields.Caption 2: The Grand Kremlin Palace, the Ivan the Great Bell Tower, and the cathedrals above the wall

fields.Name: Hermitage Museum
fields.Description: One of the largest art museums in the world, housed in the Winter Palace of the tsars in Saint Petersburg; it began in 1764 when Catherine the Great bought a collection of paintings from Berlin.
fields.Caption 2: A marble hall with crystal chandeliers, inside the museum

fields.Name: Royal Pavilion
fields.Description: The Prince Regent's seaside palace in Brighton, given onion domes and minarets in an Indo-Saracenic style outside and chinoiserie within.
fields.Caption 1: The domes and minarets from the lawn

fields.Name: Woolworth Building
fields.Description: Terracotta-clad Gothic Revival skyscraper, the “Cathedral of Commerce” and the tallest building in the world from 1913 to 1930.
fields.Caption 2: The tower rising above lower Manhattan

fields.Name: Lever House
fields.Description: A 24-storey glass curtain-wall office tower on Park Avenue, raised above a public plaza; one of the first International Style skyscrapers in New York, designed at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill.
fields.Caption 2: The columns on Park Avenue

fields.Name: Brooklyn Bridge
fields.Description: A suspension bridge over the East River between Manhattan and Brooklyn, with the world's longest suspension span when it opened in 1883; completed by Washington Roebling and Emily Warren Roebling after the designer's death.
fields.Caption 2: An approach ramp to the Brooklyn Bridge, seen from Brooklyn

fields.Name: Statue of Liberty
fields.Description: A colossal neoclassical copper figure of Libertas on Liberty Island, a gift from France in 1886; her tablet is inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI, and a broken chain lies at her feet.
fields.Architect: Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi (sculptor); Gustave Eiffel (iron framework); Richard Morris Hunt (pedestal)
fields.Caption 2: Liberty Island, with Lower Manhattan behind

fields.Name: Home Insurance Building
fields.Description: Ten-storey Chicago office block often called the first skyscraper for its load-bearing metal frame; demolished in 1931.
fields.Caption 1: A colour postcard of c. 1910, after two storeys were added (its printed title removed)
fields.Caption 2: A drawing of its iron and steel skeleton frame

fields.Name: Marina City
fields.Description: Twin corncob towers of scalloped balconies over spiralling car parks, a city within a city on the Chicago River.
fields.Caption 1: The twin “corncob” towers on the river

fields.Name: S. R. Crown Hall
fields.Description: A steel and glass pavilion on the Illinois Institute of Technology campus, its roof hung beneath four exposed plate girders so that the whole interior is one room without a single column.
fields.Caption 2: The entrance as seen from the south

fields.Name: Yale Center for British Art
fields.Description: Louis Kahn's last building, completed after his death in 1974: a concrete frame infilled with matte stainless-steel panels and glass around two skylit courts.
fields.Caption 2: Fourth floor lobby

fields.Name: Rotunda, University of Virginia
fields.Description: Thomas Jefferson's domed library at the head of the Lawn, a half-scale adaptation of the Pantheon in Rome and the centre of his “Academical Village”; gutted by fire in 1895 and rebuilt by Stanford White as one open interior, it was restored to Jefferson's three-storey plan for the 1976 Bicentennial.
fields.Caption 2: The Dome Room, the library beneath the dome

fields.Name: White House
fields.Description: The US president's residence at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, home to every president since John Adams; burned by the British in 1814 and rebuilt.
fields.Caption 2: Aerial view with Pennsylvania Avenue, closed to traffic, in the foreground

fields.Name: Washington Monument
fields.Description: A marble obelisk whose stone changes colour about a third of the way up, where building stopped for more than twenty years; at about 169 m it was the world's tallest structure until the Eiffel Tower in 1889.
fields.Architect: Robert Mills; Thomas Lincoln Casey Sr.
fields.Caption 2: The obelisk on the National Mall, from the air

fields.Name: Vietnam Veterans Memorial
fields.Description: Maya Lin's V-shaped wall of black granite in Washington, D.C., sunk into the ground and inscribed with the names of more than 58,000 Americans killed or missing in the war.
fields.Caption 1: Names etched into the granite face
fields.Caption 2: Aerial view of the memorial wall

fields.Name: Walt Disney Concert Hall
fields.Description: Frank Gehry's concert hall in downtown Los Angeles, opened in 2003 as the home of the Los Angeles Philharmonic and wrapped in curving stainless-steel panels.
fields.Caption 2: The curving stainless-steel panels

fields.Name: HSBC Building
fields.Description: The Hong Kong headquarters of HSBC, its floors hung from suspension trusses between steel masts so that the interior is free of columns, facing Statue Square.
fields.Caption 2: The atrium, looking up through the suspended floors

fields.Name: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque
fields.Description: Abu Dhabi's national mosque, with 82 white marble domes, one of the world's largest hand-knotted carpets and room for more than 40,000 worshippers.

fields.Name: Palácio da Alvorada
fields.Description: The Brazilian president's residence in Brasília, a glass box behind a veranda of slender curved columns on Paranoá Lake.
fields.Caption 2: Under construction, 1957–58

fields.Name: Sainte Marie de La Tourette
fields.Description: Concrete Dominican priory on a slope near Lyon, raised on pilotis around a cloister, with window mullions spaced in musical rhythms.
fields.Architect: Le Corbusier; Iannis Xenakis; André Wogenscky
fields.Caption 2: The convent raised on pilotis over the falling ground

fields.Name: Villa Tugendhat
fields.Description: A functionalist house of 1930 in Brno; its open main floor is divided only by a freestanding onyx wall and a curved ebony screen, and glass panes lower into the floor.
fields.Architect: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe; Lilly Reich (interior design)
fields.Caption 2: The terrace under the upper floor

fields.Name: Rietveld Schröder House
fields.Description: Built in 1924 for a widow who asked for a house with no walls. The upper floor is a single open space that sliding panels divide as needed, and the exterior is composed of intersecting planes, lines, and primary colours.
fields.Caption 2: Architectural model, ca 1985

fields.Name: Djinguereber Mosque
fields.Description: Timbuktu's great mud-brick mosque, built in 1327 for Mansa Musa after his pilgrimage to Mecca; one of the three mosques of the scholarly “University of Timbuktu”.
fields.Caption 2: Outside the mosque

fields.Name: Palmyra
fields.Description: Caravan city in the Syrian desert with a great colonnaded street and the Temple of Bel, ruled by Queen Zenobia; the Islamic State blew up the temple in 2015.
fields.Caption 2: Ruins beneath the desert hills at sunset

fields.Name: Baalbek
fields.Description: Roman temple complex at Heliopolis in Lebanon's Beqaa Valley: the vast Temple of Jupiter, set on some of the largest cut stones ever used, and the well-preserved Temple of Bacchus.
fields.Caption 1: On the photo I am standing at the front of the Bacchus temple for size comparison
fields.Caption 2: The Umayyad Mosque of Baalbek

fields.Name: Masada
fields.Description: Herod's fortress palace on a desert plateau above the Dead Sea, where Jewish rebels held out against Rome until 73 or 74 CE
fields.Caption 2: A caldarium (hot room) in northern Roman-style public bath (#35 on plan)

fields.Name: Western Wall
fields.Description: The surviving retaining wall of Herod's expansion of the Temple Mount and Judaism's holiest place of prayer; its lowest courses are huge Herodian blocks.
fields.Caption 2: The plaza below the Temple Mount and the Dome of the Rock

fields.Name: Al-Aqsa Mosque
fields.Description: The congregational mosque at the southern end of the Temple Mount (Haram al-Sharif) in Jerusalem, first built under the Umayyads and rebuilt after earthquakes; Islam's third-holiest site.
fields.Caption 2: The mosque

fields.Name: Kaaba
fields.Description: The cube-shaped shrine at the centre of the Great Mosque of Mecca, draped in the black kiswa; Muslims everywhere pray toward it.

fields.Name: Casa del Fascio
fields.Alternate: House of the Fascio, Casa del Popolo (House of the People)
fields.Description: Giuseppe Terragni's Fascist party headquarters in Como, a half-cube of white marble and glass whose ground-floor doors opened the lobby onto the square; the landmark of Italian Rationalism.
fields.Caption 2: The Palazzo Littorio of Montevarchi

fields.Name: Imhotep
fields.Description: Egyptian chancellor to King Djoser, traditionally the architect of the Step Pyramid of Djoser and high priest of Ra at Heliopolis.
fields.Works: Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara (the first monumental building in dressed stone)
fields.Caption 2: The step pyramid of Djoser
fields.Caption 3: Ernest Board, An Invocation to I-em-hetep

fields.Name: Ictinus
fields.Description: Athenian architect of the Parthenon with Callicrates, and of the Temple of Apollo at Bassae, which held the earliest known Corinthian capital.
fields.Works: Parthenon; Temple of Apollo Epicurius in Bassae
fields.Caption 1: Depiction of Ictinus and Callicrates on the façade of the historical building of the University of Athens
fields.Caption 2: The Parthenon, Athens (447–432 BCE), west front

fields.Name: Filippo Brunelleschi
fields.Description: Italian Renaissance architect who engineered the double-shelled dome of Florence Cathedral and rediscovered linear perspective.
fields.Works: Dome of Florence Cathedral; Ospedale degli Innocenti (Hospital of the Innocents); Pazzi Chapel; San Lorenzo; Santo Spirito
fields.Caption 1: Brunelleschi as portrayed by Masaccio in the Brancacci Chapel
fields.Caption 2: Santa Maria del Fiore towering above the city, Florence
fields.Caption 3: Silver figure of a seated saint, attributed to Brunelleschi

fields.Name: Leon Battista Alberti
fields.Description: Renaissance humanist whose treatise De re aedificatoria revived Vitruvius, and who adapted the Roman triumphal arch to church façades.
fields.Works: Sant'Andrea (Mantua); Santa Maria Novella façade; Palazzo Rucellai (Rucellai Palace); Tempio Malatestiano (Malatesta Temple)
fields.Caption 2: Palazzo Rucellai, Florence
fields.Caption 3: Tempio Malatestiano

fields.Name: Donato Bramante
fields.Description: An Italian architect and painter who introduced Renaissance architecture to Milan and the High Renaissance style to Rome, where his centrally planned design for St. Peter's Basilica became the basis of everything built there afterwards.
fields.Works: Tempietto; Santa Maria presso San Satiro; Saint Peter's Basilica (original plan); Belvedere Courtyard
fields.Caption 1: Bramante on a medal attributed to Caradosso, about 1506
fields.Caption 2: Tempietto of San Pietro in Montorio, Rome
fields.Caption 3: Bramante's ground plan and sections for St. Peter's

fields.Name: Andrea Palladio
fields.Description: Renaissance architect of villas and churches in the Veneto whose Four Books of Architecture (1570) spread temple-fronted classicism across Europe and America.
fields.Works: Villa La Rotonda (Villa Capra); San Giorgio Maggiore; Il Redentore (Church of the Redeemer); Basilica Palladiana; Teatro Olimpico (Olympic Theatre)
fields.Caption 2: Villa La Rotonda, Vicenza
fields.Caption 3: San Giorgio Maggiore, Venice

fields.Name: Giulio Romano
fields.Description: An Italian painter and architect. He was a pupil of Raphael, and his stylistic deviations from High Renaissance classicism help define the sixteenth-century style known as Mannerism.
fields.Works: Palazzo del Te; Sala dei Giganti (Hall of the Giants) frescoes; his own house in Mantua
fields.Caption 2: Palazzo del Te
fields.Caption 3: Fall of the Giants

fields.Name: Gian Lorenzo Bernini
fields.Description: The leading sculptor of Roman Baroque, who as architect framed Saint Peter's Square with its oval colonnade and designed Sant'Andrea al Quirinale.
fields.Works: Saint Peter's Square colonnade; Baldacchino (canopy) of Saint Peter's; Sant'Andrea al Quirinale; Scala Regia (Royal Staircase)
fields.Caption 2: The colonnade enclosing Saint Peter's Square, 1656–1667
fields.Caption 3: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, Rome, 1658–1670

fields.Name: Francesco Borromini
fields.Description: Roman Baroque architect of complex geometric plans and undulating façades, and Gian Lorenzo Bernini's great rival.
fields.Works: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane; Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza; Sant'Agnese in Agone (façade); Palazzo Spada colonnade
fields.Caption 2: Sant'Agnese in Agone

fields.Name: Carlo Maderno
fields.Description: An Italian architect from Ticino who carried Roman building out of Mannerism into the early Baroque, and who added the long nave and the façade to St. Peter's Basilica.
fields.Works: Saint Peter's Basilica (nave and façade); Santa Susanna; Palazzo Barberini

fields.Name: Christopher Wren
fields.Description: English architect and astronomer who rebuilt London's churches after the Great Fire of 1666, above all St Paul's Cathedral.
fields.Works: <u>St Paul's Cathedral</u>; Royal Hospital Chelsea; Greenwich Hospital; Sheldonian Theatre; St Stephen Walbrook
fields.Caption 2: St Paul's Cathedral, London
fields.Caption 3: Old Royal Naval College

fields.Name: Inigo Jones
fields.Description: The first English architect to build in the Palladian classical style: the Queen's House, Greenwich, and the Banqueting House, Whitehall.
fields.Works: Queen's House (Greenwich); Banqueting House (Whitehall); St Paul's Church (Covent Garden); Queen's Chapel
fields.Caption 1: Inigo Jones, after Anthony van Dyck
fields.Caption 2: Bust of Inigo Jones by John Michael Rysbrack, 1725

fields.Name: Nicholas Hawksmoor
fields.Description: A leading architect of the English Baroque and Christopher Wren's assistant. Designed six London churches including Christ Church, Spitalfields, and worked with John Vanbrugh on Castle Howard and Blenheim Palace.
fields.Works: St Alfege Church (Greenwich); St George's (Bloomsbury); St George in the East; St Mary Woolnoth
fields.Caption 1: King William Block (1699–1702), Greenwich Hospital, west façade

fields.Name: John Vanbrugh
fields.Description: English Baroque architect and Restoration playwright (The Relapse) who designed Castle Howard and Blenheim Palace with Nicholas Hawksmoor.
fields.Works: <u>Blenheim Palace</u>; Castle Howard; Seaton Delaval Hall
fields.Caption 2: Sketch of the Bastille, where Vanbrugh was imprisoned

fields.Name: Robert Adam
fields.Description: Scottish neoclassical architect and interior designer of delicate Roman-inspired stucco rooms, as at Syon House and Kedleston Hall.
fields.Works: Syon House; Lansdowne House; Culzean Castle; Kedleston Hall
fields.Caption 2: Edinburgh from Calton Hill, c. 1865–95

fields.Name: Jules Hardouin-Mansart
fields.Description: Louis XIV's First Architect, who enlarged Versailles with the Hall of Mirrors and designed the Dôme des Invalides and the Place Vendôme.
fields.Works: Palace of Versailles (Hall of Mirrors); Dôme des Invalides (Les Invalides); Place Vendôme; Grand Trianon

fields.Name: Louis Le Vau
fields.Description: French Baroque architect of Vaux-le-Vicomte and the Hôtel Lambert, whose work for the Sun King began the transformation of Versailles.
fields.Works: Château de Meudon; Palace of Versailles; Château du Raincy; Vaux-le-Vicomte
fields.Caption 1: The Collège des Quatre-Nations (now the Institut de France), Paris, in an engraving
fields.Caption 2: Palace of Versailles

fields.Name: Claude Perrault
fields.Description: French physician and amateur architect credited with the colonnaded east front of the Louvre; he also designed the Paris Observatory and translated Vitruvius.
fields.Works: <u>Louvre Colonnade</u>; Paris Observatory
fields.Caption 2: Louvre Colonnade

fields.Name: Étienne-Louis Boullée
fields.Description: French visionary neoclassicist of vast, mostly unbuilt geometric designs, above all a hollow sphere to honour Isaac Newton.
fields.Works: Cenotaph for Newton (unbuilt); Hôtel Alexandre (Paris)
fields.Caption 2: Cénotaphe à Newton (1784)

fields.Name: Claude-Nicolas Ledoux
fields.Description: French Neoclassical visionary behind the Royal Saltworks at Arc-et-Senans and the toll-gates of Paris.
fields.Works: Royal Saltworks at Arc-et-Senans; Rotonde de la Villette (Paris); Hôtel d'Hallwyl
fields.Caption 2: Madame du Barry, for whom Ledoux designed a Music Pavilion at her Château de Louveciennes
fields.Caption 3: Plan view of the facilities

fields.Name: Karl Friedrich Schinkel
fields.Description: A Prussian architect, city planner, and painter who also designed furniture and stage sets. His most famous buildings are found in and around Berlin, where he influenced the city's design and landscape profoundly.
fields.Works: Altes Museum (Old Museum); Schauspielhaus (Konzerthaus Berlin); Neue Wache (New Guardhouse); Bauakademie (Building Academy)
fields.Caption 1: Karl Friedrich Schinkel, Castle by the River, 1820
fields.Caption 2: Franz Ludwig Catel, Schinkel in Naples, 1824
fields.Caption 3: Floor plan of the proposed Orianda Palace

fields.Name: Gustave Eiffel
fields.Description: French engineer whose firm built the Garabit Viaduct, the iron frame inside the Statue of Liberty, and the tower for the 1889 Paris Exposition.
fields.Works: <u>Eiffel Tower</u>; Garabit Viaduct; Statue of Liberty (iron framework); Maria Pia Bridge
fields.Caption 2: The Budapest Nyugati railway station

fields.Name: Joseph Paxton
fields.Description: English gardener and engineer who designed the Crystal Palace for the Great Exhibition of 1851.
fields.Works: <u>Crystal Palace</u>; Great Conservatory at Chatsworth; Mentmore Towers
fields.Caption 1: Portrait of Paxton in The Illustrated London News, 1865

fields.Name: Augustus Pugin
fields.Description: English Gothic Revival designer and polemicist (Contrasts) who designed the interiors and clock tower of the Palace of Westminster.
fields.Works: <u>Palace of Westminster</u>; St Giles' Catholic Church (Cheadle); The Grange (Ramsgate)
fields.Caption 1: The Grange, designed by Pugin as his family home
fields.Caption 2: The Palace of Westminster, London, with Charles Barry (1840–70)

fields.Name: William Morris
fields.Description: English designer, poet, and socialist who led the Arts and Crafts movement; his firm made textiles and wallpapers such as Strawberry Thief.
fields.Works: Red House (with Philip Webb); Strawberry Thief; Kelmscott Press
fields.Caption 1: Water House, Morris's childhood home, now the William Morris Gallery
fields.Caption 2: King Arthur and Sir Lancelot, stained glass by Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co.
fields.Caption 3: Queen Guenevere and Isoude les Blanches Mains, stained glass, 1862

fields.Name: Antoni Gaudí
fields.Description: Catalan Modernista of organic curves and broken-tile mosaic (trencadís), whose Barcelona works include Casa Batlló, Casa Milà, Park Güell, and the unfinished Sagrada Família.
fields.Works: Sagrada Família; Casa Milà (La Pedrera); Casa Batlló; Park Güell
fields.Caption 1: Portrait photograph of Antoni Gaudí i Cornet
fields.Caption 2: El Mas de la Calderera, the Gaudí family home
fields.Caption 3: The Sagrada Família, Barcelona, begun 1882, and still unfinished

fields.Name: Victor Horta
fields.Description: Belgian founder of Art Nouveau architecture, whose Hôtel Tassel in Brussels (1893) is its first full expression.
fields.Works: Hôtel Tassel; Hôtel Solvay; Hôtel van Eetvelde; House & Atelier Horta
fields.Caption 2: Hôtel Solvay

fields.Name: Hector Guimard
fields.Description: French Art Nouveau architect best known for the cast-iron Paris Métro entrances.
fields.Works: Castel Béranger; Paris Métro entrances; Hôtel Guimard
fields.Caption 2: Castel Béranger
fields.Caption 3: Paris Metro entrances by Hector Guimard

fields.Name: Otto Wagner
fields.Description: Viennese architect and teacher who led the move from historicism to modernism: the Stadtbahn stations, the Majolica House, and the Postal Savings Bank.
fields.Works: Austrian Postal Savings Bank; Majolica House; Karlsplatz Stadtbahn station; Kirche am Steinhof (Church of St Leopold)
fields.Caption 1: Façade of the Rumbach Street Synagogue
fields.Caption 2: Interior of the Rumbach Street Synagogue
fields.Caption 3: Ceiling detail of the Rumbach Street Synagogue

fields.Name: Josef Hoffmann
fields.Description: A founder of the Vienna Secession and of the Wiener Werkstätte, whose Palais Stoclet in Brussels is a total work of art in marble and gold.
fields.Works: Sanatorium Purkersdorf; Stoclet Palace
fields.Caption 1: Overdoor relief designed for the Secession building foyer, 1902
fields.Caption 2: The 1902 Beethoven Exhibition at the Vienna Secession, installation designed by Hoffmann

fields.Name: Adolf Loos
fields.Description: Viennese modernist whose essay Ornament and Crime (1908) attacked applied decoration; designed houses around the Raumplan, a plan of interlocking levels.
fields.Works: Looshaus (Michaelerplatz, Vienna); Villa Müller; Steiner House; American Bar (Vienna)
fields.Caption 2: American Bar

fields.Name: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
fields.Description: Glasgow designer of an austere Art Nouveau: the Glasgow School of Art, the Willow Tearooms, and tall high-backed chairs.
fields.Works: Willow Tearooms; <u>Glasgow School of Art</u>; Queen's Cross Church; Scotland Street School Museum
fields.Caption 1: Mackintosh in a study by Francis Newbery for a group portrait of the Glasgow School of Art’s building committee
fields.Caption 2: The Glasgow School of Art (1897–1909), the entrance on Renfrew Street
fields.Caption 3: Design for a stencilled mural decoration for the Willow Tearooms (1896–1897)

fields.Name: Louis Sullivan
fields.Description: American architect called the “father of skyscrapers”, who coined “form follows function”.
fields.Works: <u>Wainwright Building</u>; Guaranty Building; Carson Pirie Scott Building; Auditorium Building
fields.Caption 2: Prudential Building

fields.Name: Daniel Burnham
fields.Description: Chicago architect and planner who directed the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition and wrote the 1909 Plan of Chicago; his firm built the Flatiron and Reliance Buildings.
fields.Works: Washington Union Station; <u>Flatiron Building</u>; Reliance Building; Ellicott Square Building
fields.Caption 2: Childhood home
fields.Caption 3: The Montauk Building, c. 1886

fields.Name: William Le Baron Jenney
fields.Description: Chicago engineer and architect of the Home Insurance Building (1885), often called the first skyscraper for its load-bearing metal frame.
fields.Works: <u>Home Insurance Building</u>
fields.Caption 2: House designed for Walter Cass Newberry (1889)
fields.Caption 3: Second Leiter Building, photographed in 1963

fields.Name: Henry Hobson Richardson
fields.Description: American architect of massive round-arched stone buildings, in a Romanesque Revival later named after him: Trinity Church in Boston and the Marshall Field Wholesale Store.
fields.Works: Trinity Church (Boston); Marshall Field Wholesale Store; Allegheny County Courthouse
fields.Caption 1: Trinity Church (1872), Richardson's most acclaimed early work
fields.Caption 2: The Thomas Crane Public Library (Quincy, Massachusetts)

fields.Name: Frank Lloyd Wright
fields.Description: American architect of the Prairie style and organic architecture, designer of Fallingwater, the Robie House, and the spiral Guggenheim Museum.
fields.Works: <u>Fallingwater</u>; Robie House; Guggenheim Museum; Unity Temple; Johnson Wax Headquarters; Taliesin West
fields.Caption 1: Portrait photograph of Frank Lloyd Wright
fields.Caption 2: His home and studio (1889)
fields.Caption 3: The Walter Gale House (1893)

fields.Name: Le Corbusier
fields.Description: Swiss-born French pioneer of modernism, author of the Five Points of architecture and Towards an Architecture, who planned the capital of Punjab at Chandigarh.
fields.Works: Villa Savoye; Unité d'Habitation (Marseille); Notre-Dame du Haut (Ronchamp); Chandigarh Capitol Complex
fields.Caption 2: Villa Savoye, Poissy
fields.Caption 3: Unité d'habitation

fields.Name: Walter Gropius
fields.Description: German founder and first director of the Bauhaus, whose Fagus Factory and Dessau school building made the glass curtain wall a modernist signature; he later taught at Harvard.
fields.Works: Bauhaus Dessau; Fagus Factory; Pan Am Building
fields.Caption 2: The Fagus Factory, Alfeld (1911–1913), designed with Adolf Meyer
fields.Caption 3: Monument to the March Dead (1921)

fields.Name: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
fields.Description: German-American modernist, last director of the Bauhaus, whose steel-and-glass buildings — the Barcelona Pavilion, Farnsworth House, Seagram Building — followed “less is more”.
fields.Works: <u>Barcelona Pavilion</u>; Farnsworth House; Seagram Building; S. R. Crown Hall
fields.Caption 1: Mies in 1934, in a portrait by Hugo Erfurth
fields.Caption 2: The Farnsworth House (1951), Plano, Illinois
fields.Caption 3: The Seagram Building (1958), with Philip Johnson, New York City
fields.Caption 4: The Barcelona Pavilion, built for the 1929 International Exposition

fields.Name: Marcel Breuer
fields.Description: Hungarian-born Bauhaus designer of the tubular-steel Wassily chair who became an American Brutalist, designing the Whitney Museum on Madison Avenue.
fields.Works: Whitney Museum (Madison Avenue); Saint John's Abbey Church; UNESCO Headquarters (Paris); Wassily Chair
fields.Caption 1: The Isokon building, where Breuer lived in the 1930s

fields.Name: Gerrit Rietveld
fields.Description: A Dutch furniture designer and architect of De Stijl. Designed the Red and Blue Chair and the Schröder House in Utrecht (1924).
fields.Works: <u>Rietveld Schröder House</u>; Red and Blue Chair; Zig-Zag Chair; Van Gogh Museum
fields.Caption 2: Red and Blue Chair

fields.Name: Alvar Aalto
fields.Description: Finnish modernist of warm, organic buildings in brick and timber such as the Paimio Sanatorium and Finlandia Hall; also designed bent-plywood furniture and the Savoy vase.
fields.Works: Vyborg Library; Finlandia Hall; Baker House; <u>Paimio Sanatorium</u>
fields.Caption 2: Exterior of Aalto's studio (1954-56)
fields.Caption 3: Interior of the studio

fields.Name: Eero Saarinen
fields.Description: Finnish-American architect of expressive shells and the Tulip chair: the TWA Flight Center and the Gateway Arch in St. Louis.
fields.Works: <u>Gateway Arch</u>; TWA Flight Center; Ingalls Rink; Dulles Airport terminal; Tulip chair
fields.Caption 2: Gateway Arch, St. Louis
fields.Caption 3: TWA Flight Center, New York City

fields.Name: Eliel Saarinen
fields.Description: Finnish architect of the National Romantic Helsinki Central Station, whose second-placed 1922 Chicago Tribune design shaped Art Deco skyscrapers; later head of Cranbrook.
fields.Works: <u>Helsinki Central Station</u>; Cranbrook Academy of Art; Christ Church Lutheran (Minneapolis)
fields.Caption 2: Christ Church Lutheran

fields.Name: Louis Kahn
fields.Description: Estonian-born American architect of monumental, light-filled masonry and concrete: the Salk Institute, the Kimbell Art Museum, and the National Assembly in Dhaka.
fields.Works: <u>Salk Institute</u>; Kimbell Art Museum; National Assembly of Bangladesh; Yale Center for British Art
fields.Caption 2: Louis Kahn's Salk Institute, La Jolla
fields.Caption 3: Kimbell Art Museum (1966–1972), Fort Worth

fields.Name: Philip Johnson
fields.Description: American architect of the Glass House (1949) and later postmodern towers; the first winner of the Pritzker Prize.
fields.Works: Glass House; Seagram Building (with Mies); AT& T Building (550 Madison Avenue); Crystal Cathedral
fields.Caption 2: The Glass House, New Canaan, Connecticut
fields.Caption 3: The AT&T Building (now 550 Madison Avenue), New York City (1984), with its broken pediment

fields.Name: Oscar Niemeyer
fields.Description: Brazilian modernist of sculptural reinforced concrete who designed the civic buildings of Brasília.
fields.Works: Cathedral of Brasília; National Congress of Brazil; Palácio da Alvorada (Palace of the Dawn); Niterói Contemporary Art Museum; Church of Saint Francis of Assisi (Pampulha)
fields.Caption 2: Cathedral of Brasília
fields.Caption 3: Palácio da Alvorada, Brasília

fields.Name: Kenzo Tange
fields.Description: Japanese modernist who designed Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Park and mentored the Metabolists; his Yoyogi National Gymnasium hangs its roof from cables.
fields.Works: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum; Yoyogi National Gymnasium; St. Mary's Cathedral (Tokyo); Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building
fields.Caption 1: Tange visiting the construction site of his own house
fields.Caption 2: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, view along the axis (1955)

fields.Name: Tadao Ando
fields.Description: Self-taught Japanese architect of smooth exposed concrete and light, whose Church of the Light slits its altar wall with a cross; Pritzker Prize 1995.
fields.Works: <u>Church of the Light</u>; Row House in Sumiyoshi; Water Temple (Honpuku-ji); Pulitzer Arts Foundation
fields.Caption 1: Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth, showing the restaurant
fields.Caption 2: Table of Pirosmani
fields.Caption 3: Blue Rose in the Cube study, Armani/Silos exhibition (2019)

fields.Name: Toyo Ito
fields.Description: Japanese architect of light, “conceptual” buildings joining the physical and virtual, above all the Sendai Mediatheque.
fields.Works: Hotel Porta Fira; National Stadium; Sendai Mediatheque
fields.Caption 2: Sendai Mediatheque (2001)

fields.Name: Kisho Kurokawa
fields.Description: Japanese founder of Metabolism, whose Nakagin Capsule Tower (1972) plugged replaceable living pods onto concrete cores.
fields.Works: Nakagin Capsule Tower; Kuala Lumpur International Airport; National Art Center (Tokyo)
fields.Caption 2: The National Art Center

fields.Name: Arata Isozaki
fields.Description: Japanese architect who moved from Metabolism to a postmodern classicism; designed the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles and the Palau Sant Jordi; Pritzker Prize 2019.
fields.Works: Museum of Contemporary Art (Los Angeles); Palau Sant Jordi; Ōita Prefectural Library; Team Disney Building (Orlando)
fields.Caption 2: Palau Sant Jordi

fields.Name: Kengo Kuma
fields.Description: Japanese architect who wraps buildings in slats of timber, bamboo, and stone, as at the Japan National Stadium for the Tokyo Olympics and V&A Dundee.
fields.Works: Japan National Stadium; Nezu Museum; V& A Dundee
fields.Caption 2: M2 Building (1991)
fields.Caption 3: V&A Dundee, 2018

fields.Name: Kazuyo Sejima
fields.Description: Japanese architect who founded SANAA with Ryue Nishizawa in 1995; their light, white, transparent buildings won the Pritzker Prize in 2010.
fields.Works: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art (Kanazawa); New Museum (New York); Rolex Learning Center; Louvre-Lens
fields.Caption 2: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa

fields.Name: Robert Venturi
fields.Description: American postmodernist who wrote Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture and answered “less is more” with “less is a bore”.
fields.Works: Vanna Venturi House; Guild House; Sainsbury Wing (National Gallery; London)

fields.Name: Denise Scott Brown
fields.Description: American architect and theorist who wrote Learning from Las Vegas with Robert Venturi and Steven Izenour and was a partner in their firm.
fields.Works: Learning from Las Vegas; Sainsbury Wing (National Gallery; London); Allen Memorial Art Museum addition
fields.Caption 1: Denise Scott Brown on her 81st birthday

fields.Name: Michael Graves
fields.Description: An American postmodern architect, member of the New York Five, and the Memphis Group. Designed the Portland Building and the Humana Building, and household objects for Alessi and Target.
fields.Works: Portland Building; Humana Building; Team Disney Building (Burbank); Walt Disney World Swan and Dolphin
fields.Caption 2: Walt Disney World Dolphin

fields.Name: Carlo Scarpa
fields.Description: Venetian architect of exquisite detailing who reworked historic buildings, above all the Castelvecchio Museum in Verona, and designed the Brion tomb at San Vito d'Altivole.
fields.Works: Castelvecchio Museum; Brion Cemetery; Olivetti Showroom (Venice); Fondazione Querini Stampalia
fields.Caption 2: Brion tomb

fields.Name: Renzo Piano
fields.Description: Italian architect of the Centre Pompidou (with Richard Rogers), The Shard in London, and Kansai International Airport.
fields.Works: The Shard; Kansai International Airport; Stadio San Nicola (San Nicola Stadium); Intesa Sanpaolo Building
fields.Caption 2: The Menil Collection
fields.Caption 3: The Menil Collection's covered walkway

fields.Name: Richard Rogers
fields.Description: British high-tech architect of the Centre Pompidou, with Renzo Piano, and of Lloyd's of London, both wearing their services outside; Pritzker Prize 2007.
fields.Works: Centre Pompidou; Lloyd's building; Millennium Dome; Madrid–Barajas Airport Terminal 4
fields.Caption 1: The atrium of the Lloyd's building, London (1986)

fields.Name: Norman Foster
fields.Description: English pioneer of high-tech architecture: the HSBC Building in Hong Kong, the Reichstag dome, and 30 St Mary Axe (the “Gherkin”).
fields.Works: <u>30 St Mary Axe</u>; HSBC Building (Hong Kong); Reichstag dome; Millau Viaduct; Apple Park
fields.Caption 1: Sir Norman Foster at the inauguration ceremony of Dresden's refurbished central railway station
fields.Caption 2: The HSBC Main Building
fields.Caption 3: The Century Tower, built in 1991

fields.Name: Zaha Hadid
fields.Description: Iraqi-British architect of flowing, deconstructivist forms such as the Heydar Aliyev Center; the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize (2004).
fields.Works: London Aquatics Centre; <u>Heydar Aliyev Cultural Center</u>; Guangzhou Opera House; Contemporary Arts Center
fields.Caption 1: Zaha Hadid at the Heydar Aliyev Center (2013)
fields.Caption 2: Vitra Fire Station, Weil am Rhein (1993)
fields.Caption 3: Bergisel Ski Jump (2002)

fields.Name: Rem Koolhaas
fields.Description: Dutch architect and theorist, founder of OMA, and author of Delirious New York; designed the CCTV Headquarters in Beijing.
fields.Works: CCTV Headquarters; Seattle Central Library; Kunsthal (Rotterdam); Casa da Música (House of Music) (Porto); Maison à Bordeaux (Bordeaux House)

fields.Name: Frank Gehry
fields.Description: Canadian-American deconstructivist of crumpled titanium and steel forms: the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, the Walt Disney Concert Hall and his own remodelled house in Santa Monica.
fields.Works: <u>Guggenheim Museum Bilbao</u>; Walt Disney Concert Hall; Dancing House; Fondation Louis Vuitton; Gehry Residence
fields.Caption 2: His own house in Santa Monica
fields.Caption 3: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (1997)
fields.Caption 4: Walt Disney Concert Hall, Los Angeles (2003)

fields.Name: Daniel Libeskind
fields.Description: Polish-American deconstructivist of the zigzag Jewish Museum Berlin and master planner of the rebuilt World Trade Center site.
fields.Works: Jewish Museum Berlin; Felix Nussbaum Haus; Royal Ontario Museum (Michael Lee-Chin Crystal); Imperial War Museum North
fields.Caption 2: Felix Nussbaum Haus (1998)
fields.Caption 3: Addition to the Royal Ontario Museum (2007)

fields.Name: Peter Eisenman
fields.Description: An American architect of the New York Five and a leading deconstructivist. Designed the Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus and the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe in Berlin.
fields.Works: Wexner Center for the Arts; <u>Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe</u>; City of Culture of Galicia; State Farm Stadium
fields.Caption 1: What happened to the architectural manifesto?
fields.Caption 2: The Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe
fields.Caption 3: Another view of the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe

fields.Name: Bernard Tschumi
fields.Description: Swiss-French deconstructivist whose Parc de la Villette in Paris scatters red steel follies across a grid; also designed the New Acropolis Museum.
fields.Works: Parc de la Villette; Acropolis Museum; Le Fresnoy
fields.Caption 2: A red folie in the Parc de la Villette, Paris (1982–98)

fields.Name: Santiago Calatrava
fields.Description: Spanish-Swiss architect and engineer of white, skeletal bridges, stations, and museums modelled on living forms, such as the City of Arts and Sciences in Valencia.
fields.Works: City of Arts and Sciences; Milwaukee Art Museum (Quadracci Pavilion); World Trade Center Transportation Hub; Turning Torso
fields.Caption 2: The underground shops at the railway stations

fields.Name: Jean Nouvel
fields.Description: French architect of the Institut du Monde Arabe, with light-sensitive mashrabiya panels, and the Louvre Abu Dhabi.
fields.Works: Quartier 207; Tour bleue (Blue Tower); Cologne Tower; Torre Glòries (Agbar Tower)
fields.Caption 2: Torre Glòries

fields.Name: Álvaro Siza
fields.Description: Portuguese modernist of white, site-sensitive buildings, from the Leça swimming pools to the Serralves museum; Pritzker Prize 1992.
fields.Works: Leça Swimming Pools; Porto School of Architecture; Serralves Museum; Boa Nova Tea House
fields.Caption 2: “Bonjour Tristesse” apartment block
fields.Caption 3: Faculty of Architecture of the University of Porto

fields.Name: Luis Barragán
fields.Description: A Mexican architect of walls in saturated pink, yellow, and violet, and the second winner of the Pritzker Prize (1980). Designed his own house and studio in Mexico City, the Cuadra San Cristóbal and, with Mathias Goeritz, the Torres de Satélite.
fields.Works: Casa Luis Barragán; Cuadra San Cristóbal (San Cristóbal Stables); Torres de Satélite (Satellite Towers)

fields.Caption 2: A fountain wall designed by Barragán
fields.Caption 3: The indoor pool of Casa Gilardi

fields.Name: César Pelli
fields.Description: Argentine-American architect of some of the world's tallest buildings, including the Petronas Towers.
fields.Works: Petronas Towers; One Canada Square; World Financial Center (Brookfield Place); Salesforce Tower
fields.Caption 1: César Pelli with Argentine president Cristina Fernández
fields.Caption 2: Pacific Design Center, Red Building (2013)
fields.Caption 3: Pacific Design Center, Green Building (1988)

fields.Name: I. M. Pei
fields.Description: Chinese-American architect of the Louvre Pyramid, the National Gallery's East Building, and Hong Kong's Bank of China Tower; Pritzker Prize 1983.
fields.Works: <u>Louvre Pyramid</u>; East Building of the National Gallery of Art; Bank of China Tower; Museum of Islamic Art (Doha)
fields.Caption 2: The East Building of the National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C. (1978)
fields.Caption 3: The Bank of China Tower, Hong Kong (1990)

fields.Name: Minoru Yamasaki
fields.Description: American architect of the original World Trade Center and the Pruitt-Igoe housing project, and with Edward Durell Stone the leading practitioner of New Formalism.
fields.Works: BOK Tower; <u>World Trade Center</u>; McGregor Memorial Conference Center; Pruitt–Igoe (St Louis)
fields.Caption 2: Pruitt–Igoe housing project (1954; demolished 1972–1976)
fields.Caption 3: Northwestern National Life Building (1965)

fields.Name: Buckminster Fuller
fields.Description: American inventor and futurist who popularized the geodesic dome (the Montreal Biosphère) and coined “Spaceship Earth”.
fields.Works: Montreal Biosphère; Nine Chains to the Moon; Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth; Critical Path
fields.Caption 2: Dymaxion map

fields.Name: Moshe Safdie
fields.Description: Israeli-Canadian architect whose student thesis became Habitat 67 in Montreal; he later designed Marina Bay Sands in Singapore.
fields.Works: <u>Habitat 67</u>; Marina Bay Sands; National Gallery of Canada; Yad Vashem Holocaust History Museum
fields.Caption 2: Jewel Changi Airport (2019)

fields.Name: Balkrishna Doshi
fields.Description: An Indian architect who worked with Le Corbusier and Louis Kahn, and the first Indian winner of the Pritzker Prize (2018). Designed the Indian Institute of Management Bangalore, the Aranya low-cost housing in Indore and his own studio, Sangath.
fields.Works: Sangath; Indian Institute of Management Bangalore; Aranya Low Cost Housing; Amdavad ni Gufa (Gufa, Ahmedabad)
fields.Caption 2: Doshi with Le Corbusier at the unfinished Shodhan House, c. 1955
fields.Caption 3: C. K. Mehta presenting the Dhirubhai Thakar Savyasachi Saraswat Award to Doshi

fields.Name: Charles Correa
fields.Description: Indian modernist who fitted building to climate and culture: the Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya, the Kanchanjunga Apartments, and the Jawahar Kala Kendra.
fields.Works: Jawahar Kala Kendra; Kanchanjunga Apartments; Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya; Navi Mumbai plan
fields.Caption 1: Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalay at Sabarmati Ashram
fields.Caption 2: Madhyapradesh Legislative Assembly

fields.Name: Francis Kéré
fields.Description: A Burkinabé-German architect, recognized for creating innovative works that are often sustainable and collaborative in nature. In 2022, he became the first native African to receive the Pritzker Architecture Prize.
fields.Works: Gando Primary School; Serpentine Pavilion (2017); Benin National Assembly
fields.Caption 2: Gando Primary School

fields.Name: David Adjaye
fields.Description: Ghanaian-British architect of the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington; the first African winner of the RIBA Royal Gold Medal (2021).
fields.Works: Skolkovo Moscow School of Management; National Museum of African American History and Culture
fields.Caption 2: Winter Park Library & Events Center

fields.Name: Peter Zumthor
fields.Description: Swiss architect of a few meticulous, material-led buildings in stone, timber, and concrete; Pritzker Prize 2009.
fields.Works: Therme Vals (Vals Thermal Baths); Bruder Klaus Field Chapel; Kolumba Museum (Cologne); Kunsthaus Bregenz (Bregenz Art Museum)
fields.Caption 2: Therme Vals

fields.Name: Glenn Murcutt
fields.Description: Australian architect of lightweight, climate-responsive houses in corrugated iron, working alone; Pritzker Prize 2002.
fields.Works: Marika-Alderton House; Magney House; Australian Islamic Centre
fields.Caption 2: Bowali Visitor Centre, designed with Troppo Architects

fields.Name: Lina Bo Bardi
fields.Description: Italian-born Brazilian modernist architect and designer; architect of the São Paulo Museum of Art (MASP), SESC Pompéia and the Glass House.
fields.Works: São Paulo Museum of Art; SESC Pompéia; Glass House (São Paulo)

fields.Name: Eileen Gray
fields.Description: Irish furniture designer and architect, a pioneer of the Modern Movement, best known for the villa E-1027.
fields.Works: <u>Villa E-1027</u>; “Dragons” armchair
fields.Caption 2: “Dragons” armchair

fields.Name: Maya Lin
fields.Description: American designer who, as a Yale undergraduate, won the competition for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial's black granite wall.
fields.Works: <u>Vietnam Veterans Memorial</u>; Civil Rights Memorial (Montgomery); The Women's Table
fields.Caption 1: Maya Lin at the World Economic Forum, 2023
fields.Caption 2: Lin's winning submission for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial design competition
fields.Caption 3: Lin's The Women's Table in front of the Sterling Memorial Library, commemorating the role of women at Yale University

fields.Name: Charles and Ray Eames
fields.Description: An American husband-and-wife design team working across architecture, furniture, graphic design, and film: moulded plywood and fibreglass chairs, Case Study House No. 8 in Pacific Palisades, and the film Powers of Ten.
fields.Works: Eames House; Eames Lounge Chair; LCW chair; Powers of Ten
fields.Caption 2: Moulded plywood leg splint (1941–42)
fields.Caption 3: Stacking chair for children

fields.Name: Richard Neutra
fields.Description: Austrian-American modernist of Southern California whose steel-and-glass houses, such as the Lovell Health House and the Kaufmann Desert House, open onto the landscape.
fields.Works: Kaufmann Desert House; Lovell Health House; VDL Research House
fields.Caption 2: Kaufmann Desert House, Palm Springs
fields.Caption 3: Lovell House

fields.Name: Bjarke Ingels
fields.Description: Danish founder of the firm BIG, known for playful, diagram-driven buildings such as VIA 57 West in New York and CopenHill, a power plant with a ski slope on its roof.
fields.Works: VIA 57 West; CopenHill; 8 House; Mountain Dwellings; VM Houses
fields.Caption 1: Bjarke Ingels at a press conference
fields.Caption 2: Mountain Dwellings

fields.Name: Shigeru Ban
fields.Description: Japanese architect known for innovative work with paper, especially recycled cardboard tubes, for temporary housing for disaster victims.
fields.Works: Centre Pompidou-Metz; Nomadic Museum; Cardboard Cathedral
fields.Caption 2: Takatori Catholic Church (1995), a temporary paper-tube church built after the Great Hanshin earthquake

fields.Name: Paolo Soleri
fields.Description: Italian-American architect who began Arcosanti in the Arizona desert as a prototype of “arcology”, architecture fused with ecology.
fields.Works: Arcosanti; Cosanti

fields.Name: Cass Gilbert
fields.Description: American architect of the Gothic-clad Woolworth Building, once the tallest in the world, the United States Supreme Court Building, and three state capitols.
fields.Works: United States Supreme Court Building; <u>Woolworth Building</u>; Minnesota State Capitol
fields.Caption 2: United States Supreme Court Building
fields.Caption 3: Minnesota State Capitol

fields.Name: Stanford White
fields.Description: Gilded Age architect of the Washington Square Arch and the second Madison Square Garden, on whose roof garden he was shot dead in 1906.
fields.Works: Washington Square Arch; Madison Square Garden (1890); Rosecliff
fields.Caption 2: Rosecliff, a Gilded Age mansion (1898–1902)

fields.Name: Richard Morris Hunt
fields.Description: American Beaux-Arts architect of the Biltmore Estate and the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty.
fields.Works: Biltmore Estate; Statue of Liberty pedestal; Fifth Avenue façade of the Metropolitan Museum of Art
fields.Caption 2: Portrait by John Singer Sargent (1895)

fields.Name: Bertram Goodhue
fields.Description: An American architect celebrated for his work in Gothic Revival and Spanish Colonial Revival design. He also designed notable typefaces, including Cheltenham and Merrymount for the Merrymount Press.
fields.Works: Rockefeller Chapel; Nebraska State Capitol; Los Angeles Central Library; St. Thomas Church (Fifth Avenue)
fields.Caption 1: The California Building, San Diego, for the Panama-California Exposition of 1915
fields.Caption 2: The Panama-California Exposition, Balboa Park, 1915

fields.Name: Ralph Adams Cram
fields.Description: American Gothic Revival architect of churches and campuses, who redesigned the Cathedral of Saint John the Divine in Gothic form.
fields.Works: Cathedral of Saint John the Divine; Princeton University Chapel; Cadet Chapel (West Point)
fields.Caption 2: Princeton University Chapel
fields.Caption 3: Cram and Ferguson Architects

fields.Name: Fazlur Rahman Khan
fields.Description: Bangladeshi-American structural engineer who pioneered skyscraper structural systems; designed the Sears (Willis) Tower and the John Hancock Center.
fields.Works: <u>Willis Tower</u>; John Hancock Center; Hajj Terminal (Jeddah)
fields.Caption 2: John Hancock Center, Chicago

fields.Name: Norman Bel Geddes
fields.Description: American industrial designer of Streamline Moderne, whose Futurama for General Motors at the 1939 New York World's Fair imagined the motorway city.
fields.Works: Futurama (1939 New York World's Fair); Motor Car Number 9; Horizons (book)

fields.Name: John Nash
fields.Description: Regency architect of London's Regent Street and the terraces of Regent's Park, and of the Royal Pavilion at Brighton.
fields.Works: All Souls Church; Langham Place; Clarence House; <u>Royal Pavilion</u>; Marble Arch

fields.Name: Charles Garnier
fields.Description: A French architect of the Second Empire, best known for the Paris Opera (1861–1875) and the Opéra de Monte-Carlo.
fields.Works: Palais Garnier; Nice Observatory
fields.Caption 2: Nice Observatory

fields.Name: Rudolph Schindler
fields.Description: Austrian-born American modernist whose most important houses, including the Kings Road House, were built in Los Angeles.
fields.Works: <u>Schindler House</u>

fields.Name: Sinan
fields.Description: Chief architect of the Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Magnificent and his successors, designer of the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne.
fields.Works: <u>Süleymaniye Mosque</u>; Selimiye Mosque (Edirne); Şehzade Mosque; Mihrimah Sultan Mosque
fields.Caption 1: The Süleymaniye Mosque, Istanbul (1550–1557), from its courtyard
fields.Caption 2: The Selimiye Mosque, Edirne (1568–1575), his masterpiece
fields.Caption 3: Şehzade Mosque

fields.Name: Aldo Rossi
fields.Description: Italian Rationalist and author of The Architecture of the City (1966), who reduced buildings to archetypal forms; Pritzker Prize 1990.
fields.Works: San Cataldo Cemetery; Teatro del Mondo (Theatre of the World); Bonnefanten Museum; Carlo Felice Theatre
fields.Caption 1: Central staircase of the Bonnefanten Museum
fields.Caption 2: San Cataldo Cemetery, Modena (designed 1971)

fields.Name: Geoffrey Bawa
fields.Description: Sri Lankan leader of Tropical Modernism, whose buildings dissolve into landscape and water, from the Kandalama hotel to the island parliament at Kotte.
fields.Works: Sri Lankan Parliament Building; Heritance Kandalama; Lunuganga
fields.Caption 1: Bawa's final resting place on Cinnamon Hill at Lunuganga, his country estate
fields.Caption 2: The backside of the main Bungalow of Lunuganga

fields.Name: Julia Morgan
fields.Description: The first woman licensed as an architect in California, who designed more than 700 buildings there, above all the hilltop estate at San Simeon.
fields.Works: Hearst Castle; Asilomar Conference Grounds; Berkeley City Club
fields.Caption 2: Berkeley City Club

fields.Name: Arcade
fields.Description: A row of arches carried on columns or piers, forming a covered walkway or a decorative band along a wall.
fields.Notes: Blind arcades, with the openings filled in, run along the outside of many Romanesque churches.
fields.Caption 1: Blind arcade on the Norman nave of Ely Cathedral
fields.Caption 2: Superimposed arcades of the Colosseum, Rome
fields.Caption 3: Arcade of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, Tunisia

fields.Name: Buttress
fields.Description: A mass of masonry built against a wall to resist the sideways push of a roof or vault.
fields.Notes: When it stands clear of the wall and is joined to it by an arch, it becomes a flying buttress.
fields.Caption 2: Manic-5 Dam in Quebec, a multiple-arch buttress dam
fields.Caption 3: The massive buttresses along the nave of Exeter Cathedral, Exeter, England

fields.Name: Dome
fields.Description: A hemispherical or rounded roof, in effect an arch rotated around a central vertical axis.
fields.Notes: Rome's Pantheon and Hagia Sophia in Constantinople set the two great Western precedents.
fields.Caption 2: Brunelleschi's dome over Florence Cathedral (1420–36)
fields.Caption 3: The dome of Hagia Sophia, Istanbul (537 CE)
fields.Caption 4: Tiled dome of the Church of the Assumption in Carcaixent, Spain

fields.Name: Arch
fields.Description: A curved structure that spans an opening and carries the load above it as compression down to its supports.
fields.Notes: The Romans made the semicircular arch the basis of their bridges, aqueducts, and vaults.
fields.Caption 1: Semicircular arches of the Pont du Gard, near Nîmes (1st century CE)
fields.Caption 2: The Gateway Arch, St Louis (1965), a weighted catenary arch
fields.Caption 3: Arches of the Roman aqueduct of Segovia, Spain

fields.Name: Column
fields.Description: A vertical, usually round support made up of a base, a shaft, and a capital, carrying the weight above it.
fields.Notes: The Greek orders differ chiefly in the proportions and ornament of the column.
fields.Caption 1: The National Capitol Columns, Washington, D.C.
fields.Caption 2: Columns of the Parliament House in Helsinki
fields.Caption 3: Columns of the Temple of Olympian Zeus, Athens

fields.Name: Capital
fields.Description: The decorated top of a column or pillar, which spreads the load from the beam or arch above onto the shaft.
fields.Notes: Its form is what tells the classical orders apart at a glance.
fields.Caption 1: Doric capital of the Parthenon, Athens
fields.Caption 2: Ionic capital from the Erechtheion, British Museum
fields.Caption 3: Corinthian capital in the Pantheon, Rome

fields.Name: Pier
fields.Description: A heavy vertical support of masonry, square or composite in section, that carries arches or vaults.
fields.Notes: Romanesque and Gothic churches use piers in place of the slender classical column.
fields.Caption 1: Cruciform pier in Wells Cathedral, England
fields.Caption 2: The Pont du Gard (c. 19 BCE): three rows of piers carry the arches, Vers-Pont-du-Gard
fields.Caption 3: Piers of the nave, Durham Cathedral

fields.Name: Nave
fields.Description: The long central body of a church, running from the entrance to the crossing or chancel, where the congregation gathers.
fields.Notes: The word comes from the Latin navis, ship, from the resemblance of the inverted hull to the roof.
fields.Caption 2: The nave of Länna Church, Sweden
fields.Caption 3: The nave of the Santa Monica Parish Church in Sarrat, Philippines

fields.Name: Aisle
fields.Description: A passage running parallel to the main space of a church, separated from it by an arcade or row of piers.
fields.Notes: Aisles make a church wider and let processions and worshippers move without crossing the central space.
fields.Caption 1: An aisle of Bristol Cathedral, England
fields.Caption 2: An aisle of Bath Abbey, England
fields.Caption 3: The north aisle of Salisbury Cathedral

fields.Name: Choir
fields.Description: The part of a church, east of the nave and often screened off, where the clergy and singers sit for the services.
fields.Notes: In cathedrals it is often the most richly furnished part, with carved stalls.
fields.Caption 1: The choir of Bristol Cathedral, seen through the screen
fields.Caption 2: The choir of Palencia Cathedral, Spain
fields.Caption 3: The choir and choir screen of Albi Cathedral, France

fields.Name: Spire
fields.Description: A tall, tapering, pointed structure rising from a tower or roof, usually of a church.
fields.Notes: Salisbury Cathedral's spire, at about 123 metres, is the tallest medieval one in Britain.
fields.Caption 1: Salisbury Cathedral, whose spire (1320) is 123 m high
fields.Caption 2: The Flamboyant north spire of Chartres Cathedral (1513)
fields.Caption 3: Rouen Cathedral, whose spire is the tallest in France

fields.Name: Parapet
fields.Description: A low protective wall along the edge of a roof, balcony, terrace or bridge.
fields.Notes: On castles it was often crenellated to give defenders cover.
fields.Caption 1: Crenellated parapet on a bastion of Kyrenia Castle, Cyprus
fields.Caption 2: Parapet of Henley Bridge, England
fields.Caption 3: A cannon on a fortress parapet

fields.Name: Balustrade
fields.Description: A rail carried on a row of short, shaped posts, used along stairs, balconies, and terraces.
fields.Notes: Renaissance architects made it a standard classical finish for the top of a building.
fields.Caption 1: Stone balusters in the Basilica of San Zeno, Verona
fields.Caption 2: Balustrade along the roofline of the Capitoline Museums, Rome
fields.Caption 3: Balustrades of the Staircase of the Princes, Versailles

fields.Name: Plinth
fields.Description: The square block or slab that forms the lowest part of a column, statue or wall.
fields.Notes: A continuous plinth, or plinth course, also protects the base of a wall from damp.
fields.Caption 1: Monument to Nicholas I in Saint Petersburg, on its plinth
fields.Caption 2: Plinth of the Alexander Column, Saint Petersburg
fields.Caption 3: The empty Fourth Plinth, Trafalgar Square, London

fields.Name: Obelisk
fields.Description: A tall, four-sided monolith that narrows as it rises and ends in a small pyramid.
fields.Notes: The Egyptians raised them in pairs before temples; Rome later carried more than a dozen home.
fields.Caption 1: An obelisk before the pylon of Luxor Temple, Egypt
fields.Caption 2: The Luxor Obelisk in the Place de la Concorde, Paris
fields.Caption 3: The Lateran Obelisk, Rome

fields.Name: Pagoda
fields.Description: A tiered tower with a row of projecting roofs, built in East and South Asia as a Buddhist monument.
fields.Notes: It descends from the Indian stupa, its dome turned into a tall, storeyed tower.
fields.Caption 1: The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, Xi'an, China
fields.Caption 2: The five-storey pagoda of Hōryū-ji, Japan
fields.Caption 3: Seokgatap pagoda at Bulguksa, Korea

fields.Name: Rotunda
fields.Description: A building with a circular ground plan, especially one covered by a dome.
fields.Notes: The Pantheon in Rome is the most famous rotunda in the world.
fields.Caption 2: The Rotunda of Galerius, Thessaloniki
fields.Caption 3: The Rotunda, University of Virginia, Charlottesville

fields.Name: Lantern
fields.Description: A small turret with glazed or open sides set on top of a roof or dome to let in light and air.
fields.Notes: St Paul's Cathedral and Florence Cathedral both crown their domes with one.
fields.Caption 2: The lantern over the dome of the Florence Baptistery
fields.Caption 3: A lantern on Seville Cathedral, Spain
fields.Caption 4: The dome and lantern of St Paul's Cathedral, London

fields.Name: Gable
fields.Description: The triangular wall enclosed between the two sloping sides of a pitched roof.
fields.Notes: The stepped or curved gables of Dutch merchants' houses are among the most recognisable.
fields.Caption 1: Gabled half-timbered houses on the Marktplatz, Tübingen
fields.Caption 2: Timber gable in Oulu, Finland
fields.Caption 3: Decorative gable on St. John's Place, Brooklyn

fields.Name: Dormer
fields.Description: A window set upright in a small projection of its own that rises from a sloping roof.
fields.Notes: Mansard roofs, from the 17th century, made dormers a standard feature of Parisian buildings.
fields.Caption 1: Gable dormers on the Hospices de Beaune, France
fields.Caption 2: Hip-roofed dormer windows on the Howard Memorial Hall, Letchworth
fields.Caption 3: A dormer on the Préfecture de police, Paris

fields.Name: Pilotis
fields.Description: Slender columns that raise a building off the ground, leaving the space beneath open.
fields.Notes: Le Corbusier made them the first of his Five Points of a New Architecture.
fields.Caption 1: Engel House in the White City of Tel Aviv
fields.Caption 2: Architecture Building, University of Florida (1979)
fields.Caption 3: Erasmus Building, Queens' College, Cambridge (1959)

fields.Name: Keep
fields.Description: The main tower of a medieval castle, a strong residence and last refuge inside its outer defences.
fields.Notes: The White Tower of the Tower of London is a well-known Norman example.
fields.Caption 2: The Norman keep of Rochester Castle, England (c. 1126)
fields.Caption 3: Henry II's great tower, the keep of Dover Castle

fields.Name: Barbican
fields.Description: A fortified outwork, often a tower or a walled passage, that guards the gate of a castle or city.
fields.Notes: Attackers had to run a gauntlet of fire in the narrow space in front of the real gate.
fields.Caption 2: The barbican of the White Tower, Nuremberg
fields.Caption 3: The barbican of the Château de Carcassonne, France

fields.Name: Niche
fields.Description: A shallow recess in a wall, often round-headed, made to hold a statue or urn.
fields.Notes: The Romans lined their temples and baths with them.
fields.Caption 1: Statue in a niche by Antoine Coysevox, Les Invalides, Paris
fields.Caption 2: Statue niches on Orsanmichele, Florence
fields.Caption 3: The mihrab niche of the Great Mosque of Córdoba

fields.Name: Chevet
fields.Description: The rounded east end of a Gothic church, where the aisle curves round the apse and opens onto radiating chapels.
fields.Notes: It is a French form, whose name means “pillow” or “head of a bed”.
fields.Caption 2: The chevet of Bourges Cathedral
fields.Caption 3: The chevet of Amiens Cathedral

fields.Name: Westwork
fields.Description: A massive west-facing entrance block of a Carolingian or Romanesque church, with towers and an upper chamber.
fields.Notes: Corvey Abbey in Germany preserves a rare surviving example, from the 9th century.
fields.Caption 1: The westwork of Corvey Abbey, Höxter, Germany
fields.Caption 2: The west front of Speyer Cathedral, Speyer, Germany, a later Romanesque westwork
fields.Caption 3: The westwork of the Onze-Lieve-Vrouwebasiliek, Maastricht

fields.Name: Onion dome
fields.Description: A bulbous roof that swells beyond its base and rises to a point.
fields.Notes: Russian churches often paint or gild them; they are also seen in Mughal and Bavarian architecture.
fields.Caption 1: Onion domes of Saint Basil's Cathedral, Moscow
fields.Caption 2: Church of the Resurrection, Kostroma (1652)
fields.Caption 3: Avraamiev Monastery, Kostroma Oblast

fields.Name: Gopuram
fields.Description: The monumental gateway tower of a South Indian Hindu temple, covered in painted sculpture.
fields.Notes: Those of the Meenakshi Temple at Madurai rise to about 50 metres.
fields.Caption 2: Gopurams of the Ranganathaswamy Temple, Srirangam
fields.Caption 3: Gopuram of the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram
fields.Caption 4: Gopuram at Tirumala, Andhra Pradesh

fields.Name: Madrasa
fields.Description: An Islamic college, usually built around a courtyard, with a mosque or prayer hall, lecture rooms, and student cells.
fields.Notes: The Sultan Hassan complex in Cairo has four iwans, one for each school of law.
fields.Caption 1: The three madrasas of the Registan, Samarkand
fields.Caption 2: The Mustansiriya Madrasa, Baghdad (1227)
fields.Caption 3: The Qarawiyyin Madrasa and mosque, Fez

fields.Name: Triumphal arch
fields.Description: A freestanding monumental gateway, with one or more arched passages, built to commemorate a victory or an emperor.
fields.Notes: The Arch of Titus in Rome, of about 81 CE, set the model for later ones such as the Arc de Triomphe.
fields.Caption 2: The Triumphal Arch of Orange, France
fields.Caption 3: The Arc de Triomphe, Paris

fields.Name: Impluvium
fields.Description: A shallow basin sunk in the floor of a Roman house, below an opening in the roof to catch rainwater.
fields.Notes: Pompeii's houses show these best preserved.
fields.Caption 1: Impluvium in the atrium of the House of the Menander, Pompeii
fields.Caption 2: An impluvium in a house in Casamance, Senegal
fields.Caption 3: Mosaic impluvium in the House of the Faun, Pompeii

fields.Name: Mashrabiya
fields.Description: A projecting window closed with a screen of turned wooden lattice, a feature of traditional Arab architecture.
fields.Notes: It lets in air and light while screening those inside from view and cooling the room.
fields.Caption 1: A mashrabiya in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia
fields.Caption 2: A mashrabiya in Tunisia
fields.Caption 3: Detail of mashrabiya lattice work

fields.Name: Michelangelo
fields.Description: Italian High Renaissance sculptor and painter who, late in life, designed the dome of St. Peter's Basilica and the Laurentian Library's dramatic entrance staircase.
fields.Works: St. Peter's Basilica (dome); Laurentian Library; Piazza del Campidoglio; Medici Chapel
fields.Caption 1: Daniele da Volterra, portrait of Michelangelo, c. 1545
fields.Caption 2: The dome of St. Peter's Basilica, Vatican City
fields.Caption 3: The Laurentian Library's vestibule and staircase, Florence

fields.Name: Jørn Utzon
fields.Description: Danish architect whose winning, initially unbuildable competition design for the Sydney Opera House took over a decade of engineering work with Ove Arup to realize.
fields.Works: <u>Sydney Opera House</u>; Bagsværd Church; Kuwait National Assembly Building
fields.Caption 2: Bagsværd Church, near Copenhagen

fields.Name: Thomas Jefferson
fields.Description: American Neoclassicist and Palladian revivalist, third U.S. President, who designed his own estate and the University of Virginia's campus around a domed library.
fields.Works: <u>Monticello</u>; University of Virginia Rotunda; Virginia State Capitol
fields.Caption 2: Monticello, Jefferson's Virginia estate
fields.Caption 3: The Rotunda, University of Virginia

fields.Name: John Soane
fields.Description: English Neoclassical architect of the Bank of England (mostly since rebuilt) known for dramatic top-lit interiors, preserved in the house-museum he left to the nation.
fields.Works: <u>Sir John Soane's Museum</u>; Bank of England (largely demolished); Dulwich Picture Gallery
fields.Caption 1: The Dome area of Sir John Soane's Museum, top-lit and packed with casts

fields.Name: Peter Behrens
fields.Description: German proto-modernist whose steel-and-glass AEG Turbine Factory anticipated the Bauhaus; his Berlin studio trained Walter Gropius, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and Le Corbusier.
fields.Works: <u>AEG Turbine Factory</u>; New Ways (Northampton); Hoechst Administration Building

fields.Name: Pier Luigi Nervi
fields.Description: Italian engineer-architect celebrated for thin, ribbed reinforced-concrete shells, built for Rome's 1960 Olympics and, with Marcel Breuer, the UNESCO Headquarters in Paris.
