fields.Works: Palazzetto dello Sport; UNESCO Headquarters (with Breuer and Zehrfuss); Pirelli Tower (with Gio Ponti)

fields.Name: Erich Mendelsohn
fields.Description: German Expressionist whose curved, streamlined Einstein Tower observatory became an icon of 1920s architecture before he emigrated after the Nazi rise to power.
fields.Works: <u>Einstein Tower</u>; Schocken Department Store (Stuttgart); Maimonides Hospital

fields.Name: Félix Candela
fields.Description: Spanish-born Mexican engineer-architect who raised thin, doubly curved concrete “hypar” shells into restaurants, churches, and sports halls on remarkably little material.
fields.Works: Los Manantiales Restaurant (Xochimilco); Palacio de los Deportes (Mexico City, roof); Church of the Miraculous Virgin
fields.Caption 2: L'Oceanogràfic, Valencia, 2003
fields.Caption 3: The Bacardi bottling plant, Cuautitlán, with Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, 1960
fields.Caption 4: Iglesia de San José del Altillo, Mexico City, 1956

fields.Name: William Van Alen
fields.Description: American Art Deco architect whose Chrysler Building, briefly the world's tallest, topped out with a stainless-steel spire secretly assembled inside the building and raised in minutes.
fields.Works: <u>Chrysler Building</u>
fields.Caption 2: Automobile ornament on the Chrysler Building's setbacks

fields.Name: Raymond Hood
fields.Description: American Art Deco architect of the Chicago Tribune Tower and, later, the streamlined GE Building at the heart of Rockefeller Center.
fields.Works: <u>American Radiator Building</u>; Tribune Tower; GE Building (30 Rockefeller Plaza)
fields.Caption 2: American Radiator Building, New York

fields.Name: Pyramid
fields.Description: A monumental tomb with a square base and four triangular faces meeting at a point, built smooth-sided in stone in Egypt and in stepped, temple-topped form in Mesoamerica.
fields.Notes: The largest, at Giza, was raised for Khufu around 2560 BCE and held the record for tallest structure on earth for nearly four millennia; the Mesoamerican kind carried a temple on a flat top and was climbed by stairs.
fields.Caption 2: El Castillo, Chichen Itza
fields.Caption 3: Santa Cecilia Acatitlan pyramid
fields.Caption 4: Edzna

fields.Name: Theatre
fields.Description: A tiered semicircular seating bowl facing a performance space, cut into a hillside by the Greeks and later built free-standing on vaults by the Romans.
fields.Notes: Epidaurus is the best-preserved Greek example and is famous for its acoustics; the Roman form, no longer needing a hill, led on to the enclosed amphitheatre.
fields.Caption 1: The seating of the ancient theatre at Epidaurus
fields.Caption 2: The theatre at Epidaurus, which Pausanias called the finest in Greece
fields.Caption 3: The Theatre of Dionysus

fields.Name: Basilica
fields.Description: A Roman public hall of justice and commerce — a long colonnaded rectangle lit from a clerestory, with an apse at one end — whose plan was taken over wholesale for the early Christian church.
fields.Notes: The word later became an honorific title conferred by the pope, which is why some churches carry it without having the plan at all.
fields.Caption 1: The Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine, Rome
fields.Caption 2: Digital reconstruction of the 2nd century BCE Basilica Sempronia, in the Forum Romanum
fields.Caption 3: 19th century reconstruction of the 2nd century CE Basilica Ulpia, part of the Trajan's Forum, Rome
fields.Caption 4: Ruins of Yererouk basilica 4th–5th century CE

fields.Name: Pueblo
fields.Description: A multi-storey mud-brick and stone village of the American Southwest, its flat-roofed rooms stacked in terraces and entered by ladder through hatches in the roof.
fields.Notes: Taos has been continuously inhabited for about a thousand years; the Spanish word for “village” gave both the buildings and their builders their name.
fields.Caption 2: Acoma Pueblo in northern New Mexico, one of the oldest pueblo towns
fields.Caption 3: Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, Albuquerque, New Mexico
fields.Caption 4: She-we-na (Zuni Pueblo), katsina tihu (Paiyatemu), late 19th century. Brooklyn Museum

fields.Name: Castle
fields.Description: A fortified private residence of a lord, combining a defended enclosure, towers, and a gatehouse with domestic apartments — distinct both from a purely military fort and from an unfortified palace.
fields.Notes: The motte-and-bailey earthwork came first; concentric stone rings, as at Beaumaris, are the developed form, and gunpowder artillery ended its usefulness.
fields.Caption 2: The White Tower, the keep of the Tower of London
fields.Caption 3: Windsor Castle, founded as a Norman fortification after 1066
fields.Caption 4: Vidin Castle on the Danube, Bulgaria

fields.Name: Caravanserai
fields.Description: A walled roadside inn on a trade route, built round a courtyard with stabling and storage below and sleeping cells above, spaced roughly a day's journey apart.
fields.Notes: Persian, Seljuk, and Ottoman rulers built them in chains along the Silk Road; the Ottoman term for the urban version is han.
fields.Caption 1: A ruined caravanserai on a Persian trade road
fields.Caption 2: The Izadkhast caravanserai (early 17th century), Fars province, Iran
fields.Caption 3: The Ganjali Khan Caravanserai (1598), in Kerman, Iran
fields.Caption 4: Khan As'ad Pasha, a caravanserai built in 1752 in Damascus, Syria

fields.Name: Skyscraper
fields.Description: A very tall habitable building whose weight is carried on a steel or concrete skeleton rather than on its walls, made practical by the safety elevator and by fireproof cladding.
fields.Notes: Chicago's Home Insurance Building of 1885 is usually called the first; once the frame carries the load the outer wall can hang off it as a thin curtain.
fields.Caption 1: The Bank of China Tower, Hong Kong
fields.Caption 2: Chicago, where the steel-frame skyscraper first appeared in 1885
fields.Caption 3: Oriel Chambers, Liverpool (1864), an early iron frame behind a glass curtain wall
fields.Caption 4: Palacio Salvo, Montevideo (1928), once the tallest reinforced-concrete building

fields.Name: Timber framing
fields.Description: Building on a skeleton of heavy squared wooden posts and beams joined by pegged mortise-and-tenon, with the panels between filled by wattle and daub, plaster, or brick.
fields.Notes: Called Fachwerk in Germany and half-timbering in England, where the infill is whitewashed between blackened members; the Tudor style is its best-known phase.
fields.Caption 1: Half-timbered houses in a German market square
fields.Caption 2: Nonsuch Palace in a hand-coloured engraving after Georg Hoefnagel
fields.Caption 3: Carved timber framing on a house in Strasbourg

fields.Name: Adobe
fields.Description: Sun-dried brick of earth mixed with straw or dung, laid in thick walls that soak up heat by day and give it back at night — the oldest building material still in ordinary use.
fields.Notes: The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest structure built of it and is replastered by the whole town each year; the Pueblo builders of the Southwest used the same material.
fields.Caption 1: A sun-dried earth wall, straw visible in the surface
fields.Caption 2: The mosque of Seku Amadu at Djenné in 1895, from Félix Dubois's Tombouctou la mystérieuse
fields.Caption 3: Sun-dried mudbricks laid out in rows
fields.Caption 4: Adobe wall (detail) in Bahillo, Palencia, Spain

fields.Name: Reinforced concrete
fields.Description: Poured artificial stone with steel bars set inside it, so that the steel takes the tension the stone cannot, allowing thin slabs, long spans, and cantilevers.
fields.Notes: Patented by the gardener Joseph Monier in the 1860s; Auguste Perret and then Le Corbusier made it the basis of a new architecture, and béton brut, left raw from the shuttering, gave Brutalism its name.
fields.Caption 1: A column cast round its steel reinforcement
fields.Caption 2: The Philips Pavilion, Brussels, Expo 58
fields.Caption 3: François Coignet's house, Saint-Denis (1853)
fields.Caption 4: Houses Coignet built for his factory workers, Saint-Denis

fields.Name: Gridshell
fields.Description: A curved roof whose structure is a single layer of slender laths bent into a lattice, taking its stiffness from double curvature rather than from the thickness of its members.
fields.Notes: Frei Otto's Mannheim Multihalle of 1975 is the classic; the Weald and Downland Museum in Sussex has a British example in green oak.
fields.Caption 1: Frei Otto's Mannheim Multihalle under construction, 1974
fields.Caption 2: The steel gridshell by Vladimir Shukhov (during construction), Vyksa near Nizhny Novgorod, 1897
fields.Caption 3: Multihalle in Mannheim, a wooden gridshell structure designed by Frei Otto
fields.Caption 4: Interior of the gridshell Savill Building

fields.Name: Charbagh
fields.Description: A walled Persian garden divided into four equal plots by axial watercourses — paradise laid out as a quartered square.
fields.Notes: The Taj Mahal and Humayun's Tomb both stand in one; the word is Persian for “four gardens”.
fields.Caption 1: A four-part Mughal garden divided by watercourses
fields.Caption 2: The charbagh at the Tomb of Jahangir in Lahore, Pakistan
fields.Caption 3: An example of chaharbagh on Naqsh-e Jahan Square (constructed 1598–1629) in Isfahan, Iran
fields.Caption 4: Babur celebrates the birth of Humayun in the charbagh of Kabul.

fields.Name: Modernism
fields.Description: The 20th-century movement that stripped away ornament and historical reference in favour of flat roofs, white walls, steel, glass, and plans organized by use.
fields.Notes: Its slogans were “form follows function” and “less is more”; the International Style, the Bauhaus, and De Stijl are its branches, and Postmodernism defined itself against it.
fields.Caption 2: Walter Gropius, the Bauhaus building, Dessau, 1926
fields.Caption 3: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, the Barcelona Pavilion, 1929 (rebuilt 1986)
fields.Caption 4: Mies van der Rohe and Philip Johnson, the Seagram Building, New York, 1958

fields.Name: Functionalism
fields.Description: The principle that a building's shape should follow only from its purpose and its structure, ornament being at best irrelevant and at worst dishonest.
fields.Notes: Louis Sullivan's “form ever follows function” is the ancestor; Hannes Meyer, as director of the Bauhaus, took it furthest by reducing design to a calculation of needs.
fields.Caption 2: The Bauhaus building, Dessau (1925–1926)
fields.Caption 3: The tower of the Helsinki Olympic Stadium (1934–1938)
fields.Caption 4: Houses in Södra Ängby, Stockholm (1938)

fields.Name: Futurism
fields.Description: A short-lived Italian movement that drew, but barely built, a machine-age city of stepped terraced towers, external lifts, and traffic stacked on several levels.
fields.Notes: Antonio Sant'Elia's Città Nuova drawings of 1914 are almost all that survives of it; he was killed in the war in 1916, aged 28.

fields.Name: Moorish architecture
fields.Description: The Islamic building tradition of the western Mediterranean — horseshoe arches, interlaced arcades, honeycomb vaulting, and carved stucco — developed in al-Andalus and North Africa.
fields.Notes: The Great Mosque of Córdoba and the Alhambra are its monuments; 19th-century Europe revived it for synagogues and pleasure pavilions.
fields.Caption 1: The arcades of the Great Mosque of Córdoba
fields.Caption 2: Decorated façade of the Mosque of Ibn Khayrun in Kairouan (866)
fields.Caption 3: The Reception Hall of Abd ar-Rahman III at Madinat al-Zahra (10th century)

fields.Name: Islamic architecture
fields.Description: The architecture of the Muslim world from the 7th century, built around the courtyard and the prayer hall facing Mecca, with domes, minarets, pointed and horseshoe arches, muqarnas vaulting, and ornament of arabesque, geometry, and calligraphy in place of human figures.
fields.Notes: Its regional branches — Umayyad, Moorish, Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal — differ sharply; the minaret and the prayer niche are the constants.
fields.Caption 1: The Dome of the Rock, Jerusalem
fields.Caption 2: The Mosque of the Prophet, Medina, on the site of Muhammad's first mosque
fields.Caption 3: The Umayyad Mshatta façade, from a palace near Amman, now in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin
fields.Caption 4: Great Mosque of Damascus (early 8th century)

fields.Name: Hindu temple architecture
fields.Description: South Asian religious building organized around a small dark sanctum under a tower, approached through pillared halls, with the whole exterior carved in tiers of figures.
fields.Notes: The northern Nagara type has a curved shikhara; the southern Dravida type a stepped pyramidal vimana and enormous gateway gopurams.
fields.Caption 2: Diagram of a Nagara-style Hindu temple
fields.Caption 3: The temples at Pattadakal, 7th–8th century
fields.Caption 4: The Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved from a single rock under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (r. 756–773)

fields.Name: Khmer architecture
fields.Description: The sandstone and laterite temple-mountains of the Cambodian empire: quincunx towers rising over concentric galleries inside a moat, carved with narrative reliefs.
fields.Notes: Angkor Wat, built for Suryavarman II in the 12th century and unusually facing west, is the largest religious structure in the world.

fields.Name: Rock-cut architecture
fields.Description: Building made by taking material away rather than putting it up: halls, facades, and whole churches carved down into living cliff or bedrock.
fields.Notes: Petra's tombs, the Ajanta and Ellora caves, Abu Simbel and the monolithic churches of Lalibela are the great examples.
fields.Caption 1: The temple of Abu Simbel, cut from the cliff
fields.Caption 2: The Kailasa temple, part of the Ellora Caves
fields.Caption 3: The Church of Saint George, Lalibela, Ethiopia, cut down into the rock
fields.Caption 4: The Treasury (Al-Khazneh), Petra, Jordan

fields.Name: Perpendicular Gothic
fields.Description: The last and longest English phase of the pointed style, marked by strong vertical mullions running unbroken to the arch head, huge windows, four-centred arches, and fan vaults.
fields.Notes: King's College Chapel, Cambridge, and the choir of Gloucester Cathedral are its masterpieces; it is the only phase of the style with no continental counterpart.
fields.Caption 2: King's College Chapel, Cambridge, Great East Window (four-centred arch, straight mullions and transoms)
fields.Caption 3: The chancel of Gloucester Cathedral (c. 1337–1357)
fields.Caption 4: Chapter house by William de Ramsey (c. 1332) at Old St Paul's Cathedral (by Wenceslaus Hollar); destroyed in the Great Fire of London in 1666

fields.Name: Flamboyant
fields.Description: The final French phase of the pointed style, named for window tracery whose S-curves lick upward like fire, with structure dissolved into ornament.
fields.Notes: Saint-Maclou at Rouen and the north spire of Chartres are examples; the Tour Saint-Jacques in Paris is a late one.
fields.Caption 1: A late French Gothic west front
fields.Caption 2: Notre-Dame de l'Épine, west front (1405–1527)
fields.Caption 3: West porch of the Church of Saint-Maclou, Rouen, (1434–1521)

fields.Name: Plateresque
fields.Description: An early Spanish Renaissance manner in which dense, finely cut ornament is spread across a wall like a silversmith's work, framing otherwise plain late medieval structure.
fields.Notes: Named from platero, “silversmith”; the facade of the University of Salamanca is the standard example.
fields.Caption 2: New Cathedral of Salamanca (1513-1733) in the Plateresque made city of Salamanca, Castile and León, Spain
fields.Caption 3: Hospital of the Catholic Monarchs (1501-1511), in Santiago de Compostela, Galicia, Spain
fields.Caption 4: Altar plateresque of the Cistercian monastery of Santa María del Salvador, in Cañas, La Rioja, Spain

fields.Name: Churrigueresque
fields.Description: The extravagant late Spanish and Latin American Baroque, in which altarpiece-like facades are encrusted with broken pediments, inverted obelisk pilasters, and swarming sculpture.
fields.Notes: Named after the Churriguera family of Salamanca; the sacristy of the Cartuja in Granada and Mexico City's Sagrario Metropolitano are high points.
fields.Caption 1: The Obradoiro facade of Santiago de Compostela
fields.Caption 2: Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Spain. Churrigueresque Obradoiro façade
fields.Caption 3: Basilica and Convent of Nuestra Señora de la Merced, Lima
fields.Caption 4: The Santa Prisca temple, in Taxco, Mexico.

fields.Name: Safavid architecture
fields.Description: The Persian style of the 16th and 17th centuries: vast tile-clad courtyards, bulbous double-shelled domes in turquoise and blue, and towering vaulted portals.
fields.Notes: Shah Abbas I's Naqsh-e Jahan Square at Isfahan, with the Shah and Sheikh Lotfollah mosques, is the great ensemble.

fields.Name: Eclecticism
fields.Description: The practice of picking a historical style to suit each building's purpose, so that a bank comes out classical, a church medieval, and a town hall whatever the committee prefers.
fields.Notes: Also called historicism; its training ground was the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, and the battle between its Gothic and classical camps was fought openly over London's Foreign Office.

fields.Name: Spanish Colonial Revival
fields.Description: An early 20th-century American style of white stucco walls, low-pitched red tile roofs, arcades, wrought iron, and carved doorways, drawn from the missions and from Latin America.
fields.Notes: Launched by the 1915 Panama-California Exposition in San Diego; Santa Barbara rebuilt its centre in it after the 1925 earthquake.
fields.Caption 2: Palm Beach Town Hall in Palm Beach, Florida (1925)

fields.Name: Minimalism
fields.Description: A manner that reduces a building to a few large planes, one or two materials, and the behaviour of light, with services, fixings, and joints hidden entirely.
fields.Notes: Tadao Ando's board-marked walls and John Pawson's interiors are the type; the debt is to Mies van der Rohe and to Japanese building.
fields.Caption 1: Tadao Ando, Church of the Light, Ibaraki, 1989
fields.Caption 2: Peter Zumthor, Therme Vals, Switzerland, 1996

fields.Name: Rationalism
fields.Description: The Italian interwar movement that tried to reconcile modern building with classical order: stripped colonnades, square proportion, and Roman monumentality without ornament.
fields.Notes: Giuseppe Terragni's Casa del Fascio at Como (1936) is the key work; under Mussolini it became a state manner, as at the EUR district in Rome.

fields.Name: Mid-century modern
fields.Description: The domestic strand of postwar American design: open plans, post-and-beam frames, walls of glass onto a patio, flat or low-pitched roofs, and honest cheap materials.
fields.Notes: The Case Study Houses in Los Angeles, the Eames House among them, and the desert houses of Palm Springs are the emblem; the term was coined in a 1984 book.
fields.Caption 2: Tulip chair (designed 1955–56) by Eero Saarinen
fields.Caption 3: Frank Sinatra's Home, in Palm Springs
fields.Caption 4: Eichler Homes – Foster Residence, Santa Clara

fields.Name: New Classical architecture
fields.Description: The contemporary practice of designing new buildings in traditional orders and proportions, as a living tradition rather than as historical pastiche.
fields.Notes: Léon Krier's Poundbury in Dorset, built for the Prince of Wales, is the best-known scheme; the Driehaus Prize was founded as its answer to the Pritzker.
fields.Caption 2: Ciudad Cayalá in Guatemala City, Guatemala, 2011, by Léon Krier
fields.Caption 3: Schermerhorn Symphony Center in Nashville, Tennessee, opened in 2006
fields.Caption 4: Darden Graduate School of Business Administration at the University of Virginia, 1992, by Robert A.M. Stern Architects

fields.Name: Sudano-Sahelian architecture
fields.Description: The mud-brick building of the West African savannah: tapering buttressed walls, projecting palm-wood beams left in place as permanent scaffolding, and conical pinnacles.
fields.Notes: The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest example and is replastered by the whole town each year; Timbuktu's mosques belong to the same family.
fields.Caption 1: The Great Mosque of Djenné, Mali
fields.Caption 2: The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali, the largest mud-brick building in sub-Saharan Africa
fields.Caption 3: Sankore Mosque in Timbuktu (16th century with later renovations)
fields.Caption 4: Chinguetti Mosque in Mauritania (13th century), built of sandstone with a flat wooden roof

fields.Name: Tropical Modernism
fields.Description: A postwar approach to building in hot, wet climates: deep overhangs, perforated screen walls, open plans, and courtyards that cool a building without machinery.
fields.Notes: Geoffrey Bawa in Sri Lanka, and Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew in West Africa, are the names usually attached to it.
fields.Caption 1: Geoffrey Bawa's Sri Lankan Parliament at Kotte

fields.Name: Ideal city
fields.Description: The Renaissance idea of a town planned whole on geometric principles — usually a radial star or a grid inside a polygonal wall — laid out as a diagram of good government.
fields.Notes: Filarete's Sforzinda was the first fully described; Palmanova in the Veneto was actually built, and three famous panel paintings from Urbino show the type.
fields.Caption 1: The Ideal City, panel painting from Urbino, c. 1470
fields.Caption 2: The ideal city attributed to Fra Carnevale, c. 1480–1484
fields.Caption 3: Caliph Al-Mansur's Round city of Baghdad, City of Peace, c. 8th century
fields.Caption 4: The ideal city attributed to Luciano Laurana or Melozzo da Forlì

fields.Name: Garden city movement
fields.Description: Ebenezer Howard's scheme of self-contained new towns of limited size, each ringed by a permanent agricultural belt and owned by its own community, combining the advantages of town and country.
fields.Notes: Set out in To-morrow: A Peaceful Path to Real Reform (1898); Letchworth and Welwyn were built to it, and it shaped Britain's postwar new towns.
fields.Caption 2: An attempt at a garden city: Zlín in Czechia (architect: František Lydie Gahura)
fields.Caption 3: The Workers Academy in Kauniainen, the garden city of Finland
fields.Caption 4: Avenida Ámsterdam in Colonia Hipódromo de la Condesa, Mexico City, laid out in 1926

fields.Name: Prefabrication
fields.Description: Making a building's parts in a factory and assembling them on site, which turns construction into delivery and makes repetition cheaper than variety.
fields.Notes: The Crystal Palace of 1851, built from standard iron and glass units in nine months and later taken down and moved, is the landmark; postwar housing shortages made the method general.
fields.Caption 1: The transept of the Crystal Palace, 1851
fields.Caption 2: Levittown, Puerto Rico
fields.Caption 3: “Loren” Iron House, at Old Gippstown in Moe, Australia
fields.Caption 4: A house being built with prefabricated concrete panels.

fields.Name: Sustainable architecture
fields.Description: Building designed to keep its energy use and its damage to the environment as low as possible — through orientation, insulation, daylight, natural ventilation, recycled materials, and power made on site.
fields.Notes: Also called green building; the BREEAM and LEED rating systems, of 1990 and 1998, made it something that could be measured and certified.
fields.Caption 2: Energy-plus-houses at Freiburg-Vauban in Germany

fields.Name: Imperial Hotel, Tokyo
fields.Description: A hotel of carved Oya stone on a floating foundation over soft ground; it opened the day of the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake and survived it, which made Frank Lloyd Wright's reputation in Japan. Demolished in 1968, its entrance was re-erected at the Meiji Mura museum.
fields.Caption 1: The hotel across its reflecting pool, 1930s
fields.Caption 2: The entrance wing, re-erected at Meiji Mura in 1976
fields.Caption 3: The lobby at Meiji Mura, carved Oya stone and terracotta
fields.Caption 4: Wright's elevations and sections for the hotel

fields.Name: Larkin Administration Building
fields.Description: A sealed brick office block built around a top-lit central atrium, air-conditioned, with built-in metal furniture and the first wall-hung toilets; demolished in 1950 for a parking lot.
fields.Caption 1: Before Wright was hired to design the Administration Building, he designed the George Barton House (pictured) for Darwin

fields.Name: Hollyhock House
fields.Description: Frank Lloyd Wright's first Los Angeles work, a concrete house for the oil heiress Aline Barnsdall whose ornament abstracts a single flower, the hollyhock, into a repeated motif.
fields.Caption 2: The living-room hearth
fields.Caption 3: The colonnade around the garden court, 1921

fields.Name: Price Tower
fields.Description: Frank Lloyd Wright's only completed skyscraper, a nineteen-storey tower cantilevered from a central trunk, with copper louvres, adapted from an unbuilt New York apartment scheme; he called it “the tree that escaped the crowded forest.”
fields.Caption 1: The tower and its copper louvres
fields.Caption 2: The entrance court under a copper-panelled canopy
fields.Caption 3: The lobby ceiling

fields.Name: Marin County Civic Center
fields.Description: A low arcaded government building bridging between hills, with a blue roof and a gold spire: Frank Lloyd Wright's last major commission, finished after his death, and a location in Gattaca.
fields.Caption 2: One of its long arcaded wings

fields.Name: Taliesin
fields.Description: Frank Lloyd Wright's own hillside home and studio of local limestone, growing by accretion for decades and twice destroyed by fire; in 1914 a servant set it alight and murdered seven people, including Wright's partner Mamah Borthwick.
fields.Caption 2: The house from below the hill
fields.Caption 3: A terrace

fields.Name: Royal Naval College, Greenwich
fields.Description: Paired domed blocks framing a deliberate gap so that the river view stays open, built as a hospital for retired seamen; James Thornhill took nineteen years to paint its Painted Hall.
fields.Caption 2: The Painted Hall, decorated by James Thornhill

fields.Name: Sheldonian Theatre
fields.Description: A university ceremonial hall, Christopher Wren's first major building, designed while he was Professor of Astronomy; its trussed roof spans the hall without internal columns, a span no timber then available could cross in one piece.
fields.Caption 2: Interior of the theatre

fields.Name: Monument to the Great Fire of London
fields.Description: A fluted Doric column topped by a gilded urn of flame, its height equal to its distance from where the fire began; designed with Robert Hooke, it doubled as a zenith telescope, with a hinged lid and a laboratory below.
fields.Caption 1: View of the Monument, designed by Robert Hooke
fields.Caption 2: Viewing platform at the top of the Monument

fields.Name: St Stephen Walbrook
fields.Description: A City church whose dome on eight arches is widely treated as the trial run for Saint Paul's, and the finest of the fifty-one churches Christopher Wren built after the Great Fire.

fields.Name: Guaranty Building
fields.Description: A steel-framed office block clad in terracotta, its piers running unbroken to the cornice, designed with Dankmar Adler; Louis Sullivan's essay of the same year, 1896, gave the phrase “form ever follows function.”
fields.Caption 2: The top floors: arched windows, round oculi, and the cornice, all in ornamented terracotta

fields.Name: Auditorium Building
fields.Description: A massive stone block combining a theatre, hotel, and offices in one structure, designed with Dankmar Adler, whose acoustics made its name; the young Frank Lloyd Wright worked on it as a draftsman.
fields.Caption 2: The theatre's arches, from the balcony
fields.Caption 3: Box seats in the theatre

fields.Name: Teatro Olimpico
fields.Description: The oldest surviving indoor theatre, finished by Vincenzo Scamozzi after Andrea Palladio's death: a permanent scenic wall pierced by streets in forced perspective, narrowing sharply so that a short stage reads as a long street.
fields.Caption 1: The scaenae frons, with Scamozzi's perspective streets behind its openings
fields.Caption 2: The central arch, with a street built in forced perspective

fields.Name: Basilica Palladiana
fields.Description: A medieval hall wrapped in a marble loggia of arches flanked by narrow openings, a unit since named the Palladian or Serlian motif; the commission made Andrea Palladio's name.

fields.Name: Basilica of San Lorenzo, Florence
fields.Description: The Medici parish church, laid out on a strict module of grey stone framing white plaster, with Filippo Brunelleschi's Old Sacristy and Michelangelo's New Sacristy.
fields.Caption 2: Interior looking toward the high altar

fields.Name: Santo Spirito, Florence
fields.Description: Filippo Brunelleschi's last church, built after his death to his module: a basilica of repeated bays in which the whole plan derives from one square, its façade never finished and still blank.
fields.Caption 2: The interior, with its colonnades and high altar

fields.Name: Tempio Malatestiano
fields.Description: A Gothic church encased in a Roman triumphal-arch front, left incomplete, built for Sigismondo Malatesta, whom Pius II condemned for turning a church into a pagan monument to his mistress.
fields.Caption 2: Doorway of the Malatesta Temple by Leon Battista Alberti.

fields.Name: Sant'Agnese in Agone
fields.Description: A concave church front on Piazza Navona that draws its twin towers and dome together, facing Gian Lorenzo Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers; the story that one river god shields his eyes from it is a later invention, as the fountain came first.
fields.Caption 2: View into frescoed cupola and pendentives; apse on left, entrance with organ and tomb of Pope Innocent X on right

fields.Name: Saint Peter's Square
fields.Description: An oval piazza held by four rows of columns reaching out from the basilica front, which Gian Lorenzo Bernini described as the maternal arms of the church; from two marked discs, the four rows line up as one.
fields.Caption 1: The piazza from the dome: Bernini's two colonnades enclose an oval around the obelisk
fields.Caption 2: Inside the colonnade: four rows of Tuscan columns

fields.Name: MAXXI
fields.Description: A museum of intersecting concrete tubes with no single route through it, winner of the 2010 Stirling Prize; Zaha Hadid had been the first woman to win the Pritzker, in 2004.
fields.Caption 2: The foyer, with its suspended black staircases

fields.Name: Vitra Fire Station
fields.Description: Angled concrete planes that seem frozen mid-movement: Zaha Hadid's first completed building, after years of work known only through her paintings, and used as a fire station only briefly.
fields.Caption 2: The cantilevered canopy from the side

fields.Name: East Building, National Gallery of Art
fields.Description: Two triangles cut on the diagonal from an awkward trapezoidal site, meeting at a knife-edge stone corner that visitors have worn smooth by touching it.
fields.Caption 2: The west front, with the plaza's glass pyramids
fields.Caption 3: The atrium under its space-frame skylight, with Alexander Calder's mobile

fields.Name: Museum of Islamic Art, Doha
fields.Description: Stacked stone cubes on an artificial island, stepping back to a domed atrium; I. M. Pei came out of retirement at ninety-one, toured Islamic architecture for months, and took the ablution fountain of the Mosque of Ibn Tulun in Cairo as his source.

fields.Name: Step Pyramid of Djoser
fields.Description: Six mastabas of decreasing size stacked into the earliest large stone building; its architect, Imhotep, is the first whose name survives, and was later worshipped as a god of medicine.
fields.Caption 1: The six-stepped pyramid, designed by Imhotep
fields.Caption 2: Restored buildings of Djoser's funerary complex
fields.Caption 3: The stepped courses of limestone blocks

fields.Name: Virginia State Capitol
fields.Description: A state house modelled by Thomas Jefferson on the Maison Carrée at Nîmes, with a giant portico: the first public building of the modern era in the form of a classical temple.
fields.Caption 2: Jean-Antoine Houdon's George Washington in the rotunda

fields.Name: Casa Vicens
fields.Description: Antoni Gaudí's first major house, built for a tile manufacturer of brick and tile covered in green-and-white checks, its ornament drawn from the marigolds and palms found on the site.
fields.Caption 2: Tiles painted with marigolds

fields.Name: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
fields.Description: A glass tent-pyramid on the shore of Lake Erie, recalling I. M. Pei's Louvre entrance, with a tower and cantilevered geometric volumes projecting over the water; Pei, who knew little about rock, toured music venues with the museum's founders before designing it.
fields.Caption 1: The glass pyramid facing the plaza
fields.Caption 2: The cantilevered volumes at night

fields.Name: Jay Pritzker Pavilion
fields.Description: An outdoor concert stage framed by curling ribbons of brushed stainless steel, with a trellis of crisscrossing steel pipes carrying the sound system over the lawn; the centrepiece of Millennium Park, beside Anish Kapoor's Cloud Gate, it was classed as a work of art to get around Grant Park's height limit.
fields.Caption 1: The stage and the steel trellis over the Great Lawn
fields.Caption 2: The trellis over the Great Lawn, from above
fields.Caption 3: The lawn and trellis from the stage

fields.Name: John F. Kennedy Presidential Library
fields.Description: A white concrete triangular tower beside a black glass pavilion ten storeys high and almost empty inside, on Columbia Point overlooking Boston Harbor; Jacqueline Kennedy chose Pei in 1964, and the library was meant for Harvard's campus until local opposition moved it.
fields.Caption 1: The concrete block and the glass pavilion
fields.Caption 2: The glass pavilion and its hanging flag
fields.Caption 3: On Columbia Point at dusk

fields.Name: John Hancock Tower
fields.Description: Boston's tallest building, a sixty-storey rhomboid slab sheathed entirely in reflective blue glass beside Trinity Church, which appears in its façade; soon after completion its windows began to fall out, and all 10,344 panes were replaced.
fields.Architect: Henry N. Cobb (I. M. Pei & Partners)
fields.Caption 2: Trinity Church reflected in the tower

fields.Name: Central Park
fields.Description: An 843-acre park in the middle of Manhattan, laid out as meadows, woods, and lakes to Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux's Greensward Plan, winner of the 1858 competition, with sunken transverse roads hiding cross-town traffic; Vaux designed Bethesda Terrace and its fountain.
fields.Caption 1: The park from the top of Rockefeller Center
fields.Caption 2: Bethesda Terrace and Fountain

fields.Name: Dulles Airport Main Terminal
fields.Description: An airport terminal whose concrete roof hangs in a catenary curve between two rows of outward-leaning piers; completed after Eero Saarinen's death, it carried passengers out to their planes in mobile lounges.
fields.Caption 1: The terminal's leaning piers and hanging roof
fields.Caption 2: The hall under its suspended concrete roof
fields.Caption 3: The terminal and control tower from the landside

fields.Name: Miller House
fields.Description: A flat-roofed, glass-walled house for the industrialist J. Irwin Miller, whose foundation brought modernist architecture to Columbus: a grid of cruciform columns, a sunken conversation pit, and skylights running along the roof, with interiors by Alexander Girard and gardens by Dan Kiley.
fields.Caption 2: Dan Kiley's honey-locust allée

fields.Name: Ennis House
fields.Description: A temple-like house on a hillside, built of interlocking concrete blocks cast with a patterned relief, the largest of Frank Lloyd Wright's four textile-block houses; its Maya look has made it a film set, most famously in Blade Runner.
fields.Caption 2: The gate and the patterned textile blocks

fields.Name: Stata Center
fields.Description: A cluster of tilting, colliding volumes in brick, brushed metal, and bright paint for MIT's computer-science laboratories, on the site of Building 20, the wartime radar laboratory; MIT sued Frank Gehry's firm in 2007 over leaks and cracks.
fields.Caption 2: The brick and steel volumes along Vassar Street
fields.Caption 3: The terraced steps of the courtyard

fields.Name: Transportation Building
fields.Description: The only coloured building in the White City of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, entered through the Golden Door, a gilded arch of concentric ornamented bands that won Louis Sullivan medals from the Union centrale des arts décoratifs in Paris; demolished after the fair.
fields.Caption 1: The Golden Door, in the official views of the fair
fields.Caption 2: The building across the lagoon, from an 1893 guidebook

fields.Name: Kansai International Airport Terminal
fields.Description: A terminal 1.7 kilometres long under a single curved roof whose profile follows the flow of air from its ducts, on an artificial island in Osaka Bay that has been sinking since construction; it came through the 1995 Kobe earthquake without a broken pane.
fields.Caption 1: The terminal's canyon of escalators and bridges
fields.Caption 2: The terminal's curved roof from the apron
fields.Caption 3: The airport's island from the air, 2022

fields.Name: British Museum
fields.Description: A Greek Revival museum fronted by a colonnade of forty-four Ionic columns. Its courtyard holds the round Reading Room (1857), designed by Robert Smirke's brother Sydney, where Karl Marx wrote much of Das Kapital; the court around it was roofed in 2000 with a glass-and-steel lattice as the Great Court.
fields.Caption 1: The south front's colonnade from the forecourt
fields.Caption 2: The Great Court under Norman Foster's roof
fields.Caption 3: The portico's Ionic columns

fields.Name: North Christian Church
fields.Description: A hexagonal church whose low slate roof rises into a needle spire 192 feet high, with the sanctuary gathered around a central communion table; the last building Eero Saarinen designed, completed after his death.
fields.Caption 1: The hexagonal roof and its spire
fields.Caption 2: The sanctuary under its oculus
fields.Caption 3: The spire above the approach steps

fields.Name: Crystal Cathedral
fields.Description: A star-shaped megachurch walled in more than 10,000 panes of mirrored glass on a white steel space frame, built for the televangelist Robert H. Schuller; its 90-foot doors open so that drive-in worshippers can follow the service. The Catholic Church bought it in 2012 and reconsecrated it as Christ Cathedral.
fields.Caption 1: The mirrored-glass church and its bell tower
fields.Caption 2: The stainless-steel bell tower

fields.Name: Palace of Westminster
fields.Description: The seat of Parliament on the Thames, rebuilt after the fire of 1834: Charles Barry planned it, Augustus Pugin designed its Perpendicular Gothic detail, and it ends in the Victoria Tower and the Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben). Westminster Hall, of 1097, survived the fire and was kept.
fields.Caption 2: The Central Lobby
fields.Caption 3: Elizabeth Tower at the north end

fields.Name: Green Building
fields.Description: A 21-storey concrete tower for MIT's earth sciences, raised on two-storey legs, with a weather radome on its roof; students have turned its grid of windows into a giant screen, playing Tetris on it in 2012.
fields.Caption 2: Above McDermott Court and Alexander Calder's La Grande Voile
fields.Caption 3: The weather-radar dome on its roof

fields.Name: Dallas City Hall
fields.Description: An inverted pyramid of concrete over a plaza with a pool, each floor projecting beyond the one below at 34 degrees to shade the offices from the Texas sun; it played the headquarters of Omni Consumer Products in RoboCop.
fields.Caption 2: The north front leaning out over the plaza
fields.Caption 3: From Reunion Tower

fields.Name: Jacobs House
fields.Alternate: Herbert and Katherine Jacobs First House
fields.Description: The first Usonian house, an L-shaped, single-storey house of brick and board-and-batten wood built for about $5,500 as a home the middle class could afford; its heated concrete slab and carport became Usonian standards.
fields.Caption 1: The garden side, its glass doors opening onto the lawn
fields.Caption 2: The living room

fields.Name: MIT Chapel
fields.Description: A windowless brick cylinder in a moat, lit by light reflected up through low arches and by an oculus over the altar, where Harry Bertoia's screen of metal leaves shimmers.
fields.Caption 1: The altar under Harry Bertoia's screen
fields.Caption 2: The undulating brick wall

fields.Name: 8 Spruce Street
fields.Description: A 76-storey apartment tower in Lower Manhattan whose stainless-steel skin ripples like draped cloth; it was marketed as New York by Gehry.
fields.Caption 1: The rippling tower above the Potter Building
fields.Caption 2: The rippling stainless-steel skin

fields.Name: Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts
fields.Description: Le Corbusier's only building in North America, a concrete block for Harvard pierced by an S-shaped ramp that carries a path through the building.
fields.Caption 1: The concrete studios and their brise-soleil
fields.Caption 2: The ramp that runs through the building
fields.Caption 3: A curved studio wall

fields.Name: Museum of Pop Culture
fields.Description: Colliding masses of coloured stainless steel and aluminum, said to evoke smashed electric guitars, with the Seattle Center Monorail running through them; built for Microsoft's co-founder Paul Allen as a tribute to Jimi Hendrix, its main hall is the Sky Church.
fields.Caption 1: From the air, beside the Space Needle
fields.Caption 2: The Seattle Center monorail running through it
fields.Caption 3: The coloured metal skins

fields.Name: General Motors Technical Center
fields.Description: A research campus, the “Industrial Versailles”, of long steel-and-glass buildings around a lake, with glazed-brick end walls in bright colours and a stainless-steel water tower; begun by Eliel Saarinen and completed by his son Eero.
fields.Caption 1: A glazed-brick end wall and the blue stair towers
fields.Caption 2: The stainless-steel Design Dome
fields.Caption 3: The campus and its lake from the air

fields.Name: Cardboard Cathedral
fields.Description: A temporary A-frame cathedral of cardboard tubes coated in polyurethane, with a triangle of coloured glass at its front, built after the 2011 earthquake wrecked Christchurch Cathedral.
fields.Caption 1: The A-frame and its coloured-glass front
fields.Caption 2: Inside: the cardboard-tube roof and the coloured-glass end wall

fields.Name: Banqueting House
fields.Description: The first building in England in the Renaissance classical manner, a double-cube hall that is the only surviving part of Whitehall Palace; Peter Paul Rubens painted its ceiling for Charles I, who was executed on a scaffold outside it in 1649.
fields.Caption 2: The hall under Rubens's ceiling

fields.Name: Pennsylvania Station
fields.Description: A Beaux-Arts railway terminal whose waiting room was modelled on the Baths of Caracalla; its demolition in 1963 launched the historic-preservation movement in New York, and the historian Vincent Scully wrote: “One entered the city like a god; one scurries in now like a rat.”
fields.Caption 1: The south façade, photographed for the Historic American Buildings Survey before demolition
fields.Caption 2: The concourse, photographed for the Historic American Buildings Survey before demolition
fields.Caption 3: The steel-and-glass concourse

fields.Name: AEG Turbine Factory
fields.Description: A factory hall of steel and glass under a massive gable, a temple of industry designed by the company's artistic adviser; Walter Gropius, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and Le Corbusier all worked in Behrens's office at the time.
fields.Caption 1: The hall from the street corner: the gable end and the long glazed side
fields.Caption 2: The glazed side wall between its steel piers

fields.Name: Nakagin Capsule Tower
fields.Description: Two concrete cores carrying 140 prefabricated capsules, each a tiny apartment with a round window, meant to be replaced as they wore out: the icon of Japanese Metabolism. None was ever replaced; the tower was demolished in 2022 and some capsules preserved.
fields.Caption 2: Inside a capsule, with its built-in fittings
fields.Caption 3: A single capsule, preserved after the 2022 demolition

fields.Name: New York Public Library
fields.Description: A Beaux-Arts marble library on Fifth Avenue, guarded by the stone lions Patience and Fortitude, whose Rose Main Reading Room runs almost two blocks.
fields.Caption 2: The Rose Main Reading Room

fields.Name: Transamerica Pyramid
fields.Description: A 48-storey tapering white pyramid with two wings for the elevators and stairs, the emblem of San Francisco's skyline.
fields.Caption 1: The pyramid above the Financial District
fields.Caption 2: From above
fields.Caption 3: The angled columns of its base

fields.Name: Hill House
fields.Description: A harled grey house for the publisher Walter Blackie, for which Charles Rennie Mackintosh designed everything from the furniture to the light fittings; its porous render let in so much water that since 2019 it has stood inside a protective steel-mesh box.
fields.Caption 1: The house under its protective steel-mesh enclosure, 2019
fields.Caption 2: The hall, with Mackintosh's lanterns and furniture
fields.Caption 3: Inside the steel-mesh box built over it in 2019

fields.Name: St. Vitus Cathedral
fields.Description: The Gothic cathedral inside Prague Castle, begun for Charles IV in 1344 and finished only in 1929, with Peter Parler's net vaults over the choir.
fields.Caption 2: The west front
fields.Caption 3: The Golden Gate's Last Judgement mosaic

fields.Name: Biltmore Estate
fields.Description: The largest private house in the United States, a French Renaissance château built for George Washington Vanderbilt II, with grounds by Frederick Law Olmsted.
fields.Caption 2: The entrance front
fields.Caption 3: The Winter Garden

fields.Name: Abraj Al-Bait
fields.Description: A seven-tower hotel complex for pilgrims beside the Great Mosque, crowned by the largest clock faces in the world; at 601 metres it was the third-tallest building on earth when finished, built by the Saudi Binladin Group on the site of the Ottoman Ajyad Fortress, whose demolition Turkey protested.
fields.Caption 2: The clock faces, each 43 metres across
fields.Caption 3: Rising above the Great Mosque during construction, 2010

fields.Name: St. Regis Chicago
fields.Description: Three stacked, interlocking towers of stepped glass that shades from blue to green, with an open floor left for the wind; at 363 metres it is the tallest building in the world designed by a woman, and Jeanne Gang's rippling Aqua tower stands nearby.
fields.Caption 2: Above the skyline, from Navy Pier

fields.Name: Rijksmuseum
fields.Description: The Dutch national museum, a Gothic- and Renaissance-revival palace with a public passage through its centre, home of Rembrandt's The Night Watch and Vermeer's The Milkmaid; Pierre Cuypers also designed Amsterdam Centraal station, and the 2013 renovation by Cruz y Ortiz kept the bicycle passage.
fields.Caption 2: Architectural sculpture on the facade

fields.Name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
fields.Description: The largest art museum in the Americas, set in Central Park behind a Beaux-Arts facade on Fifth Avenue that Richard Morris Hunt's son finished in 1902; it holds the Egyptian Temple of Dendur and Emanuel Leutze's Washington Crossing the Delaware, and its medieval branch, The Cloisters, rebuilds parts of five European monasteries.
fields.Architect: Calvert Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould (first building); Richard Morris Hunt (Fifth Avenue facade)
fields.Caption 2: The Great Hall

fields.Name: Museum of Modern Art
fields.Description: Founded in 1929 by Abby Aldrich Rockefeller and two friends, with Alfred H. Barr Jr. as its first director; its 1939 building on 53rd Street was the first International Style museum in America, Philip Johnson designed its sculpture garden in 1953, and it holds The Starry Night and Les Demoiselles d'Avignon.
fields.Architect: Philip L. Goodwin and Edward Durell Stone (1939 building); Yoshio Taniguchi (2004 expansion)
fields.Caption 2: The Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden

fields.Name: Art Institute of Chicago
fields.Description: Built for the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 and guarded by two bronze lions on Michigan Avenue, it holds A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, American Gothic, and Nighthawks; Renzo Piano's Modern Wing made it the second-largest art museum in the United States.
fields.Architect: Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge (1893 building); Renzo Piano (Modern Wing)
fields.Caption 1: The Michigan Avenue building in a 1901 postcard
fields.Caption 2: One of Edward Kemeys's bronze lions at the entrance
fields.Caption 3: Renzo Piano's Modern Wing, opened in 2009
fields.Caption 4: Edward Hopper's Nighthawks in its gallery

fields.Name: National Gallery
fields.Description: Britain's collection of Western European painting before 1900, in a long Neoclassical building with a portico on the north side of Trafalgar Square; Prince Charles called a rejected modern extension “a monstrous carbuncle”, and Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown built the Sainsbury Wing instead. It holds The Arnolfini Portrait and The Hay Wain.
fields.Architect: William Wilkins (main building); Venturi, Scott Brown and Associates (Sainsbury Wing)
fields.Caption 1: The portico across Trafalgar Square, beside Nelson's Column, about 1890–1900
fields.Caption 2: Giuseppe Gabrielli, The National Gallery, Interior of Room 32, 1886
fields.Caption 3: A gallery today

fields.Name: Museo del Prado
fields.Description: Designed for Charles III as a natural history cabinet and opened in 1819 as a royal picture gallery, it holds Las Meninas, The Third of May 1808, and The Garden of Earthly Delights; Rafael Moneo's 2007 extension wraps the cloister of the neighbouring church of San Jerónimo el Real.
fields.Caption 1: The Puerta de Velázquez, the main facade
fields.Caption 2: The central gallery

fields.Name: Uffizi Gallery
fields.Description: Built for Cosimo I de' Medici as offices for the city's magistrates (its name is Italian for “offices”), a long U-shaped block around a narrow courtyard running down to the Arno; its top floor became the gallery of The Birth of Venus and Primavera, and Vasari's raised corridor runs from it across the Ponte Vecchio to the Pitti Palace.
fields.Caption 1: The courtyard, looking toward the Palazzo Vecchio
fields.Caption 2: The east wing and the Tribuna

fields.Name: Louvre
fields.Description: The palace of the French kings, begun as a fortress of Philip II Augustus around 1190, until Louis XIV moved to Versailles; opened as a public museum in 1793, it holds the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo, and the Winged Victory of Samothrace, and I. M. Pei's glass pyramid became its main entrance in 1989.
fields.Architect: Pierre Lescot (Lescot Wing); Claude Perrault (East Colonnade)
fields.Caption 1: The west wing of the Cour Carrée
fields.Caption 2: Claude Perrault's East Colonnade, 1667–1670

fields.Name: Tate Britain
fields.Description: The national gallery of British art, opened on the site of the Millbank Penitentiary with money from the sugar refiner Henry Tate; it holds the Turner Bequest and hosts the Turner Prize exhibition, and its modern collection moved to Tate Modern at Bankside in 2000.
fields.Caption 2: The dome over the central hall
